articles.title: Diese Solarzellen erzeugen in 10 Meter tiefem Meerwasser Strom
articles.text:
10 Meter unter dem Meeresspiegel: Wie Solarzellen auch in größerer Tiefe Strom erzeugen
China treibt längst Photovoltaik-Projekte in großem Umfang auf dem Meer voran, um für die Energiegewinnung keine teuren Flächen in Küstennähe zu verschwenden. Allein die Provinz Jiangsu an der Ostküste China hat zuletzt ein Offshore-Solarprogramm im Umfang von gut 27 Gigawatt gestartet.
Solarzellen erzeugen unter Wasser Strom
Kombiniert werden die Vorhaben jeweils mit Energiespeichern, wie pv magazine schreibt. Doch in China sollen Solaranlagen offenbar nicht nur auf, sondern künftig auch tief im Meer Energie erzeugen. Entsprechende Solarzellen haben Forscher:innen der chinesischen Yunnan University jetzt entwickelt.
Konkret handelt es sich um Unterwasser-Perowskit-Solarzellen, die genau jene Wellenlängen von Sonnenlicht absorbieren können, die tief ins Meer vordringen. Die Forscher:innen bauten dazu zunächst ein Testsystem, um das Sonnenlicht in verschiedenen Meerestiefen zu simulieren, wie die Futurezone berichtet.
Perowskit-Zelle verwertet blaues Licht
Die mithilfe der aus den Tests erzielten Daten entwickelten die Forscher:innen eine Perowskit-Zelle, die blaues bis orangenes Licht verwerten kann. Die Solarzelle wurde anschließend skaliert. Entstanden ist ein Modul in der Größe, die auch bei kommerziellen Projekten zum Einsatz käme.
Montiert auf einem Unterwasserroboter erzeugte das Modul in zehn Meter Meerestiefe innerhalb von zwei Stunden 324 Milliwattstunden Strom. Weil es sich überhaupt um den ersten Test unter Realbedingungen handelte, zeigten sich die Forscher:innen von dem Ergebnis überrascht. Die Menge an Energie würde nämlich ausreichen, um einen kleinen Lithium-Ionen-Akku zu laden oder ein LED-Licht zu betreiben.
Energieerzeugung in noch größeren Tiefen
Die Forscher:innen wollen in weiteren Tests nicht nur die Stromausbeute erhöhen, sondern auch austesten, bis zu welcher Tiefe Solaranlagen im Meer Energie erzeugen können. Schon jetzt soll feststehen, dass das Modul in zehn Meter tiefem Salzwasser rund 5,5 Jahre Energie liefern könnte.
Die Einsatzmöglichkeiten sind jedenfalls vielfältig. Laut den Forscher:innen könnten damit etwa Tauchroboter mit Strom versorgt werden, die Wartungsarbeiten an Unterwasser-Infrastruktur vornehmen. Auch ließen sich Kommunikationsbojen und Unterwasserkameras sowie Sensoren betreiben.
Einsatzmöglichkeiten für Unterwasser-Solarzellen
Denkbar wäre auch die Möglichkeit, Schiffen eine Art Steckdosenboje zur Verfügung zu stellen, damit diese den Einsatz von klimaschädlichen Generatoren minimieren können. Ihre Ergebnisse haben die Forscher:innen in Form einer Studie im Fachmagazin Joule veröffentlicht.

articles.title: How Togo’s Nihtael Dynasty is helping musicians build more sustainable careers - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nodjigno Pierre Yao Nihtael is well-known in the Togolese music scene, with his Façonné Music label having contributed to the digital distribution of music by more than 50 artists, including Togo Joachin Migos, SCENARIO and IROK.
But though Façonné Music serves as the main platform for Nihtael’s activities in the music sector, he is now taking it a step further with Nihtael Dynasty, which is being developed as a music-industry and creative-economy platform focused on digital distribution, artist development, media strategy, project structuring and market access.
“The objective is not simply to upload music to streaming platforms, but to help artists understand and organise the business around their music so they can build stronger and more sustainable careers,” Nihtael told Disrupt Africa.
Nihtael Dynasty has developed progressively out of his practical work in the Togolese music ecosystem, rather than being launched as a conventional startup on one single date. It is currently being structured into a broader entrepreneurial platform around the services and relationships already developed through Façonné Music.
“The model is collaborative and project-based, working with artists, producers, managers, media contacts, digital-distribution partners and event professionals depending on the needs of each project,” he said.
The main gap is that access to digital distribution has become easier, but professional support around that distribution is still limited for many independent artists in Togo and similar emerging markets.
“An artist may be able to place a song on Spotify, Apple Music or other platforms, but still struggle with metadata, release planning, branding, media relations, audience development, rights awareness, catalogue strategy and international market access,” Nihtael said.
There are distributors, labels, managers and promoters operating in the market, including himself, but Nihtael Dynasty’s approach is to connect several of these functions around the artist, instead of treating distribution as an isolated service.
The response has been encouraging.
“More than 50 artists and projects have already been supported across different stages of development. Demand is increasingly coming not only from artists who want distribution, but also from artists who need help with positioning, media visibility, release strategy and professional development,” said Nihtael.
The core market is Togo, with relationships and project activity extending into the wider West African and African music ecosystem and to international digital platforms.
“The next stage is to strengthen regional connections, particularly across West Africa, while building more direct bridges between African artists, international media, distribution networks and music-industry partners,” Nihtael said.
“The longer-term ambition is for Nihtael Dynasty to become a recognisable support structure for independent African artists seeking both digital access and professional development.”
Revenue is generated through music-industry services and project-based activity, including digital distribution support, artist development, release strategy, media and promotional coordination, and related music-business services.

articles.title: How Will We Train Developers If AI Does the Routine Work: A Conversation with Scott Hanselman
articles.text:
In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Scott Hanselman about developing new software engineers when artificial intelligence agents are doing most of the work on which junior developers were trained. Hanselman suggests the software industry should adopt a preceptorship model similar to the nursing profession. Under this model, the industry needs preceptors whose sole job is to train new engineers, and these preceptors would be evaluated on how well they train people rather than how much code they ship. The use of AI agents requires experienced engineers because while they are capable of generating software features, they perform poorly at software architecture because they often miss the larger context. In addition, engineers must maintain oversight of artificial intelligence tools by acting as reviewers and coordinators to ensure that human judgment remains central to the development process.
The conversation then broadened to discuss the environment in which agentic AI should be used. When businesses prioritize short term, hyper-optimization, they neglect the longer term investments in human capital and mentorship which will make it impossible to cultivate future senior talent. Beyond that, Hanselman addressed the sociological impacts of modern development, observing that the intersection of remote work, social media, and artificial intelligence severely isolates developers. To counter this isolation and ensure healthy growth, intentional human connection and in-person interactions are vital for the next generation of users and developers of technology.
Key Takeaways
- The software industry should adopt a preceptorship model for developing software engineers. With AI taking over the tasks on which junior engineers were traditionally trained, industry needs preceptors, whose sole job is to train new engineers. This is a model that has worked quite well in the nursing profession. Preceptors are evaluated on how well they train engineers, not how much code they have shipped.
- AI is highly capable of generating software features but performs poorly at designing overarching software architecture, often missing the big picture.
- Engineers must maintain oversight of AI tools by acting as reviewers and coordinators, ensuring that human judgment remains central to the development process.
- Businesses need to prioritize long-term investments in human capital and mentorship over short-term hyper-optimization to prevent the collapse of the junior engineer pipeline.
- The intersection of remote work, social media, and AI isolates developers, making intentional human connection and in-person interaction vital for their healthy growth.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Michael Stiefel: Welcome to the Architects Podcast, where we discuss what it means to be an architect and how architects actually do their job. We are very lucky today to have as our guest, Scott Hanselman, who is a programmer, teacher, and speaker. He works out of his home office in Portland, Oregon for Microsoft GitHub as a vice president and member of the technical staff. He works on open source and agentic coding tools like GitHub, Copilot, CLI, along with the Windows development platform. Before Microsoft, he was the chief architect at Corillian Corporation, now a part of CheckFree for six plus years. Previously, he worked as a principal consultant at Step Technology, speaking, writing, consulting, and very much not getting rich during Web 1.0, although he worked on a bunch of websites you probably have heard of. He also worked at Intel, Nike, and consulted all over the world.
He was an adjunct professor at OIT teaching C and Web Services and created the first Palm Pilot diabetes management system in 1998 and sold it to a healthcare company some years later. It's great to have you here on the podcast.
How Did You Become An Architect? [01:30]
And I'd like to start out by asking you, were you trained as an architect? How did you become an architect? It's not something you woke up and decided, today I'm going to be an architect.
Scott Hanselman: I mean, architect is one of those titles that one could probably just give themselves like CTO. You'll meet a CTO at somewhere like a big Fortune 5000 company or a Fortune 500 company and they're an architect or they're a CTO and then you'll meet someone who's at Panera with their buddy and they're a founder and they're a CTO as well. So, these are titles that are kind of made up, but I am trained in software engineering. I do point out interestingly enough that I don't have a computer science degree. I have a software engineering degree, which is the practice of shipping, which is different than compiler theory, computer theory, and the things that one learns in computer science many, many, many years ago. I helped write some of the tests for the Microsoft certified software architect stuff with Clemens Vasters lo these 20, 25 years ago.
But what is an architect? Is it someone that knows UML or knows how to do Visio? Are they the one in the room with good taste? Are they the software sommelier? I don't know.
Michael Stiefel: Maybe with AI, we'll get the PowerPoint compiler and that will be-
AI is Not A Good Software Architect [02:49]
Scott Hanselman: We definitely have the PowerPoint compiler. It compiles crap though. But I have said recently on podcasts that AIs generate features extremely well. They do not generate architecture very well. They tend to be somewhat myopic in their view and they definitely miss the big picture. And I'm currently working through a problem with an application that I'm working on where the AI has over the last several weeks created a god object. Just a super struct that I would not have created, but it's kind of a cancer that's building inside the application and I need to get it out of there before it collapses under its own weight. So, the AI did a very poor job of designing an architecture.
How Will the Next Generation of Software Engineers Be Trained? [03:32]
Michael Stiefel: That's an interesting segue into something I know we want to talk about is that you and Mark Russinovich wrote an opinion piece in the Communications of the ACM last April on redefining the software engineering profession for AI. And in it, you discuss the difficulty of training new software engineers when AI is doing all the work we traditionally trained entry-level software engineers. Can you explain what you meant by this and the culture of being a preceptor at scale?
The Preceptor Model For Training Software Engineers [04:04]
Scott Hanselman: So, the idea is in any internship, apprenticeship, master student, teacher student scenario, often the student is doing the wax on, wax off work. They're doing the toil, they're doing the tedium. And it is through the “wax the car” that you learn karate. And if that job is now done by AI, then at what altitude, as I mix my metaphors, does an early in career person enter? Do they just skip the boring bits? Is it important to do the pushups and pull-ups and stuff? And I think that it is important. I think that we are skipping the easy bits and it is extremely dopamine positive and very exciting. And it's certainly a thrill. I'm watching my early-in-career and non-technical coworkers get very, very excited creating software and vibing stuff. But without trying to gatekeep the work, I don't believe that you can vibe into production, or at least not yet.
The Role of a Preceptor is to Create Engineers [05:15]
I feel like early in-career, people need guidance. They need a mentor. But the term mentor or apprentice, journeyman, these are kind of outdated. So, Mark and I looked towards successful industries that are regulated and managed and create successful seniors. And we found that in nursing. My wife is a nurse and she is a nurse preceptor. And a preceptor is an interesting word that is almost exclusively currently used in medicine to refer to the teaching nurse. And that job is an explicit and specific job. Not every nurse is a nurse preceptor. And by having that level of formality, such that the nurse preceptor, the nurse trainer is metriced and their job performance is measured on whether or not they can make nurses. They can mint new senior nurses. In software though, like if I joined your team and you're the CTO or the architect, and you're the boss and you make me the intern or the apprentice, upon entrance, I'm less than.
And that I have to dig myself out of the hole that you've put me in. And then if I don't hack it, you'll go out. Hanselman couldn't hack it. We'll grind them up and spit them out and we'll get another one. So, then interns become a dime a dozen. And if they can't crawl their way out of the bucket, then go and find more. But with preceptors, their job is to make more nurses. So, maybe if we couldn't make more nurses, it's on the trainer. Their annual review would be like, "Maybe Michael shouldn't be a trainer. Maybe he needs some more training to be a trainer". So, there's a formality to it. So, instead of a tech lead with a bunch of cleaves working for them, you have a tech lead working alongside a preceptor trainer. And that trainer's job is not to ship code, but to ship engineers.
So, like after this podcast, I'm going to have my scrum and we're going to cut a release of the product that I'm working on. And there'll be a very mixed group of young people and later in career people. And we're going to do some pair programming and we're going to do some fellowship and some working on stuff together to make sure that we are not just shipping the thing. We're going to cut a release at noon, but that we are shipping senior engineers. That's a big long answer. A lot of rambling there. But I think you understand that the idea is - focus on making people better, not just shipping more crap.
The New Role of the University [07:57]
Michael Stiefel: So, two questions come to mind right away when you say that. One is what then becomes the role of software engineering education in the universities if this is the preceptor? And also, does remote work contribute to the problem and the lack of mentorship, or does it actually help?
Scott Hanselman: As someone who has worked remotely now for many years, my entire career at Microsoft has been remote. I would say that that is hard for anyone and it's even harder for an early in career. So, I would argue that remote work is not helping grow people. Particularly like I've got young men in my house, 18 and 20, and they're going to go out into the world. There is value in them shaking hands, looking people in the eye, talking to human beings. And I know that this might sound like two old men on a podcast shaking their fist at the cloud, but human beings are meant to hang out together. We are meant to be social. I got a lot of value sitting at whiteboards with senior engineers, having them explain to me how things work. If you are an online person who does their socializing online, does their video gaming online, does their everything online, as they're dating online, and now your work is online, then that shows a fundamental collapse of the third place.
The Collapse of the Third Place [09:27]
Work, home, and the third place. And if there is nowhere, if work, home and the third place are all the same place. I don't know how you can grow into a fully formed and healthy individual. So, yes, remote work is a challenge. We can push through it, but it requires a lot of metacognition and a lot of focus on listening to your body, listening to yourself, making sure that you are a whole person. I do drive up to Seattle every four to six weeks to make sure that my badge still works and that the young people are still present. Although I do have folks that are remote in other places. It's the perfect storm of COVID, remote work, social media addiction and AI that threatens to break the young people. And I can only focus on one of those.
Michael Stiefel: So, I want to get back to university in a minute, but this is interesting. What you're saying requires acknowledgement on both sides of the equation because it's the young people, as you say, who live in this virtual world that have to learn the importance of the in-person. And you also need the companies to understand that in order to be profitable in the long term, they have to be willing to have these preceptors to help people along, in the office, if possible.
Measuring How Engineers Thrive [10:51]
Scott Hanselman: Yes. So, you have to acknowledge that hitting the ground running is not a thing and that an early in career person fresh out of school is not going to start slinging code within a couple of days. We do have a metric in our group and we call it engineering thrive, where we call it time to first PR. So, here's your laptop. Welcome to the company. It's Monday. And it's not a productivity metric. It's not, "Oh, Michael joined the company on Monday and he got a PR landed on Wednesday or Thursday". That's actually a morale metric. Think about how exciting it will be for them to land their first PR and how enabled they will be. So, when we talk about engineering thrive, we talk about how do they feel in their personal growth? Even if it's a one line change, it shows that they can begin the engineering loop.
So, back to your question I didn't answer about how this fits into the relationship with universities. They leave their parents' house, they go to university, and then they land a job. And if that entire experience is entirely online, that doesn't facilitate their growth. And if they're using AI at every step, there's also a lack of growth. So, we're trying to insert specific conscious growth moments at every step. And in doing that, we're going to have to coordinate with universities to make sure that AI ethics, AI internals, how AI is used, how AI should be used, so that they don't externalize their brains entirely and have them atrophy just like their social skills have atrophied.
The Danger For Engineers of Anthromorphizing AI [12:32]
Michael Stiefel: I find this across the board, this almost anthropomorphizing of AI. I remember one time I was in the car with my sister and brother-in-law and they were arguing over the instructions that came from the GPS. And the GPS happened to have a woman's voice. And they were saying, "She said this or she said that". And I said, "Stop. It's not a she, it's an it". But this relationship between the software and the individual, when you get to this virtual world, it seems to be very, very tight and seems to be very hard to break and to get an understanding of here's humanity and here's the computer.
Scott Hanselman: Yes. That's a whole podcast in itself. Pre-AI, the idea that we are talking and yelling at these disembodied women in our houses, telling them to turn the lights off, whether it be Cortana or Alexa or any of these things, it's not a healthy thing at all. And as much as ChatGPT is kind of ruining everything, at least it's not given a name. At least it's not Jeff or Anna. I don't think that's healthy. But the problem is that if a parrot can speak, it becomes a much more interesting pet. When dogs do things like cock their eyebrows up or make expressions or smile, we love it. We just love that stuff. I think when AI turns into a robot and starts walking around the house or when the Roomba starts talking back to you, you're going to see even more problematic behaviors. And the movie Her is not an aspirational story.
Michael Stiefel: No, it's not. When the Roomba tells you it should be cleaner and I'm going to go back and clean this even though you told me not to, we've got to another level.
Scott Hanselman: Then you've got problems.
Implementing Preceptorship in Organizations [14:29]
Michael Stiefel: So, do you see any difference in the ability to do this preceptorship with small or midsize organizations or large organizations? Is this a problem or a challenge?
Scott Hanselman: I think it would certainly be easier to do it smaller because you have full control when you have two-pizza teams. I've always been very comfortable with 400 to 500 person companies. Those are the companies that I grew up in and worked in. That's the sweet spot where you know everybody. That was the size of my high school graduating class and that's just a good size. Four or 500 people, you know everybody. Even in big companies though, if you chop it up into pieces like that, like even Microsoft, as big as we are, it's really just a bunch of thousand person companies all kind of coordinating between each other. But we've been able to do it at Microsoft as a pilot with 400 and found it to be successful. And I think if you do it in shards where you have executive buy off and executive support, it is possible.
We just finished our first cohort of preceptors and it's been very successful. I just think the trick is, do we have the organizational willpower to remind all of the bosses that this is as much a human thing as it is a “make capitalism move faster thing”. It is explicitly growing humans is the goal here. Not necessarily shipping code. And in doing that, you have to acknowledge that, yes, they're going to be slow and that's okay.
Michael Stiefel: If you take a long enough viewpoint, the actual humanity and economic incentives should line up because happier people or more productive people are going to stay in the company. But do you see the economic incentives working in your favor to do this?
Scott Hanselman: It will cost you money in the short term, but it's like working out. And this is the thing, people don't work out and then they get sad that they, "Oh, I never worked out. Too late now. Not working out in your 50s is causing you problems in your 70s, too late". Those kinds of problems are going to happen when someone does not grow senior engineers and then they need senior engineers and the only place they can find them is their competitor. And the only way that they can get senior engineers is by poaching them from their competitor. And those senior engineers use their competitor's techniques and their competitor's culture and their competitor's engineering practices. So, they need to focus on growing their own people and their own culture, but they're not going to see a benefit for a couple of years. That's going to take discipline.
AI Induced Loneliness and the Loss of "Flow State" [17:08]
Michael Stiefel: Do you know of any case studies that people have written about this that are public?
Scott Hanselman: Well, we'll do our own for preceptors, but every week there's some new thing coming out like the Harvard Business Review or somebody who is saying that AI powered engineers are getting more done, but they're lonely. There was a really good... I forgot the name of the... I don't have it in my head right now, but it was just two or three days ago, they were saying how lonely people are working in AI. That's because remote work plus social media plus AI has them sitting at home prompting and waiting and prompting and waiting. There was another one about flow state indicating that people are not getting into the flow state anymore and that's making them sad. It's important for us to say the quiet part out loud. If people are sad, that's not okay and we should do something about it.
AI Contributes to the Pre-existing Hyperoptimization of Business [18:02]
Michael Stiefel: I found a study, it was referenced in the Wall Street Journal that since 2017, there's been a general decline in entry level hiring. Is AI part of this problem or is this something more general that is going on?
Scott Hanselman: I think it's more general. I think it is shortsighted hyper optimization and late stage capitalism. I think it's just very shortsighted. And by shortsighted, I mean people don't want to plan 15, 20 years out. People have between 20 and 40 years of productivity in them. And it seems like a long time when you're at the beginning of it. But as I'm at the end of a 35, 40 year career, I'm like, "Wow, that went fast". And I'm thinking to myself, "I need to rush now to teach young people what I learned before I'm gone". Businesses need to have that kind of an attitude. Businesses need to have the same thoughtful attitude as a senior engineer who is close to retirement, but they're not. They're going quarter by quarter. So, I think that it's less about AI. AI is not going to take your job. The hyper optimization of some C-suite executive is going to take your job.
Engineers and the Future Use of AI [19:21]
Michael Stiefel: Well, it's a loaded question, but the question comes to mind is what can we as engineers do to help? Sure, this is an ROI issue. How do we present this case to people?
Scott Hanselman: Well, I think speaking truth to power is important. I think saying the quiet part out loud. Every good revolution starts at the bottom. Simply saying, "I think the engineers would be happier if we did X". Workers' rights matter. And I enjoy working with AI. I find it to be an enjoyable thing, but I find it more fun as a group, as with all activities. Sitting quietly and prompting is not fun. Going from vibes to agentic software engineering techniques. I've got a really nice DevOps framework. I can tell the AI to cut a release. It's a good release. It's tested. The harnesses are good. That's all software engineering stuff around it. I'm just at the very, very, very top. Now instead of typing build.bat, I say build. You know what I mean? It might sound silly, but I can have an idea. I can go for a walk.
I can prompt remotely and I can come and see a prototype when I get back. And then I can review the code and go through it. I'm looking at my other monitor here. I'm using the GitHub Copilot app, which still has code. Half the screen is still code, but it's a diff that I'm reviewing of code that was written. And then I'm commenting on individual lines saying, "Well, this is good and that's good". So, I feel like a sculptor, but I'm really the teacher in a sculpting class and I'm walking around making small changes to everyone else's work, if that makes sense.
Michael Stiefel: Yes. I presume a lot of this is in a context artifact of sorts.
Scott Hanselman: I'm in a session multiplexer of sorts.
Michael Stiefel: Okay.
Scott Hanselman: I'm trying to do a release of a thing today and I've got five pull requests from four different people. And I need to figure out the order in which to take them. If they are architecturally correct and if they are architecturally sound, if anything's creeping in that looks like slop, that is not the direction that we want to go, while still maintaining a pretty crisp clip and speed at which we're working. So, like all of that is, it's a very “coordinatey” job.
Michael Stiefel: But you're still looking at code because I remember the days, I'm dating myself now, when people used to argue over hand-coded assembler as opposed to what the compiler generated. And I presume we will get to some point where the AI is writing code for other AIs and the humans just don't look at it.
Scott Hanselman: Yes. I don't know what I think about that. Human beings have got to keep their hands on the wheel. That's the thing I will always fight for.
Has AI Killed Agile? [22:27]
Michael Stiefel: I personally agree with you. Humans have to be in the loop, which actually raises another thing that I've heard people talk about is that AI has killed agile. I don't know if you have a feeling about that.
Scott Hanselman: I don't think it's killed it as it has taken it to its kind of ridiculous conclusion. Everything we're doing is agile. It's just too agile.
Michael Stiefel: What do you mean by too agile?
Scott Hanselman: When agile in the '90s and the early 2000s was at its peak, people were calling it slop. And they were saying agile is just an excuse to go fast and break things. And when you combine agile, which is a very, very quick inner loop and a very, very quick outer loop and user stories and all that kind of stuff, and then you apply AI to it, you get wheels that spin so fast that they kind of wobble at speed and then the car potentially flies off the road. So, if one believes that agile was a bad idea and they think that AI is a bad idea, combining the two just makes them super bad. But I still use Kanban boards and user stories and I move them forward. So, I find that I keep coming back to agentic software engineering techniques, which is agile, smart DevOps, smart build servers, smart SDLC, except we have this new power tool that has been introduced into the mix. I'm a traditionalist with a new power tool.
Preceptorship and Teaching Software in College [23:56]
Michael Stiefel: But to get back to what we were talking about preceptorship, all this has to be taught to the potential engineer because they are not seeing this from where they sit right now. For example, take the SDLC. When you come out of college, do you understand the SDLC?
Scott Hanselman: So, no, you can't because you were making connect four or tic-tac-toe for your senior project. And even a group project in college is usually three or four people. So, this is why popping off the stack to the beginning of the conversation, I think that software engineering is a degree and a practice that is unique and different and discreet versus computer science. I mean, I like my software engineering degree. I know that there are gaps in my computer science knowledge, but I think that the ideal double major would be both of those things.
Michael Stiefel: But today we have to make those things part of preceptorship because that's the only way people are going to do it.
Scott Hanselman: We do, which is why I think internships, cohorts, senior year should almost entirely be spent in industry working. And I think that that's going to require a lot of effort on the part of industry to acknowledge that we need to invest in the early in career people lest we hollow out the pipeline completely.
Michael Stiefel: And then we're lost.
Scott Hanselman: And that's the whole point of that paper that you mentioned. The junior engineer pipeline, the early in career pipeline will collapse if we do not agree. And then we'll be bringing old people back out of retirement, just like Y2K. And they're going to go and pull me out of retirement in 2035 to go and fix the next big date bug.
Michael Stiefel: I tend to look at this as, you're a farmer and you're eating your seed corn instead of planting it for the next year.
Scott Hanselman: The analogies are legion.
Artificial Intelligence with a Humanistic Perspective [25:46]
Michael Stiefel: Before we get to the architect's questionnaire, which I like to ask all my guests, is there anything that comes to mind that we haven't talked about that you think is important?
Scott Hanselman: I keep coming back to the humanistic perspective. Everyone's talking about the benefits of AI from a, oh, it makes things better. It makes more money. It makes more this. It makes more that. But how do we feel about this? The sociology, the psychology, all of the ologies, all of the science about, are we supposed to feel this way? I think people don't sit and listen to their bodies enough. And I'll be doing my work and I'll kind of go, "I don't feel good right now. Why? Why do I feel this way? Those things need to be taught. You need to go for a walk. You need to drink more water. I don't know why I feel so bad. Everything sucks. Well, are you eating well? No. Are you sleeping well? No. Are you hydrated? No. You went from sleeping all night to sitting all day to then sitting all evening to then sleeping all night.
No wonder you feel like crap. And now you're in the AI loop. We're in the matrix. We need to acknowledge what is a reasonable amount of productivity as a society. We need to understand that we cannot improve 3% every year infinitely. That is by definition cancer. To take a finite system and grow infinitely. This idea of constant, ongoing, forever emergent, infinite growth, that's cancer. So, if AI makes me 20% more productive, okay, 20%, maybe I get Fridays off. But that's not working. Everyone else is working triply hard right now. To what end?
Michael Stiefel: That's the problem with exponential growth. You don't realize a disaster until it's almost too late because it's like the story of the guy who asked for one corn, two corns, four corns,
Scott Hanselman: Oh, yes. Yes.
Michael Stiefel: And before you know it, the king has run out of food because the nature of exponential growth is you're half full the day before disaster strikes.
Scott Hanselman: And humans just don't have any sense how bad they are at understanding how exponential growth works. It just doesn't. We can't even visualize it.
Michael Stiefel: I, for one, for example, when I go to sleep at night, my cell phone is in another room.
Scott Hanselman: That's very healthy. And this is where we need to acknowledge our age and figure out how we can help the young people be better without over-biasing them and acknowledging that we are from a different generation. And we came up with different privileges and different opportunities.
Michael Stiefel: There were disadvantages, but there are certain advantages. I mean, we went out and did free play where we didn't have location services. The point was not to be found as opposed to today where everybody wants to know where everybody is all the time.
Scott Hanselman: Yes, absolutely true.
Michael Stiefel: One of the things that's always been interesting to me is when you define the constraint space for a project, it's the subjective things that are just as much constraints as the fact that you have a latency. I mean, pick a simple example. If you can't get the engineering skills you need, you can have the best architectural design in the world and you aren't going anywhere. So, this conversation is very meaningful to me and I hope our listeners will feel the same way.
The Architect's Questionnaire [29:20]
We're talking about humanizing, because I like to ask several questions to my guests. What's your favorite part of being an architect?
Scott Hanselman: I think it is a thing that didn't exist and then I just thunk it up and now it's a thing. That's not about architecture, that's just about being a maker, a builder. My dad is a woodworker and my mom is a leather worker. And I'll just see a thing, a problem, and I'll go, "Oh, I'm going to fix that". In my garage over here, there's two buttons on the wall to open the garage. And if I pushed the wrong one, it opens the wrong door, right? And it's been bugging me for 20 years. And then I got a 3D printer and I got a pair of calipers and I made a little cover on the thing. And my dad's like, "You could just put a piece of tape over it". And I'm like, "Well, yes, but I got a pair of calipers and I made a cool 3D printed colored button". It's like a nuclear button where you flip it up and push the red button kind of thing.
That's way cooler. But the point is that it didn't exist. I thought about all the 20 ways I could have solved it from cardboard to paper to painter's tape to an over-engineered 3D printed thing. I love being able to just make a thing that didn't exist yesterday. Another example was I wanted to get a Peloton, but Pelotons are really expensive. So, I went and I went to Goodwill and I got a $30 bike and then an Android tablet. And then I made a website that lets me go on scenic bike rides in 3D. It's called PedalScape. I had that idea at 10:00 and by that evening I was riding my bike through Bavaria.
Michael Stiefel: And you realize there's a whole industry now of software that enables you to do virtual rides throughout.
Scott Hanselman: Oh, yes. I love that stuff. Yes. But I wanted one for myself and I made it.
Michael Stiefel: What is your least favorite part of being an architect?
Scott Hanselman: A younger Scott would've said waiting, but I don't think I have a least favorite part anymore. I enjoy the waiting. You can't just flash boil water to make tea. You have to kind of wait. I don't think I have a least favorite part. It's kind of all good, honestly.
Michael Stiefel: I think you may have answered this before, but is there anything creatively, spiritually, or emotionally compelling about architecture being an architect?
Scott Hanselman: I just keep coming back to humans. All of this is to make something that is delightful, that makes someone's life measurably better in some way, whether it be building architecture or drawing a picture or interior design as a kind of architecture. Software architecture is that thing will hold up under stress. I always come back to those high school classes where you make a bridge out of pickup sticks and what are those things called? Ice cream sticks.
Michael Stiefel: Popsicle sticks.
Scott Hanselman: Popsicle sticks. That's extremely satisfying to like, I made a thing and it also holds up under pressure.
Michael Stiefel: What turns you off about architecture being an architect?
Scott Hanselman: Again, I think nothing, but I would say documentation and Visio. I was doing Visio-style architecture for 10 years. And as much as I love Grady Booch, manually drawing UML diagrams was definitely not my favorite part of the experience. Shout out to Grady though.
Michael Stiefel: Do you have any favorite technologies?
Scott Hanselman: I'm a big fan of my open source artificial pancreas. When I was diagnosed diabetic 35 years ago, it was manual shots and pricking your finger. Mine's actually, it's clicking in my arm right now. I just heard it deliver insulin a moment ago and my blood sugar is as good as yours. Or dare I say better. Being a cyborg is a pretty favorite technology and it's a good solid architecture behind it.
Michael Stiefel: What about architecture do you love?
Scott Hanselman: I think the same answer as before, making stuff that holds up under pressure. I know that the argument of software architecture being a parallel to building architecture is one that has been argued many, many times. But I was in, I want to say Morocco, and I was looking at like the second or third-largest mosque in the world. You can't be unaffected by that. Holy crap, that's a building right there. You know what I mean?
Michael Stiefel: And it's lasted.
Scott Hanselman: Yes. Thousand years. You know what I mean? So, if I could get a piece of software to last more than 20 or 30 years, I think I'd be pretty thrilled.
Michael Stiefel: What about architecture do you hate, if anything?
Scott Hanselman: I don't hate as a general rule. It's a strong feeling I try not to have.
Michael Stiefel: What profession other than being an architect would you like to attempt?
Scott Hanselman: I am a teacher. I've always been a teacher. I'm not an architect. I'm a teacher. I've always been a teacher. Teaching is a very secret selfish thing because teaching is building, right? And I love the feeling of being able to build minds.
Michael Stiefel: Which is probably why you realize the importance of preceptorship, which other people may not have.
Scott Hanselman: I figured it out a couple of years ago that I've been teaching this whole time. So, I might as well quit and teach.
Michael Stiefel: Well, I was an independent consultant for a long, long time. And I found if I taught my clients, they would be less of a burden.
Scott Hanselman: Yes.
Michael Stiefel: So, teaching makes your life easier.
Scott Hanselman: Teach a man to fish. 100% agree.
Michael Stiefel: Do you ever see yourself not being an architect anymore?
Scott Hanselman: Yes. I think in 900 days when I retire, I will go and be an architect of minds. I will be a teacher.
Michael Stiefel: And finally, when a project is done, what do you like to hear from the clients or your team?
Scott Hanselman: I was thinking about that movie when the very end of Babe, when they go, "That'll do, pig". There's a project that I did for a company here called Pioneer Courthouse Square. It's basically the living room for Portland, Oregon, where it's like all these bricks in the center of the city. And on the bricks are people's names, and everyone's bought their own brick. So, my grandma has a brick and you can go, and find your brick. There's an app at the kiosk there, where you can go and look up your name, and then it'll make a printout and put an X over your brick, and then you go and you find your brick. I wrote that, I want to say in, 1996.
Michael Stiefel: Oh, my.
Scott Hanselman: I'm not joking. It's literally a 30-year-old Visual Basic app. And every five to seven years, they'll call me and make some small change. But that thing's running on Access 95 and Visual Basic, and it's still working. That is very satisfying.
Michael Stiefel: Thank you very much. I found this very, very enjoyable conversation and highlighting something I think is very important for people to realize and think about.
Scott Hanselman: Yes, it's my pleasure. And nice to see you.
Mentioned:
- Russinovich, M., & Hanselman, S. (2026). Redefining the Software Engineering Profession for AI. Communications of the ACM.
- De Cremer, D., & Koopman, J. (2024). Research: Using AI at Work Makes Us Lonelier and Less Healthy. Harvard Business Review.
- Non-paywalled summary
- Ellis, L. (2025). AI Is Wrecking an Already Fragile Job Market for College Graduates. The Wall Street Journal.
- Jonze, S. (Director). (2013). Her [Film]. Annapurna Pictures.
- OpenAPS (Open Source Artificial Pancreas System).

articles.title: Steam suma cuatro juegos gratis este domingo, con drones, estrategia y una aventura oscura
articles.text:
Steam suma cuatro juegos gratis, con una oferta que reúne carreras de drones, gestión de personajes, decisiones estratégicas y una aventura de tono oscuro. Los títulos pueden añadirse desde ahora a la biblioteca digital de la plataforma, sin necesidad de esperar a una hora de lanzamiento o a una activación posterior.
La selección amplía las opciones para quienes buscan nuevos juegos sin realizar un pago inicial. Cada propuesta se dirige a un perfil distinto de usuario: hay velocidad y reflejos para las carreras, administración de recursos para la progresión de grupos, tensión narrativa y partidas donde cada movimiento puede modificar el desenlace.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuatro títulos gratuitos disponibles
La promoción incluye cuatro propuestas independientes con mecánicas diferentes. Steam mantiene así una dinámica habitual en su catálogo: incorporar juegos sin coste que permiten descubrir producciones de estudios pequeños y géneros que suelen quedar fuera de los principales lanzamientos comerciales.
Los juegos disponibles son los siguientes:
- Split Fpv: Drone Racing propone carreras con drones de visión en primera persona, circuitos con obstáculos y pruebas que exigen precisión en cada giro.
- My Party Is Grinding se centra en la administración de un grupo, la mejora de habilidades y el progreso de sus integrantes a lo largo de la partida.
- From Below presenta una aventura de ambientación oscura, con un ritmo distinto al de las carreras o los títulos de gestión.
- Last Gambit plantea partidas basadas en la estrategia, donde resulta necesario calcular las consecuencias de cada decisión antes de avanzar.
Los cuatro pueden reclamarse desde las páginas oficiales de sus respectivos productos. La disponibilidad sin costo permite incorporarlos a la cuenta para instalarlos de inmediato o dejarlos guardados en la biblioteca para otro momento.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo añadir los juegos gratuitos a la biblioteca de Steam
Reclamar los títulos requiere una cuenta activa en Steam y puede realizarse desde la aplicación para ordenador o mediante el sitio web de la tienda. El proceso es el mismo para cada juego:
- Inicie sesión en Steam con su cuenta habitual.
- Escriba el nombre del juego en el buscador de la plataforma.
- Abra la ficha oficial del título y compruebe que el precio aparezca como 0,00 euros, dólares o la moneda correspondiente a su región.
- Seleccione el botón “Añadir a la cuenta”, “Obtener” o la opción equivalente que aparezca en la página.
- Confirme la operación cuando Steam solicite validar la adquisición.
- Revise la biblioteca para comprobar que el título quedó asociado a la cuenta.
- Descargue el juego en ese momento o instálelo más adelante desde cualquier ordenador que tenga acceso a la misma cuenta.
Antes de completar el proceso, conviene verificar si el juego es gratuito de forma permanente o si forma parte de una campaña temporal. Si existe una fecha límite, el usuario debe añadirlo a su cuenta antes de que finalice la promoción, aunque decida instalarlo después.
PUBLICIDAD
Las plataformas digitales cambiaron el acceso a los videojuegos
El crecimiento de las bibliotecas digitales modificó la relación de los usuarios con los videojuegos. Steam permite comprar, descargar y actualizar títulos desde una sola cuenta, sin depender de discos físicos ni de tiendas especializadas. También facilita el acceso a catálogos internacionales y a producciones que no siempre llegan a la distribución tradicional.
Las promociones gratuitas forman parte de ese modelo. Ayudan a atraer público hacia juegos nuevos, recuperan títulos que habían perdido presencia y permiten a estudios pequeños alcanzar a usuarios de distintos países. Para los jugadores, representan una forma de ampliar la biblioteca y probar mecánicas sin asumir el precio completo de una compra.
PUBLICIDAD
El sistema también tiene límites. La adquisición digital suele conceder una licencia de uso vinculada a una cuenta, no la propiedad de una copia física. El acceso depende de las normas de la plataforma, de la disponibilidad de los servidores y del estado de la cuenta del usuario.

articles.text:
The Download: AI’s real extinction threat and age-reversal tech for eyes
Plus: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk have called for an AI slowdown.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Roundtables: could AI really kill us all?
Employees at the world's leading AI labs are saying there's a real possibility that advanced AI could destroy humanity. Are they right? Or is this more scaremongering and hype?
Join MIT Technology Review executive editor Niall Firth, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven, and AI reporter Grace Huckins for a subscriber-only conversation unpacking the debate around AI extinction. They’ll explore where the fears come from, whether they hold any water and, if they do, what we should do about them.
Register now to attend on Tuesday, September 15 at 16:00 BST / 11:00am EST / 8:00am PST.
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.
This geneticist’s age-reversal tech could help restore sight
Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is obsessed with aging. And with eyes. As he steps outside the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, his aviator glasses darken automatically in the sun. Age-related blindness runs in his family, and his own 23andMe test came back with a mutation for macular degeneration, a top cause of vision loss in old age.
That obsession extends to his work. Lu is behind one of the coolest results in rejuvenation science and eye research: an age-reversal technique called reprogramming that repaired the optic nerves of blind mice, restoring their vision. Now, nearly the same genetic therapy he developed as a student has entered human clinical trials.
Learn more about Lu’s work on restoring sight with age-reversal therapy.
—Antonio Regalado
Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is one of the biotechnology and health honorees on our 35 Innovators Under 35 list for 2026. Meet the rest of them here, or explore the full list across the biotechnology and health, AI, computing and robotics, and climate and energy categories.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

4 South Korea has tightened espionage laws to protect its chip secrets

5 The US and Mexico are teaming up to zap drones at the border

6 AI agents are creating a new problem for the criminal justice system
The law has no clear answer when AI agents act independently. (Bloomberg $)
+ While courts face a flood of AI-generated lawsuits. (MIT Technology Review)
7 A Waymo pulled over and alerted police after detecting a gun
The riders were juveniles carrying a loaded AR-style ghost gun. (LA Times $)
8 Meta has been sued over data used to train its smart glasses
It allegedly used Facebook and Instagram photos without consent. (Wired $)

Authorities are investigating whether it stole power from a nearby dam. (Reuters $)
10 StarCraft is returning in 2030 as an open-world shooter
Fifteen years since its last release, the iconic franchise will be reborn. (Verge)
Quote of the day
“Dr. Frankenstein is telling us the monster is escaping; help us stop this.”
—Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz, calls for new AI regulation on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Inside the hunt for the most dangerous asteroid ever 
  As asteroid 2024 YR4 hurtled toward Earth, astronomers determined that this massive rock posed a higher risk of impact than any object of its size in recorded history. Then, just as quickly as history was made, experts declared that the danger had passed.
This is the inside story of the network of global scientists who found, followed, planned for, and finally dismissed the most dangerous asteroid ever found—all under the tightest of timelines and with the highest of stakes. Find out how they did it.

articles.title: Microsoft is working with the American Federation of Teachers to work out how best to use AI in the classroom
articles.text:
Microsoft is working with the American Federation of Teachers to work out how best to use AI in the classroom
Teachers will not train AI
- Microsoft and two key US teaching federations have agreed safeguards on AI use within education across America
- The American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers have made the deal with Microsoft after months of negotiations with all parties
- The AFT is in talks with other companies including OpenAI and Anthropic
After the failure to pass federal legislation to establish protections against AI overreach in schools, two teaching federations have taken the step of establishing legally-enforceable rules with Microsoft, covering the use of AI in schools.
Protections within the National AI Safety & Privacy Standard include the agreement not to use student or teacher data to train or improve AI models. Furthermore, any collected data will not be monetized, as educators attempt to find a middle ground that reduces screen time and balances technology use across all age groups.
This agreement follows various localized actions against AI use in schools, including a moratorium on AI use within the New York City school system, and a similar ban in the Los Angeles Unified School District.
Iron-clad privacy
“We have forged a hard-fought, iron-clad privacy agreement with real teeth that protects students and families, because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work,” said AFT President Randi Weingarten. “We can get angrier and angrier, or we can act decisively; anything less than legally enforceable provisions is simply a wish list.”
The concerns of the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and the United Federation of Teachers (UFT) are multiple, and ultimately center on their teachers’ comfort, focus, and ability to conduct lessons without the specter of AI intrusions. So, issues about training data, monetization, screen time, and other AI-related challenges have been sewn up by the National AI Safety & Privacy Standard, which is legally enforceable.
“This agreement ensures three foundational goals: protect the privacy and data of children, give schools real control over AI tools in the classroom, and provide transparency and information to parents," Weingarten continued.
"And with New York City adopting our framework to ban screens and AI use in the younger years, this agreement adds to the momentum around online safety for kids and educators.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Legally enforceable guardrails
The guardrails put in place by the agreement concern protecting privacy of educators, parents and students, enhancing safety of students and educators, and providing transparency and control about how AI is used in schools.
This also includes information about what data is collected and the protections that are in place. It places schools in control over the use of AI, and forces AI providers to communicate product changes and risks.
“This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” said Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith.
Along with banning the use of student and teacher data for AI model training, the data will not be sold or repurposed, and again schools will control data use, along with how it is stored and deleted. The guardrails also ensure AI systems are protected by human oversight, and are designed to block harmful actions and protect sensitive information.
The AFT reports it is in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic to also adopt the National AI Safety & Privacy Standard.

articles.title: Dix ans après sa promesse, Tesla va enfin présenter le nouveau Roadster
articles.text:
Tesla a publié le 12 septembre 2026 sur son compte X un visuel « Go for launch » accompagné de la date du 1er octobre. « C’est tout simplement incroyable », a souligné Elon Musk sous la publication originale. Oui, il s’agit bien d’un rendez-vous pour le Roadster 2.0. Un compte à rebours tourne même sur une nouvelle page dédiée au modèle.
Si l’excitation est réelle, la prudence reste autant de mise puisque le constructeur a déjà repoussé ce rendez-vous au moins huit fois depuis l’objectif de production initial, fixé à 2020.
Le Tesla Roadster se fait attendre
Rappelez-vous, le Roadster de deuxième génération a été montré pour la première fois en novembre 2017, sous la forme d’un prototype dévoilé aux côtés du camion Semi (enfin présenté lui aussi). Tesla annonçait alors environ 1 000 km d’autonomie, un 0 à 100 km/h en moins de deux secondes et une vitesse de pointe au-delà de 400 km/h.
Le prix devait être fixé à 200 000 dollars (environ 173 000 euros) pour la version de base et 250 000 dollars (environ 217 000 euros) pour la série Founders. Les livraisons qui devaient débuter en 2020 n’ont jamais eu lieu et le calendrier a glissé vers 2022, 2023, 2024, puis 2025 ou 2026.
Ces reports ont fini par lasser une partie des premiers clients. Réserver le Roadster imposait d’avancer 50 000 dollars, tandis que la série Founders exigeaient la totalité du montant. Le patron d’OpenAI Sam Altman et le vidéaste tech Marques Brownlee, réservataires de longue date, ont fini par réclamer le remboursement de leur acompte après plus de sept ans d’attente.
Une démonstration très loin de la série
On ignore encore ce que Tesla montrera le 1er octobre à Waco, au Texas. Modèle de série ? Concept revu ? Les questions demeurent et la communauté se divise en deux équipes. D’un côté, ceux qui estiment que l’image teaser est à l’envers et que les quatre halos lumineux correspondent aux fameux propulseurs de gaz à froid.
De l’autre ceux qui pensent que l’image est dans le bon sens et qui assurent que les quatre ronds font écho à un brevet déposé par la marque. Ce dernier modélise un système aérodynamique permettant de ventouser la voiture au sol par un système de succion avec justement quatre ventilateurs.
Ou peut-être les deux ? Si la voiture est à l’envers sur l’image, alors cela pourrait indiquer qu’elle est plaquée… au plafond ! Après tout, Elon Musk a promis une voiture spectaculaire. Encore faudra-t-il la produire. Pour mémoire, la marque vise un démarrage de la production d’ici à 2027 ou 2028.
L’événement se tiendra le 1er octobre à 20h30 heure de la côte Est, soit le lendemain de la clôture du troisième trimestre de Tesla. Pour les acheteurs, la seule date qui compte reste celle où une version de série, homologuée pour la route, sortira des chaînes. Et elle n’est toujours pas connue.

articles.title: Piscine, running, vélo : ce casque open-ear avec MP3 passe à 42,99€
articles.text:
Sous l’eau, le Bluetooth atteint vite ses limites, ce qui rend la mémoire intégrée particulièrement utile pour nager en musique. À 42,99 € chez Amazon, ce casque à conduction osseuse combine IPX8 et lecteur MP3 8 Go dans une formule pensée pour la piscine comme pour les entraînements à terre.
Ce modèle se présente comme un casque sportif à oreilles libres, avec conduction osseuse, certification IPX8 et lecteur MP3 intégré de 8 Go. Son intérêt est surtout concret pour la natation : le mode MP3 permet d’écouter des fichiers stockés localement lorsque la liaison Bluetooth n’est pas exploitable sous l’eau. Hors de la piscine, le Bluetooth 6.0 et le micro anti-vent sont annoncés pour la course, le vélo ou les appels, deux caractéristiques à considérer comme des données de fiche produit plutôt que comme des performances mesurées.
À ce niveau de prix, l’offre à 42,99 € chez Amazon vise donc surtout les sportifs qui veulent essayer la conduction osseuse sans s’orienter d’emblée vers une référence plus coûteuse.
Le casque à conduction osseuse IPX8 avec MP3 8 Go est proposé à 42,99 € chez Amazon, alors que le prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours indiqué pour cette offre est de 129,99 €.
Pourquoi choisir ce casque à conduction osseuse IPX8 ?
- Un mode MP3 pertinent en piscine : La mémoire intégrée de 8 Go permet de charger de la musique avant la séance. C’est essentiel sous l’eau, puisque le Bluetooth ne traverse pas correctement la surface et ne remplace pas un stockage local pendant les longueurs.
- Des oreilles qui restent dégagées : La conduction osseuse transmet le son sans obstruer le conduit auditif. Ce format peut aider à conserver davantage de perception de l’environnement à la course ou à vélo, sans dispenser de rester attentif à la circulation.
- Un ticket d’entrée nettement abaissé : À 42,99 €, le prix actuel se situe 87 € sous le prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours communiqué pour l’offre, fixé à 129,99 €. Pour découvrir le principe avant d’investir davantage, l’écart de prix est l’argument le plus concret.
Un format surtout intéressant quand le téléphone doit rester au vestiaire
En piscine, ce casque prend son sens grâce au couple IPX8 et MP3 8 Go : vous préparez vos morceaux à l’avance et il fonctionne sans dépendre du smartphone pendant la nage. À terre, il redevient un casque Bluetooth open-ear pour la course ou le vélo, sans boucher les oreilles. Clubic rappelle dans notre comparatif des meilleurs écouteurs Bluetooth pour le sport que maintien, confort et résistance aux éléments comptent autant que la qualité audio pendant l’entraînement. Ce modèle s’adresse donc davantage au nageur occasionnel ou au sportif polyvalent qu’à l’audiophile recherchant une écoute très isolante.
Un prix bas, avec moins de recul qu’une référence bien documentée
Cette offre mise d’abord sur son tarif et sa double utilisation MP3/Bluetooth, mais elle ne bénéficie pas du même recul éditorial que des références déjà testées en détail. Les modèles de marques plus établies restent plus rassurants pour un usage intensif, tandis que ce casque paraît surtout cohérent pour tester le format à moindre coût.
✅ Les points forts
- Certification IPX8 annoncée pour un usage en natation
- Lecteur MP3 intégré avec 8 Go de stockage
- Format open-ear à conduction osseuse, sans embout dans le conduit auditif
- Bluetooth pour les usages sportifs hors de l’eau
❌ Les limites
- Le Bluetooth n’est pas utilisable sous l’eau : il faut passer par les fichiers MP3 stockés localement
- Qualité sonore et performances du micro non documentées par un test indépendant fourni avec l’offre
- Peu de recul sur la fiabilité à long terme et le service après-vente de ce modèle
Si ce compromis entre natation en MP3 et usage Bluetooth à terre vous convient, vérifiez que ce casque est toujours affiché à 42,99 € chez Amazon avant de commander.
À 42,99 €, ce casque est surtout intéressant parce qu’il couvre deux contextes que les écouteurs classiques gèrent mal ensemble. Le stockage MP3 répond au problème de la connexion sous l’eau, tandis que la conception open-ear et le Bluetooth prennent davantage de sens pour courir ou pédaler. Pour un nageur occasionnel, un triathlète amateur ou un sportif curieux de la conduction osseuse, la proposition est facile à comprendre.
Il faut toutefois garder le prix en perspective avec le manque de recul sur ce modèle précis. Les performances audio, le micro anti-vent et la durabilité ne sont pas documentés ici par des mesures indépendantes, et la conduction osseuse n’est pas le format à privilégier si vous recherchez des basses puissantes ou une forte isolation. Les utilisateurs intensifs auront intérêt à comparer avec des références mieux documentées ; ceux qui veulent surtout écouter leur musique en piscine sans dépasser une cinquantaine d’euros peuvent y voir un compromis cohérent.

articles.title: Brussels-based Chift raises €10.5 million Series A to become Europe's financial connectivity layer | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Chift, a Brussels-based startup that provides a financial connectivity layer for European software, helping software vendors connect their products to the financial tools their users rely on, has raised €10.5 million in a Series A funding round.
The round was led by BlackFin Capital Partners, a specialist European FinTech investor managing more than €4 billion in assets. The round also saw participation from existing investors Entourage, Shapers, Seeder Fund, and Wallonie Entreprendre.
“Financial data connectivity is genuinely hard to build, particularly in Europe, where data sits across dozens of local systems that were never designed to talk to each other. That difficulty is what makes Chift’s position valuable. And AI raises the stakes further: agents are only as good as the data they can access,” said Pauline Brunel, Investment Director, BlackFin Capital Partners.
Founded in 2022 by Gauthier Henroz, Henry Hertoghe, and Matthieu Hertoghe in Brussels, Chift lets software companies plug into more than 120 financial systems, spanning accounting, invoicing, point-of-sale, e-commerce, payments, and property management, through a single unified API.
Its system removes the need to build and maintain each connection separately. An invoicing platform, for instance, can use Chift to route customer invoices into 40 different accounting tools without integrating with each one individually.
It’s not just about financial software; Chift is now orchestrating how AI systems and AI agents handle financial data. Through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, the company enables AI agents to securely retrieve and push data across its network of integrations, handling authentication and access control so developers building AI features don’t have to manage credentials system by system.
“AI and e-invoicing are rebuilding the entire financial software market, and businesses run on more tools than ever. Interoperability is becoming the defining problem of European SMB finance. Its fragmentation makes that harder to build than anywhere, as systems are split across 27 countries. That is exactly why we build the infrastructure that connects it all,” said Gauthier Henroz, CEO and co-founder of Chift.
The Series A funding round follows more than tenfold revenue growth since its €2.3 million Seed round in 2024. The company says its team has grown to 35 people and is now used by more than 150 software companies to connect over 50,000 SMEs in more than ten European countries. Notable clients include FinTechs, such as Revolut, Qonto, Pennylane and Mollie.
“We are proud to back Gauthier, Henry and Matthieu in making Chift the connectivity infrastructure for business software in the AI era,” added Brunel.
Chift plans to use the new capital to expand into every major European market and deepen its AI bet, connecting more AI products into financial data. It is also moving toward integrations that configure themselves rather than requiring manual setup by each customer. By 2028, the company is aiming to become Europe’s go-to provider of financial connectivity.

articles.title: Le Kia PV7 ringardise les SUV électriques : 9 passagers, batterie XXL et recharge ultra-rapide
articles.text:
En 2025, Kia se lançait dans le marché des vans électriques et annonçait toute une gamme basée sur sa plateforme dédiée PBV (Platform Beyond Vehicle). Son premier van, le PV5, fut d’ailleurs sacré utilitaire de l’année 2026 en Europe – on l’a également essayé et approuvé.
Aujourd’hui, Kia dévoile à Hanovre son grand frère, le PV7, plus long et surtout mieux né côté technique. S’il en reprend la plateforme dédiée E-GMP.S, il change de dimension : 5,35 m de long, contre 4,7 m pour un PV5 standard.
Le design reprend l’air de famille du PV5, notamment la face avant, mais adopte un design un peu plus léché. L’original biton, couvrant toute la partie supérieure et le capot du van, est conservé. Idem au niveau de la planche de bord et de l’habitacle, avec des matériaux et des couleurs plus travaillés que le PV5, franchement basique.
Le 800 volts accélère (enfin) la recharge
Kia propose deux batteries NMC de 71,5 et 96,2 kWh, là où le PV5 se contente de 51,5 et 71,2 kWh. Le moteur avant grimpe jusqu’à 200 kW (272 ch) et 420 Nm, quand le PV5 plafonne à 120 kW (163 ch) et 250 Nm. Une transmission intégrale est prévue plus tard.
Kia annonce plus de 460 km d’autonomie WLTP pour la version Cargo Long Range, quand le PV5 annonce 412 km au mieux.
La recharge est sans doute la meilleure nouvelle du lot. Là où le PV5 s’appuie sur une architecture 400 volts, limitée à 150 kW en charge rapide, le PV7 passe au 800 volts, encaisse jusqu’à 350 kW et refait ce même 10-80 % en un peu plus de 20 minutes.
Sur un utilitaire qui enchaîne les tournées et les bornes, ces minutes grattées comptent double. Pour la version « grand public », cela permettra de gagner en polyvalence sur longs trajets, notamment pour remédier en partie à la consommation qui explosera sur autoroute à cause d’un aérodynamisme peu compatible avec l’efficience.
Le PV7 Passenger vise les grandes familles et les navettes
C’est la version qui nous intéresse le plus. Le PV7 Passenger accueille jusqu’à neuf places, avec des configurations à sept ou neuf sièges selon les besoins : la version sept places mise sur des sièges qui se retirent facilement, la neuf places s’offre avec ou sans quatrième rangée. Les banquettes reposent sur de longs rails et coulissent, de quoi transformer l’habitacle en salle de réunion roulante ou en soute à bagages.
Kia soigne le détail : climatisation arrière logée dans le pavillon, prises USB-C de 100 watts, éclairage d’ambiance, rangements fermés et une console centrale qui fait aussi office de table. Les portes latérales peuvent s’ouvrir électriquement.
On garde la charge bidirectionnelle (V2L), pour brancher ses outils ou son matériel de camping, à l’intérieur comme à l’extérieur. Kia annonce sept airbags, dont celui pour le passager logé dans le pavillon pour libérer des espaces de rangement.
La version Cargo n’est pas oubliée. Elle se décline en Compact, Long et High Roof, avec jusqu’à 8 m³ de volume utile pour la plus grande et une charge utile qui grimpe à 1 200 kg. De quoi couvrir la logistique du dernier kilomètre, là où le PV5 attaque déjà le marché.
Le PV7 arrivera en Corée et en Europe au second semestre 2027, sans prix communiqué pour l’instant. À titre de repère, le PV5 démarre à 39 550 euros pour la petite batterie et 43 550 euros pour la grande, soit des tarifs très attractifs pour la catégorie.
D’ici là, le grand frère devra se frotter à un segment qui se remplit vite : Volkswagen ID. Buzz, mais aussi le nouveau Renault Trafic E-Tech présenté au même salon que le PV7, ou encore la plateforme VAN.EA de Mercedes.

articles.title: C-CAMP selects 15 bioscience startups for its National Bio Entrepreneurship Competition
articles.text:
C-CAMP selects 15 bioscience startups for its National Bio Entrepreneurship Competition
The National National Bio Entrepreneurship Competition now in its ninth edition has seen startups from the previous editions raising more than $125 million in VC funding
The Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP), a biosciences research and innovation hub, has selected 15 startups and four teams for its National Bio Entrepreneurship Competition (NBEC) 2026.
According to a statement, the winning startups received a total of Rs 35 crore in cash prizes and investment opportunities, while student-led teams secured Rs 4 lakh in cash prizes. This is the 9th edition of NBEC, a flagship platform of C-CAMP that aims to identify future bioscience entrepreneurs.
Over the past eight years C-CAMP has provided more than Rs 90 crore in cash prizes and investment opportunities to 130 plus winners. It added that the past winners have raised over $125 million in venture capital funding and launched more than 300 products.
This year’s competition saw over 3200 registrations from across 34 States and UTs with 40% of the applicants being women. The winners were selected from 25 finalists who were judged based on their novelty, scalability and business potential.
Among the solutions developed included next-gen cancer pathology, screening of kidney injury through quantum sensing, affordable insulin patch pumps, satellite imagery embedded smart spraying of agri inputs in farms,bioformulations to enhance soil health etc.
Biocon Chairman Kiran Mazumdar Shaw said, “The future of biology looks very promising as its convergence with digital technology and AI accelerates innovation at a never-before pace.”
She further added, “This (C-CAMP’s initiative) will build a strong economy for an aspiring India and lift the country’s bioeconomy from $195 billion to $2.6 trillion by 2047.”
C-CAMP CEO Taslimarif Saiyed said, “We want India’s innovators to aim higher and trust ecosystems like C-CAMP to support an ecosystem that enables your science and business growth.”
The investors in this programme include the likes of Social Alpha, Ideaspring Capital, Java Capital, TiE Global, Anicut Capital etc.

articles.title: Cuando un estudiante prometió 1.000 dólares haciéndose pasar por Bill Gates y su broma acabó siendo imposible de detener
articles.text:
Mucho antes de que hablásemos de publicaciones virales, tendencias o algoritmos, Internet ya había encontrado una forma bastante eficaz de conseguir que una misma historia circulase de una persona a otra: pedirnos que pulsáramos "Reenviar". El correo podía llegar de un amigo, un compañero de trabajo o un familiar, y ese simple vínculo podía prestarle una credibilidad que el mensaje quizá no merecía. En aquella Internet de finales de los 90, además, muchos usuarios todavía no tenían por qué saber qué podía hacer técnicamente un correo electrónico. Esa combinación resultó extraordinariamente fértil para los bulos.
El 18 de noviembre de 1997, Bryan Mack estaba en un laboratorio informático de Iowa State University cuando el estudiante sentado a su lado recibió uno de aquellos correos que prometían dinero fácil. Según contó años después a Wired, Mack respondió que podía inventar algo mejor y tardó apenas tres minutos en hacerlo. Escribió un mensaje haciéndose pasar por Bill Gates y presentó un supuesto programa capaz de rastrear cada reenvío: si la cadena alcanzaba a 1.000 personas, decía, todos sus integrantes recibirían 1.000 dólares pagados por el propio Gates.
Una broma que dejó de pertenecerle
Mack envió aquel correo a un amigo de Loras College, en Dubuque, con el asunto "bill gates here". Su amigo se rio y decidió reenviarlo. Bastaron unos días para que el mensaje llegara a desconocidos que empezaron a escribir a Mack preguntándole por el dinero prometido. El salto definitivo llegó después de Acción de Gracias: al regresar a la universidad encontró su cuenta bloqueada y, según relató, aproximadamente un gigabyte de correo acumulado, con "miles y miles" de mensajes. Para entonces, aquella broma entre amigos ya circulaba sin necesitarle.
Dos semanas más tarde, a Mack le llegó una versión de su propia broma que ya casi no le pertenecía. Su nombre había desaparecido, el remitente figuraba como gatesbeta@microsoft.com y la recompensa incluía, además de los 1.000 dólares, una copia gratuita de Windows 98. Poco después recibió otra falsamente firmada por "Walt Disney Jr." que prometía 5.000 dólares y unas vacaciones. Aquello no terminó ahí: años más tarde aparecieron decenas de versiones distintas que habían incorporado marcas como IBM, Nokia, Honda, British Airways, Disney, Coca-Cola o Gap.
Para 1999, una nueva cadena aseguraba que Honda recompensaría con 200 dólares de crédito por cada amigo al que se reenviara el mensaje, gracias a un supuesto programa capaz de seguir su recorrido por Internet. La compañía negó haber lanzado semejante promoción y publicó un desmentido, pero no consiguió evitar que algunos destinatarios llamaran para cobrar.
En realidad, ni siquiera el desmentido del propio Gates había conseguido frenarlo. En marzo de 1998 ya había calificado aquel correo de "hooey", una patraña, pero el mensaje continuó pasando de una bandeja de entrada a otra. Cuando se les preguntó años después a varias personas por qué lo habían reenviado, las respuestas resultaron reveladoras: algunos confiaban en quien se lo había enviado, otros pensaban que no tenían nada que perder y hubo quien encontró plausible que Microsoft pudiera rastrear los correos. Esa falta de familiaridad técnica es precisamente uno de los ingredientes que Microsoft identifica al recordar los grandes bulos por email de aquella época.
La parte más interesante es que nadie diseñó todo lo que vino después. Las firmas automáticas daban autoridad a algunas copias, distintos mensajes acababan mezclados y algunas variantes conseguían propagarse mucho más que otras. Mack había puesto en circulación unas pocas líneas, pero Internet terminó convirtiéndolas en algo que podía cambiar sin dejar de reconocerse. Años antes de las redes sociales, ya habíamos encontrado una forma de fabricar virales: bastaba con que cada receptor decidiera enviárselo a alguien más.
