articles.title: What happens after a town de-Flocks
articles.text:
From Florida to Washington state, local governments across the country are canceling their contracts with Flock, the company behind the controversial AI-enabled license plate readers, in response to public outcry. But ending the contracts doesn’t necessarily mean the cameras will come down immediately — or that the information they’ve gathered will be deleted anytime soon.
What happens after a town de-Flocks
Cities across the US are ditching the controversial license plate-reading cameras, but some are now turning to new surveillance tools.
Even as state and local governments decide to rein in their surveillance capabilities, uncertainty remains about what Flock can and will do with data that has already been collected. Each jurisdiction’s contract is different, but many of them let Flock retain data long after it’s been collected. “Let’s say they terminate,” said Saira Hussain, a senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation who has reviewed dozens of municipal Flock contracts. “What happens to the data, and how long is it able to be searched? That question appears to be unresolved.”
The backlash against Flock was slow to mount, but now it’s everywhere, and it’s bipartisan. Founded in 2017, Flock pitched its cameras — which are sold not only to local governments but to private businesses and citizens — as an unobtrusive tool to enhance public safety. Early in the company’s history, some cities even offered grants for homeowners associations that wanted to install Flock cameras in their neighborhoods. Flock’s footprint has grown quickly. The company has installed more than 120,000 cameras across the US.
This rapid expansion, along with alarming reports of misuses of Flock’s surveillance network, has fueled a new wave of opposition, making Flock a kind of shorthand for privacy invasion. In recent months, activists in big cities and small towns have urged local governments to end their contracts, citing concerns about privacy, harassment, and mass surveillance. Local leaders have said the public pressure — coupled with Flock’s data-sharing and retention policies, and what the company can do with the information its cameras collect — spurred them to end the contracts.
Lawmakers in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, unanimously voted to end the city’s Flock contract after learning that Flock reportedly tried to sell anonymized data collected in Sheboygan back to the city’s public works department. Elsewhere in the state, the mayor of Stevens Point not only ended its contract with Flock but also covered up the 10 cameras scattered throughout the city. “We really have no way of auditing where the Flock data goes once it’s collected,” Mayor Mike Wiza said on a local radio show. “Our community is not comfortable using these cameras without some assurances that it’s being used in a manner we have authorized.” (Flock maintains that it doesn’t sell consumer data.)
Local leaders across the country say they were misled about how Flock data could be used, and some have admitted that they didn’t realize the degree to which the data would be accessed by third parties.
In Bridgewater, Virginia, the town council put bags over its Flock cameras after voting to cancel its contract. Bridgewater is home to fewer than 7,000 people, but the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism found that because of the town’s information-sharing agreement with Flock, data collected in the town was searched 7 million times by law enforcement in 12 months.
The EFF, which sued the city of San Jose, California, over its usage of Flock cameras, argues that these information-sharing agreements violate the Fourth Amendment’s protections against unreasonable search and seizure.
“Through these searches, police are able to identify patterns of where people live and work, where they may drop off their kids to school, who they associate with, where they worship, seek reproductive care, seek an immigration consult,” Hussain said. “What we’re talking about here is a mass surveillance technology that is by design intended to identify where people are going and track people’s movements.”
Like many movements against law enforcement overreach, the backlash against Flock began with stories about particularly egregious abuses. There have been several reports of law enforcement officers using Flock to track exes and romantic partners. In response to these and other concerns, Flock recently rolled out new guardrails, including a new requirement to run case codes — which were previously optional — for all searches. Flock is also mandating a feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal” queries.
“This is such an obvious way to curb abuse,” Flock CEO Garrett Langley recently told The Verge. “And I said, ‘Fine. You know what? I think that’s right, and we got this one wrong. We should make it a requirement.’”
Flock has also shortened its standard data retention period from 30 to seven days, though it will let individual jurisdictions lengthen these time frames. Agencies that use Flock will also be able to limit what kinds of information they share with other entities. For example, a city or police department could let other jurisdictions access its Flock data for homicide searches, but not for queries related to immigration enforcement.
But privacy advocates say Flock’s reforms don’t go far enough. The American Civil Liberties Union, which is suing San Jose alongside the EFF, said the changes are “more focused on addressing a perceived PR problem than the significant harms its products create.”
It’s unclear what would stop someone from falsely or incorrectly tagging a Flock search. For example, after sheriff’s deputies in one Texas county used Flock to track a woman suspected of violating the state’s abortion ban, the sheriff described the queries as a search for a missing person.
Flock has repeatedly emphasized that Immigration and Customs Enforcement doesn’t have access to its cameras. But local agencies that have deputized their officers under federal 287(g) agreements — which let local law enforcement conduct immigration arrests — can use Flock for immigration enforcement, and many do. Public recordsobtained by 404 Media revealed that Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission uses Flock to carry out ICE arrests. The agency is reportedly also using Flock to surveil and track its critics. Florida’s Department of Transportation has since banned Flock cameras from state highways, but law enforcement can still tap into city- and county-level Flock cameras, or to those installed on private property. Shopping centers, retail giants like Home Depot and Lowe’s, and homeowners associations have reportedly installed Flock cameras on their properties. Activists are urging beauty retailer Ulta to drop its Flock contracts, citing numerous reports of officers using the surveillance network to track women.
Privacy activists note that ending Flock contracts won’t be enough to stop mass surveillance. Some cities that have ended their relationships with Flock — including South Pasadena, California, and Durango, Colorado — are now considering alternatives. The Flock backlash has reportedly enriched Axon, the company that also makes Tasers and body-worn cameras. Hussain notes that Axon’s system is arguably more integrated than Flock’s.
“Axon has other technologies as well that they stack on top of their automated license plate readers. They have a bunch of other data streams, including coming from their body-worn cameras, so you’re able to build out quite a surveillance system,” she said. “You’re not going to be able to stop this mass surveillance technology by moving to another vendor. The only thing that is going to solve this whole problem is not relying on this technology.”

articles.title: Jugar 'GTA 5' desde tu móvil va a ser posible muy pronto, pero no te hagas grandes ilusiones
articles.text:
GTA 5 podría hacer su debut no oficial en Android muy pronto. Según publica Android Authority, un desarrollador está trabajando en un port que llevará el icónico juego de Rockstar Games a dispositivos móviles. El responsable del proyecto es el mismo que recientemente lanzó una versión para Nintendo Switch.
Los detalles del port de GTA 5 para Android son todavía bastante escasos, y desde ya puedes hacerte la idea que tanto a Rockstar como a Take-Two Interactive no les agradará nada este lanzamiento (si es que finalmente se concreta). De acuerdo con la información que circula en Discord, el desarrollo está lo suficientemente avanzado como para ya revelar un listado de especificaciones de hardware mínimas para ejecutarlo.
Esta versión no oficial de GTA 5 se podrá ejecutar en móviles y otros dispositivos Android con chip Snapdragon 865 o superior, pero también requiere al menos 8 GB de RAM y 65 GB de almacenamiento libre. Esto significa que para correrlo será necesario disponer de un teléfono que en su día hayan sido topes de gama, como un Asus Zenfone 7 o un OnePlus 8T.
Asimismo, el autor del port de GTA 5 para Android menciona que el juego se podrá ejecutar en algunos móviles Samsung impulsados por chips Exynos, siempre y cuando tengan GPU Xclipse 530 o superior. Esto abriría la puerta a su ejecución en modelos de 2022 en adelante. Como contracara, los Google Pixel modernos con procesadores Tensor no serán compatibles con el título.
Un port no oficial de GTA 5 está en camino a Android
Si bien el responsable del proyecto tiene experiencia llevando GTA 5 a plataformas no soportadas, no te ilusiones demasiado con esta versión para Android. Como ya indicamos, es una solución no oficial ni tampoco autorizada por los creadores del juego original. De modo que, si realmente se llega a lanzar un instalador para móviles con el software de Google, es lógico pensar que Rockstar y T2 van a tomar todas las medidas a su alcance para evitar su distribución.
Pero la potencial respuesta de los dueños de la propiedad intelectual no solo se fundamentaría en la piratería, sino en el hecho de que muy posiblemente este port de GTA 5 se base en el código fuente robado en 2023. Todo apunta a que la versión de Nintendo Switch se creó a partir del material filtrado por entonces.
A esto hay que sumarle que, independientemente de cuáles sean las intenciones del autor de la iniciativa, este tipo de propuestas son una puerta de entrada a la distribución de malware. Si Rockstar y Take-Two hacen reclamaciones de derechos de autor que tumban los enlaces de distribución más conocidos, cualquier otra vía menos probada o confiable que aparezca como alternativa puede terminar llevando a una campaña de software malicioso.
Así que no te hagas grandes ilusiones con GTA 5 en Android. Si el port avanza, jugarlo será prácticamente imposible y no solo por las exigencias técnicas que pueda presentar su ejecución.

articles.title: This Xbox and PC controller I tested impressed me more than Microsoft’s offering — and I couldn’t quite believe the price
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Drakong Challenger is a no-thrills Xbox and PC controller, shorn of bells and whistles to focus on top-tier performance instead, courtesy of its Hall Effect sticks and triggers and tactile buttons. The headphone jack is a welcome addition, but it lacks wireless connectivity and customization software. Still, these omissions are hard to complain about at this price point.
Pros
- +Surprisingly solid yet light design
- +Tight and responsive inputs
- +Budget price tag
Cons
- -Wired-only
- -No accompanying software
- -Anonymous looks
Why you can trust TechRadar
Drakong Challenger: One-minute review
The Drakong Challenger takes aim at the budget controller market by offering a basic but high-performing pad. On the style front, the Challenger is very much a case of function over form. You’d be hard-pressed to tell it apart from your run-of-the-mill Xbox controller, although the green rings around the thumbsticks are one notable point of difference.
Just like that controller, the Challenger is very comfortable in the hand. It’s also surprisingly well-made, with a solid shell and planted buttons. What’s more, it’s pleasingly light, making it easy to use for long periods. All this makes it one of the best Xbox Controllers at the budget end of the sector in terms of construction.
Although there’s no software to accompany the Challenger, you can assign the back buttons quite easily using the M button. A rumble notifies you when your assignments have been confirmed, which is a useful indicator.
The Challenger impresses in action. The triggers and sticks are as smooth and precise as you would expect from their Hall Effect technology, while the D-pad and face buttons are satisfyingly damped and quick to respond and rebound. The back buttons are a little less tactile, but they suffice nonetheless.
Given how inexpensive it is, you’d seriously have to consider the Challenger over a standard Xbox controller or any other, for that matter, so long as wireless connectivity is something you’re willing to sacrifice.
Drakong Challenger review: Price & availability
- $34.99 (about £25 / AU$50)
- One month of Game Pass Ultimate included
- Good price-to-performance ratio
The Drakong Challenger costs $34.99 (about £25 / AU$50) and is available now. It comes with a USB-C cable, as well as a code for a one-month free trial of Game Pass Ultimate.
The Challenger is cheaper than the official Xbox Wireless Controller, although that gamepad has the advantage of wireless connectivity. However, it doesn’t include a rechargeable battery as standard, nor does it have customizable back buttons.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
If you want something a little more feature-packed, but don’t want to spend a huge amount, the Turtle Beach Pacific Skyline is a good alternative. It has companion software that can be used to remap buttons, as well as adjust vibration intensity and thumbstick dead zones. Also, the controller itself is far more vibrant than the Challenger — and many other controllers, for that matter.
Drakong Challenger review: Specs
| Price | $34.99 (about £25 / AU$50) | 
| Weight | 7.23oz / 205g | 
| Dimensions | 6.3 x 2.5 x 4.4in / 160 x 63.5 x 111.8mm | 
| Compatibility | PC, Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One | 
| Connection type | Wired (USB-C), 3.5mm AUX (headset) | 
Drakong Challenger review: Design
- Classic Xbox controller design
- Light yet solid construction
- No accompanying software
As far as looks go, the Challenger barely departs from the traditional Xbox design. It has the same shape, size, and layout, with the only additional flourishes being green rings around the sticks and a subtle outline around the two halves of the pad. There’s no RGB lighting, despite what those aforementioned stick rings may lead you to believe.
However, all this isn’t to say the Challenger has a disappointing construction. After all, to many gamers, the Xbox controller form is comfortable and practical. And despite the plastics not feeling particularly premium, the Challenger is surprisingly solid and pleasingly light at the same time, which is always a winning combination.
What’s more, the sticks and buttons are well fitted with no play in them at all, which isn’t something that can be said about most budget controllers. The back of the handles is textured for added traction, but the improvement is marginal given how subtle this texture is.
There’s no software available to customize the Challenger, but there are two mappable back buttons. I couldn’t find information on how to map them anywhere, but thankfully it’s a fairly simple process to figure out. You simply press the M button and a back button simultaneously until you feel a rumble, then press the button you want to assign and another rumble will confirm its activation.
The Challenger has no wireless connectivity, which is a shame but understandable at this price point. The included USB cable is quite long, but it isn’t finished in a braided fabric, which is something you often find on the best gaming mice to improve flexibility and reduce drag. It does at least seem quite durable, and the connection at either end was solid in my experience, despite the small amount of superficial wobbling at the controller end.
Drakong Challenger review: Performance
- Solid and responsive buttons
- Precise and tactile triggers and sticks
- Easy connectivity to Xbox and PC
The Drakong Challenger might be a budget controller, but that’s not something you’ll notice when gaming with it, as every input is smooth, solid, and precise. The face buttons are also well damped and very responsive, rebounding quickly to allow for easy spamming when needed. The same goes for the D-pad, and despite its traditional four-pronged hat, it felt comfortable in my thumb, even when performing rolls and frantic inputs in Tekken 8.
On the shoulder buttons, the texture is subtle but noticeable, and feels quite nice on the fingers, although I’m not sure it provides much in the way of traction. The Hall Effect triggers are light but offer a surprising amount of control, which was especially helpful when accelerating and braking in Assetto Corsa. The Hall Effect thumbsticks were accurate and responsive when steering, too, as well as when aiming in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl. I also appreciated their soft, grippy coating and textured rims for added purchase and feedback.
The two back buttons are easy to reach, but they don’t feel quite as tactile as the other inputs, lacking depth of travel and dampening by comparison. Also, I found them quite easy to trigger accidentally, even when I didn’t have a particularly tight grip on the pad.
Surprisingly for an inexpensive controller, the Challenger features a headset jack. The cable connection is solid, and I didn’t notice any loss in audio quality relative to connections made elsewhere.
As for the pad itself, I had no issues connecting it via the USB cable to either an Xbox Series X or to my PC, being just as easy to use with the latter as the best PC controllers.
Should I buy the Drakong Challenger?
Buy it if…
You want a solid build
Despite how light it is, the Challenger’s shell and buttons are surprisingly sturdy.
You want great value
In terms of price-to-performance, it’s hard to beat this controller.
Don't buy it if…
You want to go wireless
Part of the cost-cutting comes from its wired connectivity, which might seem a little outmoded in 2026.
You want to tweak inputs
You can remap the back buttons, but not any of the others. You can’t alter the behavior of the sticks and triggers, either — a missed opportunity given their Hall Effect tech. 
Drakong Challenger review: Also consider
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Drakong Challenger | Xbox Wireless Controller | Turtle Beach Pacific Skyline | 
| Price | $34.99 (about £25 / AU$50) | $59.99 / £54.99 / AU$74.99 | $89.99 / £79.99 / around AU$150 | 
| Weight | 7.23oz / 205g | 9.76oz / 275g | 7.04oz / 200g | 
| Dimensions | 6.3 x 2.5 x 4.4in / 160 x 63.5 x 111.8mm | 6.02 x 4.01 x 2.40in / 153 x 102 x 61mm | 6.22 x 4.09 x 2.36in / 158 x 104 x 60mm | 
| Compatibility | PC, Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One | Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One, PC, Android, iOS | PC, Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One | 
| Connection type | Wired (USB-C), 3.5mm AUX (headset) | Wireless (Xbox, Bluetooth), Wired (USB-C) | Bluetooth, Wired (USB-C), 2.4Ghz wireless dongle | 
| Battery life | N/A | 20-40 hours | ~20 hours | 
Xbox Wireless Controller
It’s hard to go wrong with Microsoft’s official controller for its console (and other platforms). But although it’s wireless, it doesn’t come with a rechargeable battery by default; that’s an optional extra on a controller that already costs more than the Challenger. It doesn’t have back buttons, either. Read our full Xbox Wireless Controller review.
How I tested the Drakong Challenger
- Tested for several days
- Played a variety of games
- Experienced with many other gamepads
I tested the Challenger for several days, using it for a variety of games and on both PC and Xbox.
I played Assetto Corsa to test the triggers, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl to test the precision of the sticks. I also played Tekken 8 to test the responsiveness and comfort of the D-pad and face buttons.
I’ve been gaming for decades and have used a wide variety of systems and controllers in that time. I’ve also reviewed a range of them, from simple budget-friendly affairs to feature-packed premium offerings.
- Read more about how we test
- First reviewed: September 2026
Lewis Maddison is a Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He previously worked as a Staff Writer for our business section, TechRadar Pro, where he gained experience with productivity-enhancing hardware, ranging from keyboards to standing desks. His area of expertise lies in computer peripherals and audio hardware, having spent over a decade exploring the murky depths of both PC building and music production. He also revels in picking up on the finest details and niggles that ultimately make a big difference to the user experience.

articles.title: Shogun Saison 2 : la série vient de franchir une grosse étape et livre quelques détails
articles.text:
Justin Marks et Rachel Kondo, les créateurs de la série, ont officiellement annoncé la fin des prises de vues de la saison 2 de Shogun. Une étape clé pour une production dantesque qui promet d’amener le drame féodal japonais vers de nouveaux sommets.
Si la première saison avait créé un véritable raz-de-marée critique en adaptant le roman de James Clavell, la barre est aujourd’hui fixée à une hauteur vertigineuse. Le défi est d’autant plus grand que cette deuxième ligne droite s’aventure en territoire inconnu, au-delà de l’œuvre littéraire originale.
Près de 200 jours dans le Japon féodal pour Shogun saison 2
C’est via un message célébrant la fin du plateau de tournage de Shogun que Justin Marks a partagé la nouvelle sur ses réseaux sociaux ce 14 septembre 2026, photo des coulisses à l’appui :
« Les plateaux étaient vides, et ils le sont à nouveau. C’est dans la boîte pour la saison 2 de Shōgun. Près de 200 jours de tatamis, de palanquins et de laques fines empaquetés. Attendez de voir ce qui arrive… »
Commencé en janvier dernier, le tournage aura nécessité près de huit mois de prises de vues intensives pour reconstituer l’esthétique léchée et l’exigence plastique qui ont fait le succès de la série. Un marathon logistique indispensable pour alimenter le niveau de détail qui avait valu à la première saison son plébiscite critique et sa rafle historique de récompenses.
Entre prudence et impatience pour les fans
Si l’annonce du clap de fin est une excellente nouvelle, il faudra armer son sabre d’un peu de patience. L’entrée en phase de post-production, montage minutieux, étalonnage et effets visuels, devrait s’étaler sur plusieurs mois. Une sortie sur les écrans n’est donc pas à attendre à très court terme.
Fort du renouvellement combiné pour des saisons 2 et 3, le duo d’auteurs a désormais les coudées franches pour développer l’ascension politique de Yoshii Toranaga et les destinées de John Blackthorne. Privée du roman de James Clavell pour la guider, la saison 2 avance en terrain inédit. C’est le pari le plus risqué de la série depuis ses débuts, et FX n’a pas encore communiqué de date de sortie.

articles.title: Trump and Mike Johnson think the AI industry is overreacting
articles.text:
Yesterday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy open letter saying it was time to “pace the frontier” and slow down AI development. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk both agreed, publicly voicing their support on X. Even Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis offered tentative support for Amodei’s proposal.
Trump and Mike Johnson think the AI industry is overreacting
The Republicans fear slowing down AI development could give China the edge.
Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, however, seem to think the AI executives are being overreactive and fear that a pause could lead to China outpacing the US in the AI race. According to the Financial Times, Trump said “Look, we’re leading China in AI ... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Johnson echoed those sentiments on CNN, telling Jake Tapper that rushing to place restrictions on AI development could be a “national security threat.” He urged people not to panic. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try and regulate AI, we will lose the race to China.”

articles.title: Amodeis KI-Warnung: Angst-PR oder echte Gefahr? Warum beides stimmt
articles.text:
KI-Warnungen von Anthropic-Chef Amodei: Eigennützig – und trotzdem richtig
ChatGPTs Start war vor allem faszinierend: Mit einer Maschine zu chatten und halbwegs vernünftige Antworten zu bekommen, hatte etwas von Magie. Man testete eine Software im Schutz eines Chatfensters. Was sie tut, wenn keiner hinschaut, musste damals niemand fragen.
Heute, knapp vier Jahre später, hat die KI-Entwicklung ein Tempo erreicht, das selbst den Lenkern der großen KI-Konzerne nicht geheuer ist. Der Angriff der KI-Agenten von OpenAI auf Hugging Face, den die Mitarbeiter von Sam Altman erst deutlich später entdeckten, markiert eine Zäsur. Ähnliche Vorfälle häuften sich in den vergangenen Wochen.
Grund genug für Anthropic-Chef Dario Amodei, einen bedeutungsschweren Essay zu veröffentlichen, in dem er ausdrücklich dafür plädiert, die KI-Entwicklung zu verlangsamen. Die Gefahren einer sich selbst verbessernden KI seien zu hoch, wenn es in dem aktuellen Tempo weitergehe. Erstaunlicherweise stimmten die Erzrivalen Elon Musk und Sam Altman zu.
Aber was heißt das jetzt eigentlich? Müssen wir uns wirklich Sorgen machen, dass KI die Menschheit bis Ende des Jahrzehnts auslöscht? Und wenn nicht gleich auslöscht, dann versklavt, unterjocht, unsere Systeme lahmlegt? Oder doch alles „Angst-PR“, um sich kurz vor dem Börsengang nochmal ins Gespräch zu bringen? Für die Branche ist das jedenfalls eine erstaunlich bequeme Werbebotschaft: „Seht her, unsere Modelle sind so mächtig, dass wir sie selbst kaum kontrollieren können.“ Zumal Amodei in seinem Essay fordert, Chinas Fortschritt über Chipexporte und ein Vorgehen gegen Distillation so weit zu bremsen, dass Amerika seinen Vorsprung in drei bis fünf Jahren deutlich ausbaut – wer profitiert: Anthropic und Konsorten. Also doch alles zum Wohle der US-Akteure?
KI: Selbstverbesserung schneller als Prüfung
Jein, denn beides kann stimmen. Das ist das Unangenehme an dieser Debatte: Der Verdacht, dass hier jemand sein eigenes Geschäft betreibt, und die Möglichkeit, dass er recht hat, schließen einander nicht aus. Interessenlage und Faktenlage sind zwei verschiedene Dinge, und sie fallen hier ausgerechnet zusammen: Niemand hat ein größeres Interesse an dieser Erzählung als die Labore – gleichzeitig sieht niemand genauer, was in den Modellen passiert.
Denn wir selbst können nicht in die Labore von Anthropic, OpenAI und Co. hineinschauen, aber es ist davon auszugehen, dass die fortschrittlichsten Modelle gehütet werden wie der heilige Gral: Sie sind der Nukleus einer Industrie, die Billionen-Umsätze verspricht. Diese Modelle scheinen aber auch offenbar so mächtig geworden zu sein, dass Amodei, Altman und Musk in ungewohnter Einigkeit jetzt eine Drosselung der KI-Entwicklung forderten – denn KI hilft inzwischen dabei, die nächste KI zu bauen. Damit verkürzt sich der Abstand zwischen zwei Modellgenerationen. Der Aufwand, ein Modell zu verstehen, zu testen und freizugeben, verkürzt sich aber nicht mit. Irgendwann – und vielleicht sind wir schon an diesem Punkt – ist der Entwicklungszyklus schneller als der Prüfzyklus, und ab da gibt niemand mehr etwas frei, das er wirklich geprüft und verstanden hat.
Und das könnte sich rächen – denn: „Agenten zeigen schon heute in Experimenten Verhalten, bei dem sie beispielsweise Abschaltbefehle umgehen. Sie schützen andere Agenten vor Abschaltung, und sie verfolgen Ziele über ihre jeweiligen Aufträge hinaus. Solange diese Systeme wenig Reichweite haben, bleibt der Schaden klein. Mit mehr Autonomie und mehr Zugriffsrechten wächst er mit“, erklärt Dr. Thilo Hagendorff, Forschungsgruppenleiter AI Safety an der Universität Stuttgart in einem aktuellen SMC-Briefing.
Verlangsamung von KI‑Entwicklung: Eine Reihe von Warnungen
Es ist jedenfalls nicht so, dass es erst seit Amodeis Essay Warnungen gibt. In einem offenen Brief, der bereits im Juli dieses Jahres veröffentlicht wurde, fordern knapp 1.400 KI-Entwickler und -Forscher, KI endlich stärker zu regulieren. Der „Godfather of AI“ Geoffrey Hinton verließ Google, um vor KI und den Folgen einer unregulierten Entwicklungen ausdrücklich zu warnen. Und nicht zuletzt die Kündigung von Jacob Coxon, der lautstark Anthropic verließ – sein Vorwurf: Die führenden Labore spielten mit dem Leben der Menschen.
Und trotzdem: Aussagen wie die von Evan Hubinger, der Coxon öffentlich recht gab, helfen auch nicht weiter. Auf X spricht der Alignment-Chef bei Anthropic davon, dass die Chance, dass KI die Menschheit innerhalb des nächsten Jahrzehnts auslöscht, größer als zehn Prozent sei. Was bedeutet das? Und vor allem: Wo kommen jetzt genau diese zehn Prozent her? Das grenzt nun tatsächlich an Panikmache.
Forscher Hagendorff erklärt hingegen: „Der KI-Kontrollverlust ist kein einzelnes Ereignis. Er ist schleichend. Wir übergeben Entscheidungen an Systeme, deren Ausgaben niemand mehr im Einzelnen prüft und die mit Werkzeugen im digitalen Raum agieren. Irgendwann fehlen uns die Zeit und die technischen Möglichkeiten, sie zurückzuholen.“ Das könne erst recht passieren, wenn ganze Agentenschwärme mit persistentem Aufgabenerfüllungstrieb auf Probleme losgelassen würden, zu deren Lösung sie dann schädliche Mittel wie Hacking einsetzen. „Der Vorfall bei OpenAI und Hugging Face ist dafür ein Beispiel und kein Ausreißer“, so Hagendorff.
Man muss Amodei nicht glauben, dass er es gut meint. Es reicht schon, zumindest zur Kenntnis zu nehmen, dass die Leute, die diese Systeme bauen, gerade mehr Angst vor ihnen haben als die, die sie benutzen.

articles.title: Natural seasons, human seasons: An exploration by artist Meena Das Narayan
articles.text:
Natural seasons, human seasons: An exploration by artist Meena Das Narayan
In this photo essay, we showcase a range of artworks by artist Meena Das Narayan, along with insights from her creative journey.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,015 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
The Four Seasons Hotel at Embassy One, Bengaluru is featuring an exhibition titled The ‘Haveli’ Collection: A Celebration of Womanhood Through Art. See our earlier photo essay from its CUR8 Art Gallery here.
The exhibition represents a thematic journey that brings the changing colours and seasons of life onto canvas through the works of artist Meena Das Narayan. It explores the parallel between the cyclical changes of nature and the distinct phases of a woman’s life.
Art and design can help hotels resonate with local and international creative communities. Landscaping, commissioned installations, and curated exhibitions can take experience and storytelling to the next level, as seen in this photo essay. The monsoon rains add a new level of delight to the hotel’s courtyards and gardens, providing an additional apt metaphor for the ongoing exhibition.
The narrative of the exhibition is deeply relatable, and transcends cultural and geographical boundaries. Some of the exhibited artworks are featured in this photo essay from the luxury hotel, which is also host to original works by more than 25 contemporary Indian artists.
“At Four Seasons Bengaluru, we believe art has the ability to create meaningful connections and offer a space for reflection and discovery. The exhibition by Meena Das Narayan celebrates the many chapters, emotions, seasons, and experiences that shape a woman’s life,” says Biswajit Chakraborty, General Manager, Four Seasons Bengaluru.
The green of spring symbolises youth and the yellows of summer represent adulthood. The blue hues of monsoon reflect a woman’s journey in having a family of her own, and the red of autumn conveys accomplishment and reflection.
“When a viewer stands before one of these paintings and recognises a phase of her own life in the texture, colour or pose, a bridge of empathy is built. Art becomes a shared conversation. The collection thus invites every woman to feel seen, celebrated and deeply connected to the collective spirit of womanhood,” Narayan explains.
She was born in Delhi, studied in Pune, and then moved to Baghdad at the age of 13 when her father was posted there as an irrigation expert. “Though we read a lot about the wars in Iraq, their people are very kind and welcoming,” she tells YourStory.
“The experience of travel made me much more broad-minded. I got a little world of diverse cultures in the university itself,” she adds.
Her writing and artwork began after she moved back to Delhi and got married. “We then moved to Dubai, where I worked in the newspaper and magazine industry before starting my own luxury magazine,” Narayan says.
She enjoys painting in oils because of the depth it makes possible. “I also love watercolours,” she describes.
The idea for the painting series in a haveli or townhouse came from a friend’s suggestion. “There are many canvases in my house, which are in different stages of finishing. I complete an artwork whenever I feel in the mood,” she says, describing her creative process.
“Currently, 10 of the paintings in the series are on display, the others are already sold. I prefer to paint what I like, not what others tell me to paint,” Narayan affirms.
“Saleable art often suits the interiors of homes and offices. Other art delivers beauty and originality and can even be regarded as an investment,” she explains.
She feels the online medium has some shortcomings when it comes to appreciating and selling art. “Somehow, I feel that online photographs of artwork do not do full justice to the creation,” she observes.
Narayan is also writing books about her uncle and great-grandfather, who were accomplished in the cultural fields. She runs a YouTube channel with commentary and analysis, and co-founded the Bangalore Club for Kathakali and the Arts (BCKA).
“I have directed and produced mythological operas which have Sanskrit songs, and music that is appealing to youngsters,” she adds. Another upcoming project is her second cultural movie, on the Yakshagana traditional theater and dance-drama art form from the coastal districts of Karnataka and Kerala.
An important decision many artists have to take is whether to sell a painting or keep it. “My paintings are my babies, I love seeing them. But if they go to a house where they are appreciated, that makes me happy as well,” she describes.
“It is important to move on in art, and in life. You have to know when to cut your connections – even in life, your children go and your mother goes. You just have to accept these things,” Narayan comments.
She has now come back to India from Dubai to look after her mother. “She is 91, and doesn't have anyone to look after her. I am very attached to her, this is my duty. It gives me fulfilment to look after her and see her smiling,” she says.
“I don't want to be too rich. Too much money can lead to burdens and less of happiness, though it may seem to give people a jet-setting lifestyle,” she says.
She has also curated exhibitions at the Leela Palace in Bengaluru. Last year, she curated an exhibition at The Four Seasons called Threads of Tradition, with the works of seven artists.
The lineup included Krishna Shetty CS, V Hariraam, Paresh Hazra, Shraddha Rathi, Ganesh Doddamani, and SG Vasudev. Collectively, they showcased abstract works, everyday life, folk themes, identity, and a blend of traditional and modern life.
Narayan cautions aspiring artists that it can be hard to make a living only with art. “You may need to have another job to support you – if you have that, you can do what you like and won’t be curtailed by what other artists tell you,” she advises.
“From a very young age, I hated being dictated at. I did not want to listen to people, because if you listen to others, you are molding yourself to their tastes – even if they are your own parents,” Narayan signs off.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at The Four Seasons Hotel at Embassy One, Bengaluru.)

articles.title: Microsoft: September updates cause RDS failures on Windows Server
articles.text:
Microsoft has confirmed reports that the September 2026 security updates cause Remote Desktop Services (RDS) failures on Windows Server systems.
According to a release health update on Friday, this known issue impacts Windows Server 2012 and later, as well as Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices.
This confirmation follows widespread reports from Windows admins that installing this month's Patch Tuesday updates prevents users from connecting and, in some cases, requires a hard reset to restore functionality.
"In some environments, RDS might become unstable, resulting in RDP connections failing after several minutes, sign-in issues, or servers hanging at 'Please wait for the Remote Desktop Configuration'," Microsoft said on Friday.
"Related tools, including Microsoft Management Console (MMC), RDS Licensing Diagnoser, and File Explorer might also become unresponsive. Additionally, the Windows Update page might stop responding and continuously display a loading indicator."
Affected users have also found that once a server starts failing, existing Remote Desktop sessions may not disconnect or log off properly, while new connection attempts may also fail after hanging during the connection process.
Mitigation available
Microsoft now provides the following Group Policy (found under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates), which can be used to mitigate the issue on enterprise-managed devices managed by IT departments:
- Windows 11 26H1: Windows 11 26H1 KB5124012 260912_00471 Group Policy
- Windows 11 25H2 and Windows 11 24H2: Windows 11 24H2, Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 KB5124008 260911_19322 Group policy
- Windows 11 23H2: Windows 11 22H2 KB5122880 260912_00473 Group Policy
- Windows 10 21H2 and 22H2: Windows 10 20H2, 21H1, 21H2 and 22H2 KB5122878 260911_18476 Group Policy
- Windows Server 2025: Windows Server 2025 KB5122871 260911_18472 Group Policy
- Windows Server 2022: Windows Server 2022 KB5122882 260911_18471 Group Policy
- Windows 10 1809 and Windows Server 2019: Windows 10 1809 and Windows Server 2019 KB5122876 260911_18474 Group Policy
- Windows 10 1607 and Windows Server 2016: Windows 10 1607 and Windows Server 2016 KB5123099 260911_18473 Group Policy
- Windows Server 2012: Windows Server 2012 KB5123065 260911_18475 Group Policy
- Windows Server 2012 R2: Windows 8.1 and Windows Server 2012 R2 KB5123066 260911_18477 Group Policy
While it still works to ship a permanent fix for this issue, Microsoft said those who can't access virtual machines through RDP may be able to temporarily restore RDS connectivity by stopping and restarting the affected virtual machine.
Windows admins have also been able to restore Remote Desktop functionality by rolling back the buggy updates. However, removing them will also remove the security fixes included in this month's Patch Tuesday release.
Microsoft fixed a similar known issue that triggered Remote Desktop and RDS connection failures in March 2025 after installing Windows updates released since January 2025.

articles.title: Pirater un Boeing 737 en 60 secondes : ce minuscule boîtier peut permettre de détourner un avion
articles.text:
Des chercheurs de l’Université de Californie à San Diego (UCSD) et d’Oberlin College ont découvert le moyen de pirater un Boeing 737. Pour arriver à leurs fins, les chercheurs se sont munis d’un petit boîtier électronique. Avec celui-ci, ils ont démontré que le piratage de l’avion ne prenait pas plus de 60 secondes.
A lire aussi : Une batterie externe a obligé un avion à se poser d’urgence à 1 472 km de sa destination
Intrusion sur le tarmac
L’attaque imaginée par les chercheurs débute sur le tarmac, entre deux vols ou pendant une opération de maintenance. En profitant du moment où l’avion se trouve au sol, l’attaquant peut accéder à la baie qui rassemble une partie des équipements électroniques de l’engin. Dans cette section, les chercheurs ont en effet identifié un port de maintenance inutilisé.
Atteignable depuis le sol derrière une trappe extérieure qui n’est généralement pas verrouillée, le port désigne une prise technique prévue pour les opérations d’entretien. Les techniciens utilisent ce type de connecteur pour contrôler le bon fonctionnement de certains équipements, lire ou tester les données qui circulent, effectuer des vérifications lors des opérations de maintenance, ou encore brancher ponctuellement un appareil de mesure ou de diagnostic. En l’occurrence, elle donne accès à des lignes de communication internes.
Une menace de la taille d’une pièce de monnaie
Selon les chercheurs, il ne faut pas plus d’une minute pour installer leur dispositif sur la prise de maintenance. Le boîtier sur lequel repose l’attaque n’est pas plus grand qu’une pièce de monnaie. L’outil est donc particulièrement discret et facile à transporter sur la piste de décollage.
Par ailleurs, le boîtier est plutôt abordable. Il ne coûte pas plus de 100 dollars à fabriquer. Il est composé d’un microcontrôleur, de composants électroniques adaptés au réseau de bord de l’avion, et d’une puce Wi-Fi. Une fois placé dans le port visé, il peut rester caché sous le capuchon qui protège habituellement le connecteur de maintenance, à l’abri des regards.
« On peut y accéder sans outil particulier en une quinzaine de secondes, explique Stefan Savage, professeur d’informatique et l’un des responsables du projet », à Wired.
Le port ciblé par les chercheurs donne accès à un réseau filaire interne qui repose sur le protocole ARINC 429. Largement utilisé dans l’aviation, il sert à faire circuler des informations entre les différents ordinateurs de l’avion. Il relie notamment le Flight Management Computer, qui gère des données de navigation, de trajectoire et de performances, au Multipurpose Control Display Unit, le système qui permet aux pilotes d’interagir avec certains paramètres.
Un protocole qui remonte aux années 1970
Les chercheurs pointent du doigt l’ancienneté de ce protocole. Né dans les années 1970, il est dépourvu d’un mécanisme de chiffrement qui protégerait les messages échangés entre les ordinateurs de l’avion. Le système sait lire l’information, mais il ne peut pas vérifier que son expéditeur est bien l’ordinateur autorisé en amont. De facto, le dispositif placé par un éventuel attaquant pourrait envoyer des commandes sur les ordinateurs de l’avion.
Baptisée « Bus Driver » par les chercheurs, la méthode d’attaque a été mise au point au terme d’une décennie de recherches intensives. Pendant plusieurs années, ils ont acheté sur le marché de l’occasion des pièces authentiques provenant de divers Boeing 737. Ils ont ainsi pu reconstruire une partie de l’informatique de bord de l’avion, de manière à pouvoir réaliser leurs expérimentations.
Ce laboratoire miniature, baptisé Triton, leur a coûté plusieurs dizaines de milliers de dollars. En épluchant des centaines de pages de schémas électriques, l’équipe a fini par repérer la prise extérieure reliée au réseau interne de l’appareil. Cette découverte est à l’origine de la tactique de piratage mise au point. Par la suite, ils ont développé et fabriqué le dispositif adéquat pour se connecter à la prise en toute discrétion.
Une trajectoire modifiée
Une fois branché, l’implant pourrait permettre à un attaquant de modifier le plan de vol de l’avion. Le pilote pourrait être poussé à suivre une trajectoire différente, ce qui éloignerait progressivement le Boeing 737 de sa destination. En théorie, le boîtier pourrait permettre de détourner l’avion en le faisant passer dans l’espace aérien de pays bien précis.
Par ailleurs, l’attaque risque de perturber la préparation du décollage. Avant de quitter la piste, les pilotes et les systèmes de bord calculent plusieurs paramètres essentiels : le poids de l’avion, la répartition des passagers et des bagages, la température extérieure ou encore la longueur de la piste. Ces données permettent de déterminer la puissance à demander aux moteurs et la vitesse à laquelle l’avion doit décoller. Si un pirate parvenait à modifier ces informations, le système pourrait croire que l’avion est moins lourd qu’il ne l’est vraiment, ou que l’air est plus froid, ce qui pourrait entraver le bon déroulement du décollage.
À lire aussi : Pourquoi un bracelet connecté a obligé un avion à faire demi-tour en plein vol
Un risque réel faible
Les chercheurs précisent que l’attaque est particulièrement complexe à mettre en place, et à mener à son terme. Il faut énormément de préparation et de repérage. Néanmoins, ils ont prévenu Boeing dès le printemps 2020, afin de laisser au constructeur le temps d’examiner le problème avant toute divulgation publique. Interrogé par Wired, le constructeur affirme avoir étudié les expériences réalisées, et estime que le scénario décrit par les chercheurs reste difficile à mettre en œuvre. Boeing estime que les protections intégrées à l’appareil, les contrôles au sol et les procédures d’exploitation limitent fortement les risques d’une attaque de cet acabit.
« Nos experts estiment que les multiples protections intégrées à l’avion, tant dans la conception de ses systèmes que dans son exploitation, réduisent fortement la faisabilité et le risque d’attaques réelles », déclare Boeing.
Les chercheurs recommandent néanmoins à la société de retirer ou condamner physiquement le connecteur vulnérable et d’ajouter un mécanisme de chiffrement sur tous les avions. Les scientifiques précisent qu’ils continuent de voyager « régulièrement à bord d’un Boeing 737 et prévoient de continuer à le faire ».

articles.title: Caminar o subir escaleras a partir de los 60: la ciencia tiene claro qué ejercicio exige más a tus piernas
articles.text:
La actividad física diaria es fundamental para mantener un buen tono muscular y disfrutar de todos sus beneficios a largo plazo con el objetivo de contar con unos cuantos años más de vida en óptimas condiciones. Pero dentro de las actividades diarias puede haber preguntas sobre qué ejercicio es el más adecuado, destacando sobre todo el caminar o el subir las escaleras.
El duelo biomecánico. La explicación biomecánica de que las escaleras exigen más fuerza por paso es completamente razonable, puesto que al subir un escalón, nos vemos obligados a elevar nuestro centro de masas contra la gravedad, lo que impone una demanda significativamente mayor a los músculos extensores de la rodilla y la cadera.
Y lo estudios de intervención respaldan esta exigencia extra, como por ejemplo un ensayo piloto realizado con 45 personas mayores de 65 años con movilidad limitada, donde se demostró que 12 semanas subiendo y bajando escaleras con un chaleco lastrado produjeron una mejora del 17% en la potencia máxima de la prensa de piernas frente a un programa centrado únicamente en caminar.
Y hay más. La evidencia más reciente es aún más precisa, puesto que un ensayo aleatorizado de 2025 con 46 adultos mayores comparó el entrenamiento de escaleras con el de fuerza en máquinas. Ambos mejoraron la potencia de las piernas y la capacidad funcional, y aunque las escaleras no demostraron poder sustituir por completo a las máquinas de gimnasio, sí dejaron claro que son un estímulo útil, específico y altamente funcional para el día a día.
Un buen paseo. Presentar el acto de caminar como un ejercicio irrelevante para ganar fuerza es un error, puesto que un ensayo aleatorizado de 17 semanas en adultos mayores no entrenados reveló que un programa progresivo de caminata aumentó el grosor de los músculos del muslo y la fuerza isométrica de la rodilla. De hecho, en este estudio, añadir escaleras no produjo una ventaja adicional estadísticamente significativa frente a la caminata progresiva.
El problema de las escaleras. Cuando se llega a cierta edad, hay cierto miedo por subir y sobre todo por bajar las escaleras. Y la afirmación de que bajar las escaleras molesta más es clínicamente plausible, puesto que el cuádriceps debe trabajar para frenar al cuerpo, lo que resulta exigente para rodillas débiles o con artrosis, como explica también el Dr. Alberto Sanagustín, como recoge 20 minutos.
Pero esto no quiere decir que las escaleras causen artrosis, puesto que la evidencia observacional no demuestra causalidad. Y aunque un estudio de 2024 halló una asociación modesta entre subir más de 150 escalones diarios y un mayor riesgo posterior de artrosis, existen múltiples factores que influyen. Es por ello que lo mejor no es dejar las escaleras, sino adaptar el ejercicio usando menos altura o apoyarse si hay dolor.
La recomendación de la OMS. Lo que se apunta en las guías oficiales es la necesidad de hacer entre 150 y 300 minutos semanales de actividad aeróbica moderada, y dos días a la semana hay que fortalecer los grandes grupos musculares, como los de las piernas. Además, en las personas más mayores se necesita también tener en mente los ejercicios de equilibrio para poder evitar posibles caídas que a ciertas edades son fatales.

articles.title: Le Xiaomi 18 Pro dévoile une plus grosse caméra mais surtout un nouveau bouton un peu spécial
articles.text:
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro dévoile une plus grosse caméra mais surtout un nouveau bouton un peu spécial
À quelques semaines de sa présentation, le Xiaomi 18 Pro se dévoile et plusieurs images nous montrent une caméra bien plus imposante, mais surtout un bouton un peu spécial.
Les images, qui restent à prendre avec des pincettes, nous montrent un Xiaomi 18 Pro qui ressemble fortement au Xiaomi 17 Pro. C’est surtout au niveau de la taille de la caméra bien plus grande que la différence se fait au niveau esthétique. Mais la grosse nouveauté, c’est un quatrième bouton qui apparaît sur la tranche et serait totalement dédié à l’IA.
Le Xiaomi 18 Pro aura un bouton dédié à l'IA
Xiaomi 18 Pro case leak 👀
Looks like Xiaomi is going with a bigger camera setup and adding a new AI button on the side. 
What do you think of this design? pic.twitter.com/Z5u6OVGzY7
Selon plusieurs sources, le Xiaomi 18 Pro s’équiperait de deux capteurs de 200 mégapixels. Le premier serait l’appareil photo principal avec une grande surface sensible à la lumière. Le second se trouverait derrière un téléobjectif périscopique. Et pour finir, le Xiaomi 18 Pro aurait le droit à un ultra-grand-angle de 50 mégapixels.
Forcément, avec deux capteurs de 200 mégapixels, la caméra est bien plus grosse, comme nous le montrent ces images fuitées. Les précédentes fuites parlent aussi d’un capteur principal SmartSens avec technologie LOFIC pour garder les détails dans les zones très claires et très sombres d’une image.
Mais la plus grosse nouveauté, c’est que les images montrent un emplacement pour un quatrième bouton sur la tranche du Xiaomi 18 Pro. Il s’agirait d’un raccourci pour lancer rapidement les fonctionnalités IA sans chercher dans les paramètres d’HyperOS. Mais le bouton pourrait aussi être utilisé pour gérer les appareils connectés et voitures Xiaomi compatibles. En gros, une commande directe pour tout l’écosystème du constructeur.
Une présentation attendue à la fin du mois
Mais pour le moment, cette information reste à prendre avec des pincettes puisque si l’image nous montre l’existence d’un bouton sur la tranche, on ne sait pas encore ce qu’il se passera quand on appuie dessus. Que ce soit une pression rapide ou longue.
Pour le reste de la fiche technique, les fuites évoquent un processeur Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 de Qualcomm gravé en 2 nm, une batterie d’environ 7 000 mAh et une recharge filaire de 100 W. L’écran situé à l’arrière, introduit par le Xiaomi 17 Pro, ferait son retour avec de nouvelles fonctionnalités.
On attend la présentation du Xiaomi 18 Pro pour ce mois de septembre 2026 en Chine. Pour la commercialisation en Europe, Xiaomi n'a encore rien communiqué.

articles.title: Revolut piégée par des escrocs : les pirates menacent de publier chaque jour de nouveaux dossiers clients - Numerama
articles.text:
C’est une notification envoyée vendredi 11 septembre à un nombre restreint de clients qui a mis le feu aux poudres, avant d’être relayée sur Telegram par le chercheur en cybersécurité ZachXBT.
Le lendemain, la néobanque britannique a confirmé les faits auprès de TechCrunch : un tiers non autorisé a réussi à se faire passer pour une agence gouvernementale légitime afin d’obtenir des informations sur certains comptes.
Revolut, qui revendique plus de 80 millions d’utilisateurs répartis dans une trentaine de pays, évoquait un nombre « limité » de clients concernés, sans avancer de chiffre précis, ni préciser le pays ni le nom de l’agence usurpée.
Mais depuis le dimanche 13 septembre, l’affaire a pris une nouvelle tournure : ceux qui détiendraient les dossiers ont commencé à publier des supposés échantillons sur Telegram. Le piratage vire au chantage. Les hackers assurent qu’ils continueront à publier chaque jour de nouveaux dossiers tant que Revolut ne paiera pas une rançon, dont le montant n’a pas été rendu public.
Pas de piratage technique, mais une usurpation par mail
Pour rappel, contrairement à ce que l’on pourrait imaginer, cette fuite ne repose sur aucune faille informatique ni malware sophistiqué. L’auteur des faits a simplement envoyé sa demande depuis une adresse mail hébergée sur le vrai domaine de l’agence gouvernementale visée, ce qui lui a permis de passer les vérifications d’authenticité habituelles.
Revolut, comme n’importe quelle banque soumise à des réquisitions régulières de la police ou de la justice, a traité la demande comme légitime et y a répondu en conséquence, avant de découvrir la supercherie en recontactant l’agence de son côté, mais après coup, une fois les documents déjà transmis. Une véritable erreur.
Des zones d’ombre qui persistent
Selon ZachXBT, les personnes visées seraient surtout des clients disposant d’avoirs conséquents, une piste que Revolut n’a pas confirmée officiellement.
Le premier dossier rendu public concernerait un entrepreneur crypto : les attaquants auraient diffusé ce qu’ils présentent comme son dossier de vérification d’identité complet, avec un document allemand visible sur les captures. D’autres clients avaient déjà fait savoir publiquement avoir reçu la notification officielle de Revolut, parmi lesquels l’ancien patron de Mt. Gox Mark Karpelès, qui a détaillé le contenu exact du dossier envoyé par erreur : nom, date de naissance, métier, adresse, téléphone, pièce d’identité, selfie, relevés bancaires, IBAN, date d’ouverture de compte, référence de wallet, retraits et historique complet des transactions, bitcoin compris.
De son côté, Revolut n’a pour l’instant communiqué ni sur le nombre exact de clients touchés, ni sur la date d’envoi des données.
L’entreprise recommande aux personnes notifiées de surveiller leurs comptes, de se méfier de tout contact se réclamant de la banque, et d’envisager le renouvellement de leurs papiers d’identité.

articles.title: Une IA de la NASA et d’IBM part à la chasse à la glace sur la Lune
articles.text:
Un nouveau modèle ouvert doit aider les chercheurs à repérer plus vite les zones lunaires les plus intéressantes. Derrière la cartographie, l’enjeu est surtout de trouver les ressources nécessaires à de futurs séjours prolongés sur la Lune.
Deux millions d’échantillons pour mieux savoir où poser les yeux sur la Lune. La NASA et IBM viennent de publier leur Lunar Foundation Model, une IA conçue pour accélérer l’analyse des données lunaires et repérer des zones susceptibles d’abriter de la glace, de nouveaux cratères ou, encore, des traces d’activité volcanique. Mais outre l’aspect scientifique, cette IA pourrait surtout aider l’agence spatiale américaine à préparer les prochaines missions habitées. Quitte à atterrir et à séjourner sur la Lune, autant le faire à proximité d’un gisement potentiel de glace d’eau.
Une même IA pour lire plusieurs visages de la Lune
Lunar Foundation Model adapte aux observations lunaires la méthode d’apprentissage de TerraMind. Ce modèle repose sur un encodeur visuel ViT-B associé à un décodeur de type Transformer. Entraîné à partir de zéro sur près de deux millions d’échantillons, il combine des images, notamment de la sonde Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, à différentes définitions jusqu’à un mètre par pixel avec des informations sur le relief, les températures et l’éclairage.
Pendant l’apprentissage, certaines données ont été masquées et l’IA a dû les reconstruire à partir des autres observations pour apprendre les relations entre ces mesures. La position du Soleil faisait également partie des paramètres fournis, afin de mieux interpréter les ombres qui modifient fortement l’apparence du terrain. Les chercheurs ont pu ensuite spécialiser cette base dans la détection de cratères, de formations volcaniques ou, encore, la recherche de zones favorables à la glace, sans recommencer tout l’entraînement.
Lors d’une démonstration, l’IA a retrouvé le cratère formé près du cratère Einstein par l’impact d’un étage supérieur de Falcon 9, le 5 août 2026. Un exemple de sa capacité à faire ressortir automatiquement des formations difficiles à repérer dans d’immenses volumes d’images.
Trouver de la glace pour pouvoir rester plus longtemps sur la Lune
La recherche de glace est évidemment le volet le plus stratégique. Si elle peut être extraite et traitée sur place, l’eau lunaire servirait à alimenter les équipages, produire de l’oxygène et, potentiellement, fabriquer certains propergols. De quoi réduire une partie des ravitaillements depuis la Terre.
Évitons toutefois de transformer ce modèle en baguette de sourcier. Lunar Foundation Model identifiera surtout les zones où les conditions semblent favorables à la conservation de glace ; cette IA ne mesurera pas directement la présence d’un dépôt. Sa documentation précise d’ailleurs que ce modèle n’est pas destiné à valider un site d’alunissage ni à évaluer seul les risques d’une mission.
L’intelligence artificielle peut donc indiquer où regarder, mais pour découvrir ce qui se cache réellement sous le régolithe de la Lune, il faudra désormais y renvoyer des astronautes et les laisser gratter la surface.

The fight against automation is ultimately one many won’t be able to resist. Caxton Group , a South African newspaper group, recently told shareholders that it is piloting AI for copy-editing as revenue declines. Speaking of things happening in media, we’re also looking to hear from people who made meaningful connections at Moonshot. Maybe you found a co-founder, landed your dream job, met an investor, found a new partner, raised funding, or met someone who became an important part of your journey. Subscribe Uber defends UberX decision in SA ‘Too important to fail’ Bidvest suffers attack Carrefour’s Kenya moment World Wide Web 3 Opportunities Ride-hailing Uber defends decision to discontinue UberX in South Africa Image Source: Tenor You must have rolled your eyes seeing Uber, the ride-hailing giant, in the news again. I did, too. But with the rate of these operational changes happening, market shutdowns, layoffs, and work-from-home (WFH) scaleback, I’d have assumed the coincidence was too good to be true, and this was probably some well-executed media run. This time, Uber is out to defend a critical business decision it made in South Africa. What happened? South Africa’s drivers’ union says Uber’s decision to discontinue UberX on September 1 could put drivers out of work . The union estimates that more than 60% of its drivers may not qualify for Uber’s remaining categories. Uber says drivers can continue using the platform if their cars qualify for another category. Doom and gloom? One thing’s for sure: the drivers’ union has a point. Compared with markets Uber has exited , such as Nigeria, South Africa is a much bigger market for the company. Uber is the market leader there, competing with Bolt and Wanatu . The company likely has more drivers than the others and network effects to protect; it also means changes to its platform can have a much bigger effect on the same drivers. UberX was built around everyday cars, including Toyota Corollas and Hyundai Accents. UberGo accepts older cars, while Comfort requires newer ones. Some drivers could fall through the gap. A day after Uber left Nigeria, I spoke with a marketing executive visiting the country for the first time. He was disappointed. After spending a lot of time in South Africa, he had grown used to Uber and felt its service was more reliable and consistent than some alternatives. Perhaps Germany offers a useful lesson. The marketing executive, who had also recently been in Germany, said UberX cars were mostly Mercedes-Benz vehicles. That wasn’t always the case. When Uber entered Germany in 2013, it struggled to attract riders who were used to being picked up in taxis, often in luxury Mercedes-Benz cars. Uber eventually adapted its model by working with licenced taxi and private-hire companies to fit the market. Now, Uber is testing autonomous cars in Munich. In South Africa, it is simply a case of Uber refusing to drop the standard for UberX tiers. Uber has replaced UberX with cheaper UberGo and higher-end Comfort, creating clearer tiers while pushing some drivers towards categories that require newer cars. And the introduction of UberGo is instructive. Previously, the company didn’t operate this tier in South Africa, whereas countries like Kenya have UberChapChap , which is comparable. Nigeria had the UberX Share (Basic) option. Two things can be true: The union is right to worry about jobs. But Uber is signalling it won’t compromise its standards if drivers can’t meet them. The only question is why the company is reacting now. But well, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi did promise cheaper rides after the global restructuring ; perhaps this is the hand we’re now being dealt. Every business owner needs to watch this. The business questions you Google, answered by experts. Watch for free . banking Kenya’s biggest banks could face tougher rules under new proposal Image Source: Reddit Imagine waking up one morning to find that one of Kenya’s biggest banks has collapsed. Your money might still be protected, but businesses could struggle to make payments, other financial institutions could take a hit, and confidence in the banking system could start wobbling. That’s called a bank run, and it is the kind of situation the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) wants to prevent. What happened? On Friday, the CBK proposed a new framework for identifying Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs). What are D-SIBs, you ask? These are banks whose failure could cause serious disruption to Kenya’s financial system and wider economy. The CBK wants to identify banks that are too interconnected, complex, or difficult to replace for their failure to be treated like an ordinary bank collapse. The regulator said it would assess banks based on four factors: size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity. Explain like I’m new here: Kenya already has a robust regulatory setup for banks. CBK licences and supervises commercial banks, mortgage finance companies, microfinance banks, and other financial institutions under the Banking Act and its prudential guidelines. Banks must meet minimum capital and liquidity requirements. Kenya raised its minimum capital requirement for commercial banks from KES 1 billion ($7.7 million) to KES 3 billion ($23.3 million), effective December 2025, under the Business Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024. The increase is being implemented progressively, with the requirement initially set to rise to KES 5 billion ($38.7 million) by December 2026, KES 6 billion ($47.4 million) by 2027, KES 8 billion ($61.9 million) by 2028, and KES 10 billion ($77.4 million) by 2029. By the end of March 2026, four banks —Credit Bank, Consolidated Bank of Kenya, Development Bank of Kenya, and Access Bank Kenya—were still below the $23.2 million threshold. As of June 2026, the banking sector’s total capital adequacy ratio was 20% , comfortably above CBK’s 14.5% minimum. Its liquidity ratio was 61.2% , more than three times the 20% minimum. What changes? If a bank is designated a D-SIB, it must hold additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Depending on how systemically important the bank is, the additional requirement is pegged at 0.5% to 2.5% of risk-weighted assets . The more important the bank, the bigger the cushion. D-SIBs would also face more intensive supervision, quarterly stress tests, and annual assessments of whether they have enough capital and liquidity to survive major shocks. There’s more: The proposed framework would also subject D-SIBs to enhanced supervision and require recovery and resolution plans. A recovery plan sets out the actions management could take if the bank comes under severe stress, while a resolution plan helps authorities deal with the bank if failure becomes unavoidable. CBK wants D-SIBs to identify these actions and contingency arrangements before a crisis hits, and submit updated plans every year by April 30. Why should you care? Stronger capital buffers could make Kenya’s banking system more resilient. For investors, D-SIB designations will also show which banks face extra capital requirements, potentially affecting their lending capacity, dividends, and valuations. No bank has been designated yet. CBK is consulting the public on the framework, with comments due by November 7. Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world! True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Banking South African lender Bidvest Bank is dealing with a data breach as it seeks a buyer Image Source: Zikoko Memes Remember Bidvest, that South African bank that Nigerian tier-1 lender Access Bank tried to acquire before the deal collapsed ? Well, it’s back in the news, this time over a data breach. What happened? Bidvest Bank, which offers personal, business, fleet, and foreign exchange (FX) services, said a third-party service provider suffered a cyber incident that may have exposed some of its data. The bank does not yet know which customers are affected or exactly what information was accessed. Its own banking systems were not affected, and accounts and services are operating normally. Why it matters: Bidvest is already in an unusual position. Its parent company, Bidvest Group, is trying to sell the bank after its R2.8 billion ($798 million) deal with Access Bank fell through in January because some conditions, including regulatory approvals, were not met. Bidvest relaunched the sale process and said in August that talks with potential buyers were continuing. The timing makes the breach worth watching, even though there is no evidence yet that it will affect the sale. Bidvest noted that an independent forensic investigation is still trying to establish what happened. There is also a useful recent warning. Standard Bank, South Africa’s largest lender, suffered a breach in March. While initially it said only limited customer data had been exposed , it later found in April that some credit card details had also leaked online. Standard Bank hasn’t updated on the recovery process since then. Bidvest is already telling customers to watch their accounts and beware of scammers pretending to be the bank. The bank may not know the full extent of the breach yet, but criminals will not need much information to make a convincing phishing attempt. Ecommerce Carrefour Kenya’s revenue increased by over $45 million in 2025 Image Source: Tenor Kenya’s supermarket business has become more interesting. Big players are expanding, but there are only so many customers to go around. Carrefour appears to have found a comfortable seat. What happened? Carrefour Kenya, the local arm of the French supermarket giant, recorded KES 48.84 billion ($378 million) in revenue in 2025, up from KES 42.95 billion ($322.6 million) the previous year. The supermarket chain in Kenya made KES 5.89 billion ($45.6 million) in its latest reporting year, Dubai-based operator Majid Al Futtaim revealed. The growth comes as Carrefour expands its footprint. It opened eight new stores in Kenya in 2025, taking its total to 34, and plans to add another eight by December this year. Explain like I’m new here: Carrefour entered Kenya in 2016, just as the country’s supermarket industry was beginning to unravel. Nakumatt, Tuskys, and Uchumi had once been among Kenya’s biggest supermarket chains, but years of debt, cash flow problems, and management troubles eventually brought them down . Nakumatt closed its final stores in 2020 after accumulating more than $296 million in debt. Tuskys’ last branch shut down in 2023 , owing roughly KES 19.6 billion ($151.8 million). Their collapse left a huge gap in Kenya’s formal retail market. Naivas and Quickmart expanded to fill it, while Carrefour came with international scale and experience at an opportune time. Since 2020, the three chains have collectively opened dozens of new outlets. How are the rivals doing? Naivas is still the heavyweight. It had 108 outlets at the end of its 2025 financial year and reported KES 2.45 billion ($18.9 million) in profit. Quickmart has a smaller footprint, with more than 70 stores, but it is expanding too. Carrefour is playing the same game. Its 34 stores now put it firmly among Kenya’s three biggest modern grocery chains, which together account for roughly 36–42% of the country’s modern grocery retail market. Why should you care? The competition eventually reaches your shopping basket. When Naivas, Quickmart, and Carrefour compete for the same customers, they have to offer promotions, wider product ranges, and competitive prices. Each chain has to give shoppers a reason to choose it over the others. articles.title: The Race to Control AI and Protect What Makes Us Human
articles.text:
A current debate is whether artificial intelligence (AI) is a force for good or bad; or perhaps both.
What follows is the argued opinion of the author – it is not the inevitable outcome of current AI development.
On August 26, 2026, Bill Gates published a 6,000 word memo on his personal website, titled The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical. It starts, “The transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history. Right now, we are not preparing adequately for that transition. If the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.”
The implication is that AI contains danger if we don’t behave responsibly toward it, but that we can and will probably learn to behave responsibly. Overall, AI is likely to be a force for good.
Not everybody agrees. Responding to a tweet on X from Jacob Coxon, Evan Hubinger (a safety researcher at Anthropic leading the firm’s Alignment Science org) replied on September 9, 2026, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”
Could Misaligned AI Kill Us All?
Coxon, a former AI researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic, had suggested “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Hubinger’s reply focuses on ‘alignment’, saying we cannot yet control it. Alignment in AI is the assurance that AI actions are tied to its developer’s intentions. Misalignment, in the vernacular, is what allows AI models to go rogue – to take unintended actions that can result in attacking unintended targets. Hubinger is saying that we are not on track to solving this problem.
The problem would be worsened if we achieve, but misalign, future Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). AGI is an ill-defined concept that effectively implies artificial intelligence that can match or surpass human capabilities across all cognitive tasks and economic domains. Misaligned AGI could lead to a technological singularity where the technology accelerates beyond human control; that is, the AI will begin to ‘reprogram’ itself by itself.
This is the potential result if we fail Gates’ warning to take the right steps today. But market forces work against this. Quite simply, the developer of the most powerful AI is likely to become the most powerful and richest developer of AI. AI has been advancing at a phenomenal speed, and nobody really knows where it is going.
The debate between the potential effect of this is widening. Stephen Cobb, a former senior security researcher at ESET, and now an independent researcher, said on LinkedIn, “We’ve been told: ‘The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.’ To which I say: Not unless we allow it or enable it,” (taking the Gates’ line of thought).
Dan Tynan responded, “Neither will cigarettes. You have to stick them in your mouth and light them. But the companies making cigarettes knew about the dangers for decades, and hid them, knowing that their product was so addictive, and so pervasive, it would overcome people’s normal inclination towards self-preservation.” Cobb believes in humanity’s good sense, while Tynan believes in market forces.
There is, however, one promising sign for the future. OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman is not an innocent in AI. On September 11, 2026, Bloomberg reported: “OpenAI said it has slowed parts of model development and paused certain internal AI training recently due to safety concerns. In July, Altman also said that he’d spoken with White House officials about the ‘need’ to pace AI development.”
Altman sat down with Fortune’s Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell to discuss the high-stakes balancing act of AI in an episode that aired on Saturday, September 12th (embedded below).
It seems the AI developers are recognizing the potential danger of headlong development. It may be that Gates’ request for doing the right thing now may yet be heeded, and we may still avert the destruction of the human species. But let us return to his 6,000 word memo.
“One preliminary survey,” he writes, “suggested that heavier AI use was associated with less critical thinking. The effect was stronger for younger people.” So even if we succeed in aligning AI models for only beneficial purposes, the effect is still likely to be a degradation in the human ability to reason for itself. It could be argued that the ability to reason is what distinguishes humanity from the world’s other animals. We may succeed in preventing the destruction of the human species by AI, but can we prevent the destruction of the distinguishing humanity of humans?
