articles.title: Après Pac-Man, Lego transforme une autre borne mythique en set collector
articles.text:
Après Pac-Man, Lego s’attaque à un autre monument du jeu vidéo d’arcade. Depuis peu, Lego propose en effet un nouveau set Donkey Kong Arcade, pensé comme un hommage XXL au jeu qui a vu naître Jumpman, le futur Mario.
Vous avez peut-être vécu cette époque (bénie), où quelques pièces de monnaie suffisaient à lancer une partie de Donkey Kong dans une salle d’arcade, dont l’odeur résultait souvent d’un doux mélange de sueur et de cigarette. Plus de quarante ans plus tard, le célèbre gorille de Nintendo retrouve une seconde jeunesse… sous forme de briques.
Une borne Lego qui promet de jouer avec la nostalgie
Le set en question porte la référence 72051 et reprend l’esthétique du jeu original de 1981, avec Donkey Kong donc, Jumpman (le Mario d’avant Mario) et les fameux éléments qui ont marqué toute une génération : les plateformes, les échelles, la demoiselle en détresse, les tonneaux…
Cette création n’est pas qu’un simple objet décoratif à exposer sur une étagère. Le set intègre plusieurs mécanismes mobiles, avec notamment un système permettant de faire descendre des tonneaux et de manipuler Jumpman à l’aide d’un joystick.
Des détails qui s’inscrivent parfaitement dans la nouvelle tendance de Lego à transformer les souvenirs vidéoludiques en véritables objets interactifs.
Une approche qui rappelle forcément d’autres créations récentes de la marque, comme le tout premier flipper Lego fonctionnel : un set rétro de 2 274 pièces qui pousse encore plus loin l’idée d’un objet de collection capable de réellement se manipuler. Une philosophie qui colle parfaitement à cette borne Donkey Kong Arcade.
Un nouveau morceau d’histoire vidéoludique à collectionner
La borne est d’ores et déjà disponible à la vente, avec un prix de vente calé à 169,99€. Le set compte précisément 1 367 pièces, ce qui le place clairement dans la catégorie des modèles destinés principalement aux adultes et aux collectionneurs plutôt qu’aux simples amateurs de briques.
Lego continue donc d’explorer son fructueux filon nostalgique en transformant les icônes du jeu vidéo en pièces de collection.
Après Pac-Man, la petite console Game Boy ou encore la NES (et bientôt la PlayStation de 1994), Donkey Kong pourrait donc bien devenir le prochain cadeau incontournable des joueurs ayant grandi dans les années 80/90.

articles.title: „Speicher voll" – der teuerste Hinweis auf deinem Smartphone
articles.text:
Speicher voll? Fünf smarte Wege, das Beste aus deinen Geräten herauszuholen
Schöne neue Welt: Wir teilen Urlaubsfotos noch vor Ort mit Freunden, laden das neue Lieblingsspiel direkt aus dem Store und drehen spontan ein Video in 4K. Dann erscheint plötzlich eine Meldung, die niemand sehen will: „Speicher voll“. Wer besonders knapp an freiem Speicher ist, kann unter Umständen nicht einmal mehr die Kamera oder Messenger-App öffnen. Also beginnt das große Aufräumen: Apps auslagern, alte Videos durchsehen, Screenshots und doppelte Dateien löschen. Das kostet Zeit und Nerven.
Das Problem kommt nicht von ungefähr. Der Datenverbrauch wächst rasant und mit ihm der Bedarf an Speicherplatz.¹ Smartphone-Kameras machen bessere Fotos, die wiederrum mehr Speicherplatz verbrauchen. Eine Minute 4K-Video kann schnell 400 MB belegen.² Aufwendige Spiele füllen mehrere Gigabyte. Gleichzeitig liegen laut einer Bitkom-Studie rund 167 Millionen alte Handys ungenutzt in deutschen Haushalten – viele davon ersetzt, obwohl sie noch funktionierten.³ Dabei lässt sich das Speicherproblem oft einfacher und günstiger lösen als mit einem Neugerät. Die richtigen Speicherlösungen können die Nutzungsdauer von Laptops, Smartphones und Konsolen verlängern.
1. Der Laptop streikt
Für viele ist der Laptop das wichtigste Arbeitsgerät. Speicherprobleme sind hier besonders ärgerlich: Updates bleiben hängen oder lassen sich gar nicht erst herunterladen, Programme starten quälend langsam. Wer kein gutes Ordnungssystem hat, steht beim Löschen von Daten schnell vor einer Mammutaufgabe. Besser also, wenn man sie gleich umgeht: Der SANDISK® Extreme Fit™ USB-C® Flash Drive ist kaum größer als eine Fingerkuppe, sodass er dauerhaft im USB-C-Anschluss stecken bleiben kann – ganz nach dem Prinzip „Plug & Stay“. Die kompakte Bauform geht nicht zulasten der Kapazität: Der Flash Drive bietet bis zu 1 TB Speicherplatz.⁴ Mit Lesegeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 400 MB/s⁵ lassen sich Dateien schnell übertragen und sind ganz ohne Cloud oder stabile Internetverbindung jederzeit zugänglich.
2. Das iPhone® absichern
Noch intensiver nutzen viele ihr Smartphone. Fotos und Videos konkurrieren mit Apps, Podcasts und Musikdateien um den verfügbaren Speicherplatz. Ist dann auch die Cloud voll, braucht es eine unkomplizierte Lösung für Backups. Schließlich schließen nur wenige ihr Handy regelmäßig an den Laptop an. Der SANDISK Phone Drive für iPhone® schafft Abhilfe. Nutzer können den Stick einfach ans iPhone anschließen und Fotos, Videos oder andere Backups mit bis zu 90 MB/s übertragen. Mit bis zu 256 GB¹ Kapazität bietet der Stick reichlich Platz für wichtige Daten.
3. Die Spielebibliothek wächst und wächst
Auch Videospiele verlangen immer mehr Speicherplatz. Die Spielwelten werden komplexer, die Dateien größer. Das Action-Game Split Fiction benötigt beispielsweise mehr als 70 GB. Da ist der interne Speicher der Handheld-Konsole schnell gefüllt. Wer Spiele nicht ständig auslagern und neu herunterladen möchte, kann sein Gaming-Setup mit der SANDISK GamePlay microSD™ Express-Karte um bis zu 512 GB erweitern. Die Karte erreicht Übertragungsgeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 880 MB/s.⁶ Dadurch verkürzen sich Ladezeiten und Spiele laufen flüssiger.
4. Unterwegs arbeiten, ohne Daten zu riskieren
Auf Reisen entstehen schnell große Datenmengen: Fotos und Videos von Stadtrundgängen, vom Strand oder aus den Bergen. Wer unterwegs noch arbeitet, füllt den Gerätespeicher im Handumdrehen. Gerade wenn nicht immer stabiles Internet verfügbar ist. Dabei sollen Bilder und Videos gesichert und jederzeit verfügbar bleiben – ob im Zug, im Hotel oder am Flughafen. Hier kommt die SANDISK Extreme® Portable SSD ins Spiel. Sie bietet bis zu 4 TB¹ Speicherplatz im kompakten Format. Mit Lesegeschwindigkeiten von bis zu 2.000 MB/s² lassen sich beispielsweise 1.000 hochauflösende Fotos in weniger als einer Minute⁷ übertragen. Die portable SSD ist gegen Wasser, Staub und Stürze aus bis zu drei Metern⁸ geschützt. Der Passwortschutz sowie die Hardwareverschlüsselung sorgen zudem dafür, dass die Daten noch sicherer bleiben – selbst wenn das Laufwerk verloren geht oder gestohlen wird.⁹
5. Überall Content drehen, schneiden und posten
Guter Content ist oft nicht geplant. In inspirierenden Momenten heißt es: Handy zücken und aufnehmen. Damit das Smartphone auch bei längeren hochauflösenden Videos mithält, braucht es eine Lösung, die direkt am Gerät sitzt, große Dateien speichert, wenn der interne Speicher schnell an seine Grenzen kommt, und einen reibungslosen Workflow ermöglicht. Hier kommt die SANDISK Creator Phone SSD ins Spiel. Sie lässt sich magnetisch an MagSafe®-kompatiblen Smartphones befestigen und speichert Aufnahmen direkt auf dem Laufwerk. Auf kompatiblen iPhones lassen sich auch Apple ProRes®-Videoaufnahmen in 4K mit 60 Bildern pro Sekunde speichern. Nach dem Dreh können die Dateien unmittelbar weiterbearbeitet werden. Das Silikongehäuse, der IP65-Schutz und der Fallschutz aus bis zu drei Metern Höhe⁸ machen die SSD zu einer robusten Begleiterin für mobile Drehs. Dank exFAT-Formatierung funktioniert sie mit Windows®, Android®, macOS® und iOS®.
Fazit: Mehr Platz, weniger Frust
Mangelnder Speicherplatz sollte nur selten ein Grund sein, ein funktionierendes Gerät zu ersetzen. Ob am Laptop im Büro, mit dem Smartphone im Urlaub, beim Gaming auf der Couch oder beim Dreh auf der Straße: Mit der passenden Speicherlösung von Sandisk lässt sich mehr aus vorhandener Hardware herausholen. So bleibt der Kopf frei für das, was wirklich zählt: Erinnerungen festhalten, neue Highscores und kreative Meilensteine erreichen.

articles.title: 6,89 kWh/100 km et 1278 km avec une recharge : on est monté à bord du concept VW Mission Efficiency - Numerama
articles.text:
C’était l’invité surprise des essais internationaux de la Volkswagen ID. Polo. Dans un coin de l’espace réservé par la marque se cachait un drôle d’engin qui n’était pas prévu au programme : le concept « Mission Efficiency ». Un coupé 2+2 de 4,77 m dont le design ne peut qu’attirer l’attention.
J’ai pu me glisser sur le siège conducteur et discuter avec l’équipe de développement de Wolfsburg pour comprendre l’idée derrière le concept. Il ne s’agit pas pour Volkswagen de créer un prototype uniquement pour battre des records, mais de montrer qu’il est possible d’obtenir ces performances avec des éléments de modèles déjà produits en série.
Le XL1 nouvelle génération
En 2013, pour créer la célèbre XL1 (qui consommait 0,9 l/100 km en cycle NEDC), Volkswagen avait sorti l’artillerie lourde : fibre de carbone, tarifs à six chiffres et production confidentielle.
En 2026, alors que l’industrie automobile s’obstine à corriger le manque d’efficience des véhicules en empilant des batteries de 100 kWh pouvant peser jusqu’à 700 kg, la Mission Efficiency prend exactement le chemin inverse : exploiter la banque de pièces d’une citadine populaire pour signer un record. Enfin, trois records plus précisément :
- Record d’aérodynamisme : un Cx de 0,158, établissant le niveau le plus bas au monde pour un véhicule homologué pour la route.
- Record d’efficience absolue : une consommation théorique minimale de 6,48 kWh/100 km mesurée lors d’un trajet idéal à vitesse constante (68 km/h), sur profil plat et sans climatisation.
- Record d’efficience réelle sur longue distance : un parcours de 1 278,36 km entre Wolfsburg et Vienne achevé avec une seule recharge intermédiaire, pour une consommation mesurée à 6,89 kWh/100 km (7,51 kWh/100 km en incluant les pertes à la prise).
De nombreux constructeurs s’attaquent à établir des records dans des domaines très précis, comme Lucid ou Mercedes. Volkswagen apparaît comme un constructeur de plus à se lancer dans la course aux records. Mais les détails du véhicule méritent le détour.
Un cousin de l’ID. Polo
Si le dessin aérodynamique impressionne, le plus captivant reste la recette technique utilisée sous cette robe de 4,77 m en forme de goutte d’eau :
- Organes de série : le train avant, le moteur électrique de 135 ch (99 kW) et la batterie de 54,9 kWh sont strictement repris de l’ID. Polo.
- L’effet traînée : en étirant le pavillon (longtail) pour canaliser l’air, le gain d’efficience dépasse 30 % au-delà de 80 km/h par rapport à la Polo classique.
- Équivalence surprenante : roulant à 140 km/h sur autoroute, la Mission Efficiency consomme la même quantité d’énergie qu’une ID. Polo se traînant à 100 km/h.
Plusieurs pistes intéressantes derrière ce design
Une fois installé au volant, on prend mieux la mesure du projet. Pour alléger la voiture et réduire la consommation des équipements auxiliaires, les ingénieurs ont sabré dans le superflu :
- Le concept Bring Your Own Device : pas d’écran multimédia géant ni d’ordinateur de bord énergivore. On fixe son propre smartphone ou sa tablette sur un rail mécanique coulissant, qui remplace ainsi l’écran d’infodivertissement. C’est bien intégré, sauf que la Citroën e-C3 d’entrée de gamme le fait aussi, mais pas pour la même raison.
- Pas d’enceintes dans les portes : l’installation audio est remplacée par une simple enceinte Bluetooth nomade. Résultat : des contre-portes 100 % recyclables d’un seul bloc et débarrassées de tout câble électrique, un peu comme la Citroën Ami.
- Pas de rétroviseurs-caméras : l’équipe m’a expliqué avoir sciemment écarté les rétroviseurs-caméras. Le gain aérodynamique marginal ne compensait pas l’électricité consommée en permanence par les caméras et les écrans intérieurs.
L’habitacle intègre également des appuis-tête alvéolés imprimés en 3D (en plastique TPU souple et recyclable) et un toit vitré photovoltaïque de 370 W capable d’injecter jusqu’à 30 km d’autonomie gratuite par jour. Forcément, les roues carrossées à l’arrière sautent également aux yeux. Au-delà du gain aérodynamique, les passages de roues cachent aussi d’astucieux rangements.
Bien sûr, ce coupé 2+2 très bas ne rejoindra jamais les concessions en l’état. Mais savoir que 80 % de ses entrailles mécaniques sont déjà prêtes pour la grande série sur la plateforme MEB+ laisse espérer que Volkswagen appliquera une partie de ces recettes d’aérodynamique et de légèreté sur ses futurs modèles du quotidien.

articles.title: Microsoft: September updates break audio on some Windows PCs
articles.text:
Microsoft has confirmed that USB audio devices may fail on some Windows systems after installing the KB5124008and KB5124012 September 2026 security updates.
This known issue affects only devices running Windows 11, version 24H2 or later, and is limited to USB Audio Class 1.0 devices.
"After installing the September 8, 2026, Windows security update [..], some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices might fail to start or produce audio," Microsoft said in a Friday update to the release health dashboard.
Affected users reported seeing "This device cannot start (Code 10)." errors in Device Manager, no audio output, and unresponsive volume controls and sound settings.
Others said the impacted USB audio speakers fail only when using multichannel audio features, including 3D audio or 8-channel modes.
While Microsoft has not yet provided an official workaround, some users have been able to restore audio on affected Windows PCs by switching to 2-channel mode.
Microsoft addressed a similar issue in January 2025, triggered by the KB5050094 optional preview cumulative update, which caused audio playback issues and Code 10 errors on Windows 11 24H2 systems with USB audio device drivers.
In September, it also lifted a safeguard hold that prevented Windows 11 24H2 upgrades on systems with Dirac audio improvement software because of compatibility issues causing Bluetooth headsets and speakers to malfunction.
Two years ago, Microsoft blocked Windows 24H2 upgrades on systems with incompatible Intel Smart Sound Technology (SST) audio drivers because of blue screen of death (BSOD) issues and confirmed an issue that caused game audio to unexpectedly increase to full volume when using USB DAC sound systems.
With the September 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft fixed known issues that wiped Windows desktop and mouse settings, as well as a bug that prevented Teams and Outlook from launching on ARM-based Windows devices.

articles.title: Voiture offerte en cas d'incendie et batterie garantie à vie : le pari fou de Xiaomi
articles.text:
Pour s’imposer en tant qu’outsider, il faut redoubler d’imagination. Souvenez-vous de la garantie 7 ans déployée par Kia sur sa Cee’d, une première qui a marqué les esprits ! 20 ans plus tard, c’est au tour des Chinois de séduire pour espérer pénétrer le marché. Et l’argument prix ne suffit plus pour faire signer le bon de commande. Xiaomi ressort donc un atout clé : une garantie massue autrement plus impressionnante que celle de Kia.
La marque chinoise garantit en effet sa nouvelle batterie Dragonscale à vie contre la combustion spontanée et les incendies survenant après un accident. Autant dire que si ça flambe pour une raison X ou Y, vous êtes normalement couvert ! Développée en partenariat avec CALB et Sunwoda, cet accumulateur prometteur dépasserait largement les normes chinoises en matière de sécurité.
Garantie à vie et voiture offerte : que cache cette offre folle ?
Li Xiaoshuang, vice-PDG de la branche automobile de Xiaomi, explique que cette prouesse a été possible par une sélection rigoureuse des matières premières combinées à une conception et une fabrication au centre de toutes les attentions. Cela permet ainsi à la marque d’être extrêmement confiante sur ses batteries en offrant carrément un nouveau véhicule en cas d’incendie dû à un défaut de fabrication.
Dans le cas d’un accident, Xiaomi prendra en charge la différence entre l’indemnisation de l’assurance et la valeur du véhicule estimée avant la collision. Il faut dire que la batterie Dragonscale possède des isolateurs haute tension avec des temps de commutation de quelques millisecondes permettant de réagir au plus vite en cas d’anomalie. Des matériaux ultra isolants englobent le tout pour éviter toute transmission de chaleur excessive.
Une protection survitaminée grâce à l’intelligence artificielle
Les cellules sont d’autre part constamment surveillées grâce à une IA basée sur le cloud. Xiaomi ajoute que ce système contrôle leur état dix fois plus fréquemment que ne l’exigent les normes locales. Ainsi, lors de tests grandeur nature menés à 55°C, les cellules isolées en feu ne peuvent provoquer un incendie généralisé de la batterie. Cet argument clé aura de quoi rassurer les sceptiques toujours effrayés par les explosions de modèles électriques.
Cela dit, il y a une poignée d’exclusions comme pour toute garantie qui se respecte. Seuls les véhicules de première main vendus aux particuliers sont éligibles à la mesure. Les véhicules utilisés professionnellement par les taxis ne sont pas concernés, tout comme les modèles d’occasion. Un entretien régulier du véhicule dans les centres agréés Xiaomi est également attendu. En Chine, la batterie Dragonscale équipe les SUV Skynomad N70 et N90.

articles.title: Meta Open-Sources Astryx, its Agent-Ready React Design System
articles.text:
Meta recently announced the beta release of Astryx, an open-source React design system developed internally over eight years. Astryx builds on React 19 and StyleX to provide over 150 accessible UI components, customizable CSS design tokens, and dedicated CLI and MCP tooling — for both engineers and AI agents.
Meta’s design system decouples behavior and accessibility compliance from aesthetic representation. The latter is specified by means of a centralized design token layer (e.g., color palettes, typographical hierarchies, border radii).
Under the hood, Astryx authors its components’ styles using StyleX, Meta’s build-time CSS-in-JS compiler that outputs deterministic, collision-free atomic CSS. Components accept an xstyle property for compile-time typed StyleX styling:
import * as stylex from '@stylexjs/stylex';
const overrides = stylex.create({
  card: { maxWidth: 400, marginBlock: 16 },
  saveButton: { alignSelf: 'flex-end' },
});
<Card xstyle={overrides.card} />
<Button label="Save" xstyle={overrides.saveButton} />
The core package, @astryxdesign/core, distributes pre-compiled CSS files alongside typed React components. Components also maintain native className support so teams can interoperate seamlessly with Tailwind, CSS Modules, or vanilla stylesheets:
<Card className="shadow-lg hover:shadow-xl transition-shadow">
  ...
</Card>
<Button label="Save" className="my-app-save-btn" />
Using pre-compiled CSS and className does not require additional compiler setup.
Astryx’s CLI exposes a swizzle command that allows developers to eject a component’s full source code into their repository. Design tokens and related classes enable developers to customize a component’s appearance. Standard React compositional patterns let developers customize a single component’s behavior or the behavior of every instance of a component (e.g., component wrapper pattern). Code ejection may, however, be required for those cases where customization requires access to an unexposed internal implementation (e.g., private state, DOM structure, or inaccessible event listeners). While ejecting offers enhanced customization flexibility, it also means that developers now own the code and with it, the associated maintenance duty.
Astryx claims native support for AI workflows through its CLI (@astryxdesign/cli) and an MCP endpoint.
Some developers on Reddit expressed concerns regarding the long-term maintenance and governance of a Meta-sponsored framework. Other developers have already begun porting the token architecture and component specifications to alternative UI runtimes, e.g., Svelte 5 and Flutter.
Astryx is distributed under the MIT license and requires React 19 or later.

articles.title: Vous pourrez bientôt installer des jeux Roblox sans télécharger l'application Roblox
articles.text:
Jusqu’ici, un jeu Roblox existe dans un seul endroit : au sein de l’application Roblox. On installe la plateforme et on cherche dans le catalogue l’expérience qui nous intéresse. L’annonce du 11 septembre, pendant la Roblox Developers Conference, bouscule cette règle de base, puisque les créateurs vont pouvoir, dans un futur proche, sortir leurs jeux de ce cadre pour les distribuer ailleurs.
D’après Roblox, l’objectif de « Roblox Everywhere » est de « permettre aux créateurs d’atteindre leur public là où il se trouve déjà ».
Bientôt, les créateurs auront la possibilité de proposer leurs jeux sous forme d’applications autonomes sur mobile, PC et consoles, Roblox fournissant la technologie et les services sous-jacents.
La plateforme, qui fête ses 20 ans, revendique 29 milliards d’heures de jeu rien qu’au dernier trimestre, dans plus de 180 pays. L’entreprise cherche à attirer les joueurs qui ne passent jamais par son application.
Pourquoi payer la nouvelle génération au prix fort ? iPhone 17, iPhone 16 Pro et iPhone 15 Pro : trouvez le modèle parfait, révisé par des experts et garanti sur Back Market.
Au-delà des applications autonomes, Roblox a détaillé d’autres façons de jouer sans passer par son application. D’ici la fin 2026, on pourra lancer un jeu directement dans le navigateur Chrome depuis sa page de détails, sans rien installer, d’autres navigateurs devant suivre. Un mode solo hors ligne est aussi prévu pour le milieu de l’année 2027.
Roblox, bientôt un moteur de jeu comme Unity ?
Pour le site spécialisé Pro Game Guides, ce virage pourrait faire passer Roblox du statut de simple plateforme à celui de moteur de jeu, à la manière d’Unreal Engine ou d’Unity. Roblox deviendrait alors la brique technique sur laquelle tourne le jeu, sans que le joueur voie forcément la marque. Tim Sweeney, le CEO d’Epic Games, a salué l’annonce en estimant que Roblox se transforme en moteur pour des jeux autonomes.
Dans les faits, un développeur pourra proposer son jeu comme une application classique sur smartphone, PC ou console, pendant que Roblox continue de fournir la technologie et les services derrière. On pourrait donc voir arriver une vague de titres conçus au départ pour Roblox, mais téléchargés comme n’importe quelle autre application. D’après le média Outlook Respawn, ces jeux autonomes resteront reliés à l’écosystème. Par défaut, leurs joueurs pourront retrouver ceux de l’application Roblox classique, et le déploiement commencera avec quelques créateurs et boutiques triés sur le volet. Roblox vise les grandes plateformes de téléchargement, sans confirmer si Steam, l’Epic Games Store ou GOG accueilleront ces jeux.
Sur mobile, le calendrier tombe bien, car les boutiques d’applications s’ouvrent justement à la concurrence même si Google s’applique à rendre la tâche plus pénible sur Android afin de protéger le Play Store.
Roblox Everywhere arrive « bientôt »
Roblox mène plusieurs chantiers en parallèle. La firme a aussi élargi Build, son outil qui permet de créer un jeu en tapant une simple phrase. Elle a aussi déployé en France des comptes adaptés aux moins de 16 ans.
Roblox n’a donné ni date précise ni liste de boutiques pour ces applications autonomes, l’entreprise parle seulement d’une arrivée « bientôt ». Si le projet tient ses promesses, des jeux nés sur Roblox pourraient débarquer sur nos plateformes habituelles sans qu’on n’installe jamais l’application mère. Pour les créateurs, c’est une porte vers un public bien plus large que le seul catalogue Roblox.

articles.title: iPhone Duo: todo lo que debes saber del primer plegable de Apple
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo, el primer teléfono plegable de Apple, llegará al mercado con un precio inicial de 1.999 dólares y una apuesta por la inteligencia artificial, las pantallas de gran formato y la productividad móvil.
El dispositivo marca la entrada de la compañía en una categoría donde Samsung, Huawei y Motorola ya tienen presencia desde hace años. Apple busca trasladar la experiencia del iPhone a un formato que combina un móvil compacto con una pantalla interna cercana a la de una tableta.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuándo estará a la venta el primer iPhone plegable
El iPhone Duo estará disponible a partir del 23 de octubre de 2026 y llegará con iOS 27, Apple Intelligence y un diseño pensado para reducir la visibilidad del pliegue central.
El dispositivo adopta un diseño tipo pasaporte, con una pantalla exterior de 5,4 pulgadas y un panel interno de 7,6 pulgadas. Cerrado, funciona como un teléfono convencional que puede utilizarse con una sola mano. Abierto, ofrece más espacio para leer, ver vídeos, trabajar con documentos o ejecutar varias aplicaciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Apple ha situado las cámaras frontales en la parte superior derecha. La cámara interior queda oculta bajo el panel, una decisión con la que la empresa busca aprovechar toda la superficie de la pantalla. El modelo estará disponible en blanco y negro, con bordes de titanio y botones configurables.
Uno de los elementos centrales será el mecanismo de plegado. La compañía sostiene que el diseño reduce la marca visible en el centro del panel, uno de los problemas que han acompañado a los primeros dispositivos de esta categoría. La pantalla interna de 7,6 pulgadas será la más grande instalada hasta ahora en un iPhone.
PUBLICIDAD
iOS 27 adapta las aplicaciones a la pantalla plegable
La propuesta de Apple depende en buena medida del software. El terminal estrenará una versión de iOS 27 ajustada al formato plegable, con un dock vertical en el borde derecho tanto de la pantalla externa como de la interna.
Cuando el dispositivo esté abierto, será posible utilizar dos aplicaciones de forma simultánea. La posición semiplegada habilitará funciones específicas, entre ellas una variante ampliada de StandBy, el modo que muestra información en pantalla mientras el equipo permanece apoyado y conectado a la corriente.
PUBLICIDAD
Los desarrolladores dispondrán de herramientas para adaptar sus aplicaciones a las diferentes posiciones del dispositivo. El objetivo es evitar que el panel ampliado se limite a mostrar una versión estirada de las interfaces diseñadas para teléfonos tradicionales.
El iPhone Duo incorporará el chip A20 Pro, creado para este modelo. Apple lo presenta como la base para ejecutar Apple Intelligence, reproducir contenido, jugar y mantener varias aplicaciones abiertas al mismo tiempo.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo es la cámara del iPhone Duo
El sistema fotográfico trasero contará con dos cámaras. La principal tendrá un sensor de 48 megapíxeles, equivalente al del iPhone 18 Pro, con grabación de vídeo en 4K y zoom óptico de dos aumentos. El conjunto se completa con una lente ultra gran angular, aunque no incluirá un teleobjetivo dedicado.
Apple sustituirá Face ID por Touch ID como sistema de desbloqueo. La decisión responde a los cambios de diseño que exige el formato plegable y devuelve al iPhone un método de autenticación que la empresa había relegado en sus modelos de gama alta.
PUBLICIDAD
La autonomía alcanzará hasta 24 horas con el teléfono plegado, según la información difundida por la compañía. La carga rápida permitirá recuperar el 50% de la batería en 20 minutos.
El precio partirá de 1.999 dólares en Estados Unidos
El modelo base, con 256 GB de almacenamiento, costará 1.999 dólares en Estados Unidos. En Europa, el precio comenzará en 2.339 euros. La versión de 512 GB tendrá un valor de 2.589 euros; la de 1 TB costará 3.089 euros y la de 2 TB ascenderá a 3.839 euros.
PUBLICIDAD
Las reservas se abrirán el 16 de octubre y las ventas comenzarán el 23 de octubre. El precio coloca al iPhone Duo por encima de los modelos convencionales de la marca y confirma que Apple se dirigirá inicialmente a un segmento de alto poder adquisitivo.
Una década de investigación detrás del proyecto
El origen del dispositivo se remonta a 2016, cuando los equipos de Apple empezaron a estudiar pantallas flexibles. Durante ese período, la empresa valoró la posibilidad de fabricar un iPad plegable, pero terminó por priorizar un iPhone por su potencial comercial.
PUBLICIDAD
Según informó Bloomberg, el proyecto ganó impulso después de un viaje de Tim Cook por Asia alrededor de 2020. El entonces director ejecutivo habría considerado que los plegables representaban una categoría en la que Apple debía participar.
La presentación del iPhone Duo coincide con el primer Apple Event encabezado por John Ternus como director ejecutivo. Ternus ha definido el modelo como el mayor cambio de la línea desde el iPhone original, una afirmación que ahora deberá sostenerse con ventas, resistencia y una experiencia de uso que justifique su precio.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Massive global price gap of iPhone Duo - international buyers pay a premium for Apple's most expensive iPhone - Tech Guide
articles.text:
When Apple revealed the iPhone Duo – it’s first foldable device – everyone was amazed and then they discovered the price which for Australians starts at $3,499.
The question we were being asked by our readers and listeners – “Why is it so expensive for Australian customers and other customers outside the US?”.
It turns out the iPhone Duo is going to be even more expensive for other countries than it will be in Australia.
The starting price for US customers is $US1,999.
Now we understand the US pricing does NOT include sales tax which would be a maximum of 10 per cent depending on which state you buy the device.
And the Australian price IS inclusive of a 10 per cent GST.
iPhone Duo
| Storage | US Price (USD) | Australian Price (AUD) | 
| 256 GB | $1,999 | A$3,499 | 
| 512 GB | $2,199 | A$3,899 | 
| 1 TB | $2,599 | A$4,699 | 
| 2 TB | $3,199 | A$5,899 | 
But even when you do the straight conversion from the US price with the added sales tax v Australian price the result is still hundreds of dollars lower than the Australia RRP.
The Australian price of $3,499 is equivalent to $US2,500 – a 22 per cent price increase.
The AUD v USD conversion rate at the time of writing is 0.7147 which means 1 Australian dollar can buy 71.47 US cents.
The rate was 0.688 on June 30. The lowest rate this year was on January 1 when it was 0.66. The exchange rate was at its highest on May 14 when it hit 0.725.
So apart from the June dip when Apple was working out pricing our exchange rate has been quite high.
So let’s do the math – we calculated the US price (including the maximum 10 per cent sales tax) and did the conversion with exchange rate at an average of 0.70.
So $US1999 plus $US199 sales tax equals $US2198. Converting $US2198 to AUD at the rate of 0.70 works out at $AUD3,140.
That means the starting price is $AUD359 dollars higher at $AUD3,499.
And it’s the same story around the world.
In Canada $CAD2,999 Canadian – works out at $US2,160 while in Germany/Eurozone will be paying €2,299 which is $US2,500.
In Taiwan the price is $74,900 Taiwanese dollars which converts to $US2,360 and the £1999 price in the UK works out at $US2,700.
If you’re in India and want the iPhone Duo it will cost 299,900 rupees – or $US3,500.
But the most expensive place on Earth to buy the new foldable iPhone will be Turkey where it will cost the equivalent in its local current to $US4,741. That’s a 137 per cent price difference.

| 🇦🇺 Australia | A$3,499 | $2,500+ |

We understand there are import costs and duties and various other fees to take the product around the world but it seems Apple has built in a lot of wiggle room and will still make a solid profit.
These prices also take into account the elevated price of memory and storage which Apple stated earlier this year would be passed on to customers.
But these prices pressures and other costs apply to other companies as well but the pricing of their products are a lot more affordable to Australians.
Let’s compare like for like with a similar product.
The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is priced at $US1,899. The Australian pricing is $2,699.
The Samsung starting US price of $US1,899 is $US100 cheaper than the iPhone Duo at $US1,999 but it managed to be $AUD800 cheaper in Australia.
That’s $AUD2,699 (Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8) v $AUD3,499 (iPhone Duo).

articles.title: Siempre hablamos del peso, pero el verdadero problema del efecto rebote podría estar en los músculos
articles.text:
Adelgazar es uno de los propósitos más comunes que vemos en nuestra sociedad para mejorar la salud o verse físicamente mucho mejor. Pero a menudo este objetivo se convierte en un ciclo interminable de pérdida y recuperación de kilos, que es lo que se conoce popularmente como 'efecto rebote' o dietas yo-yo. Sin embargo, a medida que cumplimos años, la ciencia nos advierte que este ciclo repetitivo puede afectar a la masa muscular de manera persistente.
La fluctuación de peso. Para ver el efecto que de verdad tiene algo que puede parecer tan inocuo como ganar y perder peso, los investigadores comenzaron a analizar las resonancias magnéticas y las analíticas de 1.433 personas de mediana edad.
Los resultados apuntaron a que las personas cuyo peso fluctuaba repetidamente, perdiendo y ganando kilos en ciclos constantes, perdieron casi cuatro veces más músculo en los muslos durante un periodo de cuatro años en comparación con las que mantuvieron un peso estable. En concreto, la pérdida fue de aproximadamente el 3,7% del volumen muscular del muslo en quienes experimentaron estas fluctuaciones, frente a un mero 1% en los de peso estable, incluso tras ajustar por edad, sexo, actividad física o dieta.
Declaraciones. Thomas Link, profesor de Radiología de la UCSF y director de la investigación, lo resume de forma muy gráfica: "Cuando el peso de las personas fluctuaba, perdían grandes cantidades de músculo junto con la grasa, y no lo recuperaban". Y es que, al final del estudio, estas personas terminaron con aproximadamente el mismo peso total que cuando comenzaron, pero su composición corporal había empeorado drásticamente.
Por qué ocurre. Aquí hay que tener muy presente que cuando nos sometemos a un déficit calórico para perder peso, el cuerpo no solo quema grasa, sino que también degrada el tejido magro. Esto es algo que se estudió en 2011 en 78 mujeres posmenopáusicas tras una intervención de pérdida de peso y durante el año posterior de recuperación ponderal.
Los números son demoledores, puesto que por cada kilogramo de grasa que se perdía durante la dieta, se perdían también 0,26 kg de tejido magro. Sin embargo, cuando llegaba el efecto rebote y se recuperaba un kilo de grasa, solo se recuperaban 0,12 kg de músculo. En otras palabras, en cada ciclo de dieta y rebote, se está intercambiando musculatura por tejido adiposo.
A largo plazo. El problema, por tanto, no es la pérdida de peso en sí, sino cómo se ejecuta. Una reciente investigación de 2025 estudió a 291 personas con sobrepeso u obesidad y encontró que la reducción del volumen muscular del muslo es un peaje inevitable al bajar de kilos: un 5,1% en quienes mantuvieron su peso estable, frente a un 12,8% en quienes experimentaron pérdidas de peso drásticas.
Sin embargo, este mismo estudio revela que la clave para evitar esta sangría en nuestro tejido muscular es hacer ejercicio mientras estamos en una dieta hipocalórica. En concreto, aquellos participantes que combinaron su dieta con entrenamiento físico perdieron considerablemente menos músculo frente a quienes adelgazaban basándose únicamente en restringir sus comidas.

articles.title: Une seule app pour veiller sur l'humidité, les fuites, la chaleur et le monoxyde
articles.text:
X-Sense : du thermomètre aux détecteurs connectés, un écosystème pour surveiller la maison
Une base pour jouer collectif
Après avoir testé le thermo-hygromètre STH0A et sa station SBS50, nous avons découvert trois autres capteurs de l'écosystème X-Sense. Fuite d'eau, monoxyde de carbone ou hausse anormale de température : la marque propose de surveiller toute la maison.
Le test du X-Sense STH0A nous a permis de découvrir un écosystème plus vaste qu'un simple thermomètre connecté. Reliée au wifi, la station SBS50 sert de relais entre l'application X-Sense Home Security et les capteurs radio de la marque. Elle peut accueillir jusqu'à 50 appareils.
Détecteurs de fumée, de chaleur, de fuite d'eau ou de monoxyde de carbone se retrouvent ainsi dans la même application disponible pour iOS et Android. Tous ne suivent toutefois pas la même logique : certains nécessitent la SBS50, tandis que d'autres se connectent directement au wifi. Sans aller jusqu'au test complet, puisque le fonctionnement reste identique au thermo-hygromètre connecté, nous avons pris en main trois autres de ces appareils.
Le climat sous surveillance
Le STH0A constitue la porte d'entrée la plus paisible dans cet univers. Son écran de 2,7 pouces affiche la température et l'humidité en grands caractères, avec un indicateur de confort. Il peut être posé à plat, incliné sur son pied ou accroché au mur.
Lors de notre test, nous avons apprécié sa lisibilité et la simplicité de l'application. Celle-ci conserve les mesures par heure, jour, semaine, mois ou année et permet de définir des seuils. La SBS50 peut alors sonner ou envoyer une notification si une pièce devient trop chaude, froide, sèche ou humide. L'application calcule aussi le point de rosée, utile pour anticiper la condensation, et le VPD, destiné au suivi des plantes.
L'écran perd cependant son utilité dans l'obscurité, faute de rétroéclairage, et aurait pu afficher l'heure ou une tendance. Les fonctions connectées imposent par ailleurs la SBS50. Alexa permet de demander les mesures à la voix, tandis que Home Assistant ouvre la voie à des automatisations plus avancées.
Prix : 24,99 € seul et 89,99 € pour quatre capteurs avec la SBS50.
X-Sense STH0A Thermo-hygromètre connecté
À la fuite !
Le SWS51 est conçu pour prendre place sous un évier, près d'un lave-linge, d'un chauffe-eau ou dans un sous-sol.
Quatre sondes sous son boîtier détectent une flaque, tandis que deux contacts supérieurs repèrent de l'eau tombant sur l'appareil.
En cas de fuite, le capteur et la station donnent l'alerte, avec un volume annoncé jusqu'à 110 dB. Une notification est envoyée sur le smartphone et l'alarme peut être interrompue depuis l'application ou le bouton du capteur. Sa liaison avec la SBS50 évite de dépendre du wifi sous chaque meuble. X-Sense annonce trois ans d'autonomie avec une pile remplaçable, mais seulement cinq ans de durée de vie.
Prix : 19,99 €, station SBS50 non incluse.
X-Sense SWS54 kit détecteur de fuites d'eau
X-Sense SWS51 détecteur de fuites d'eau
Le CO en ligne de mire
Le XC0C-iR surveille le monoxyde de carbone, un gaz invisible et inodore produit par une combustion incomplète. Il utilise un capteur électrochimique donné pour dix ans et affiche sa concentration en parties par million. L'application suit l'évolution des ppm et avertit en cas d'alarme, de pile faible, de panne ou de niveau jugé suspect.
Une alerte peut être coupée depuis le smartphone après vérification. La fonction est désactivée au-delà de 300 ppm afin d'éviter de faire taire une alarme réellement dangereuse. Le détecteur peut être posé ou fixé au mur, idéalement à hauteur de respiration.
Contrairement aux autres appareils présentés ici, le XC0C-iR ne fonctionne pas avec la SBS50. Il se connecte directement à l'application par le wifi 2,4 GHz : même environnement logiciel, mais réseau différent.
Prix : 31,99 €.
Chaud devant
Le XH02-M ne recherche pas de fumée, mais une hausse anormale de la température. Son thermistor NTC réagit à une élévation rapide ou à une température statique comprise entre 54 et 65 °C. Il convient ainsi aux cuisines, garages ou pièces où fumées de cuisson et poussière pourraient déclencher trop facilement un détecteur de fumée.
Les alertes sont transmises à l'application par la SBS50, qui relaie aussi les avertissements de pile faible ou de panne. Les événements peuvent servir de déclencheurs dans Home Assistant. Ce détecteur de classe A1 ne repérant ni la fumée ni le monoxyde de carbone, il complète un système de sécurité sans remplacer le détecteur de fumée obligatoire.
Prix : 29,99 €, station SBS50 non incluse.

articles.title: Telus Warns Customers of Account Breaches
articles.text:
Telus, one of Canada’s largest telecom providers, is notifying some customers that their accounts have been breached and their personal information has been accessed.
In data breach notifications sent to customers whose consumer telecom accounts were affected, Telus said the intrusions occurred between February 2025 and June 2026.
According to the company, the attacker used compromised credentials to access Telus accounts and the information they store, including names, account numbers, phone numbers, billing addresses, email addresses, partial payment card numbers, subscription details, and payment history.
Telus said the obtained account information has been used to attempt to convince customers to move their services to competitors, and in some cases the attackers made unauthorized changes to the victim’s services.
It’s unclear how many accounts the breach affected.
Telus said it has reset the compromised credentials and added enhanced security monitoring to impacted accounts. The Vancouver Police Department has been notified, and victims have been offered complimentary identity theft protection services.
Telus’ brief description of the incident suggests the accounts were targeted in a credential stuffing or other account-takeover campaign involving credentials obtained from a third party. However, the company has not said specifically that the abused passwords came from a third party.
In March, subsidiary Telus Digital confirmed suffering a data breach after the notorious ShinyHunters cybercrime group claimed to have stolen roughly 1 petabyte of information from the company’s systems.
SecurityWeek has reached out to Telus for additional information, including the number of affected accounts and clarification on the source of the credentials the attacker abused.

articles.title: StarCraft is coming back as an open-world shooter, but you'll have to wait until 2030
articles.text:
Something to look forward to: StarCraft is coming back, but it's not the real-time strategy game that became a global phenomenon. This time, Blizzard is reimagining the franchise as an open-world shooter. Sadly, we won't get to play it until 2030.
Rumors of a new StarCraft game have been circling for a while now. Its existence was confirmed during the opening ceremony of BlizzCon with a three-minute cinematic video.
The video continues Blizzard's tradition of flashy and quite gory game promos. It shows a determined young recruit going through training before being dropped on an alien planet to face a swarm of Zerg forces. With his weapon seemingly out of ammo, we next see the slushy remains of the soldier being drained from his CMC Powered Combat Suit.
There are no gameplay clips at this early stage, but we do know it's going to be an open-world shooter rather than an RTS.
Dan Hay, GM & VP of StarCraft, told IGN about why Blizzard decided to change the format of one of the genre's most famous franchises.
"For us, when we think about the themes and we think about the opportunity for you to be on the battlefield and for you to go out and think about the vista, the opportunity to explore, and then to discover, and then to disrupt," he said.
"It's incredibly unique. And then when you think about the different factions that there are, we just wanted people to go out into these worlds and actually get a sense of what it's like to meet these different groups."
Hay also talked about using enemies as a "tool" against other enemies, which sounds like a feature that may appear in the finished game.
2030 is a long time away, of course, so why did Blizzard not just wait a bit longer before revealing the next StarCraft? Hay said sharing a "solid" release date keeps the team "honest," so it should release that year and not any later – but then we've heard those sorts of promises before.
We almost had a genre-changing StarCraft game more than 20 years ago. Blizzard announced StarCraft: Ghost in 2003. It was supposed to be a third-person shooter set in the StarCraft universe slated for an Xbox release later that year, and there was even an hour-long gameplay reveal. But prioritizing World of Warcraft and the upcoming next-gen consoles pushed back development and Ghost was eventually canceled.
There were other big reveals at BlizzCon, including Diablo 5 and World of Warcraft: Forever.

articles.title: Three JFrog Artifactory Flaws Exploited for Backdoor Deployment
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting three high-severity vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to compromise deployments and install backdoors, cybersecurity firm Wiz reports.
Many organizations use Artifactory to manage software artifacts, binaries, AI models, containers, and packages.
The three flaws, CVE-2026-42016, CVE-2026-42018, and CVE-2026-82329, can allow attackers to bypass authentication and gain administrative privileges on vulnerable Artifactory instances.
An improper authentication bug patched on August 12, CVE-2026-42018 can be exploited to obtain an anonymous-user token that provides access to sensitive artifacts and repository data.
Patched on July 27, CVE-2026-42016 is an insufficient token validation issue that can be exploited for privilege escalation.
CVE-2026-82329 is an authentication bypass patched on August 28 that could be exploited remotely without authentication to gain administrative privileges. In-the-wild exploitation was reported a few days later.
According to Wiz, CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 have been chained together since mid-August to obtain the anonymous-user token and then use it to elevate privileges to administrator.
“Between August 15 and September 8, 2026, we observed multiple actors chain CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 against self-hosted Artifactory instances,” Wiz says.
The hackers were seen deploying persistent admin accounts, installing malicious plugins to gain arbitrary code execution, running shell commands through the plugin endpoint, dropping second-stage payloads, and occasionally updating the scripts for continuous access.
Multiple threat actors also started exploiting CVE-2026-82329 in the first week of September, for configuration exfiltration, persistent admin access, token minting, cluster key exfiltration, and asset enumeration.
In some instances, the attackers were seen attaching their own SSH keys to the user accounts they created.
On Friday, CISA added CVE-2026-42018 and CVE-2026-42016 to its KEV catalog, one week after it added CVE-2026-82329 to the list. In line with BOD 26-04, federal agencies were given two weeks to patch their vulnerable instances.
All organizations are advised to update their self-managed Artifactory deployments to versions 7.161.20, 7.146.38, 7.133.29, 7.125.20, 7.117.28, or 7.111.21 as soon as possible.

articles.title: Even Realities G2 smart glasses show the limits of speaker- and camera-free frames
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
While I’m generally impressed with the design and some of the features, including the teleprompter, news feed, and occasionally useful Even AI, I was left with a feeling of, “Why do we need these?” The quick access to some information — such as it is — is not life-altering, and too many of its other features are subpar and would force me to pull out my phone, which, of course, defeats the entire purpose of smart glasses. If I’m going to pay that much for a pair of smart glasses — and invest in prescription lenses for them (another $150 to $350) — I want the full raft of capabilities (yes, including a camera) and deep access to all the features of my smartphone so that my smart glasses feel truly smart and useful.
Pros
- +No camera!
- +Stylish and comfortable
- +Teleprompter is a cool feature
Cons
- -Touch operation is finicky
- -Software lacks true hooks into your smartphone
- -Maps intentionally lacks driving directions
Why you can trust TechRadar
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: 30-second Review
It's a weird time for smart glasses. After a moment in the sun (as sunglasses!) where companies like Meta sold millions of frames to willing customers seeking on-their-face intelligence and the ability to life-log with ever-present, eyebrow-level cameras, the worm has turned. Now people refer to smart glasses with cameras as "pervert glasses". Even Realities Even G2 smart display glasses (Even Realities G2) would seem to be the antidote to those concerns.
The relatively stylish specs live up to the smart expectations by connecting you to phone-based AI and delivering useful information to your eyes where and when you need it, but without the concerning cameras.
In some ways, Even Realities' approach is rather quaint. Instead of Augmented Reality, you get binocular, monochromatic waveguide displays that offer eye-level access to notifications, notes, translations, news, even a teleprompter, that only you can see. The imagery is sharp, but not rich. It's glanceable info that could be handy in a pinch, but is also stuff you can easily ignore.
These are smart lenses in the narrowest sense. They have four mics for listening, but no speakers. The microphones let you summon the AI (Even AI), which lives on the Even Realities iPhone app, but with no speakers, Even can't talk back to you. Even AI's responses appear before you as text on the waveguide screens.
The AI is not quite good enough to fully control the glasses, but that's where the gestures come in. While Even's G2 glasses look much like any other analog pair you'd wear, each arm ends in a large pill shape that houses the batteries and touch sensors. If you don't want to keep touching behind your ear, you can buy the $249 Even R1 ring, which Even Realities did supply to me. You wear the R1 on your index finger and use your thumb to recreate the taps, long presses, and swipes you'd do on the glasses. The Ring also records temperature, heart, and step measurements, readouts of which you can view on the glasses.
It's easy to see (pun intended) how useful these could be for turn-by-turn directions delivered from the app's map to the screen, and teleprompter text gently scrolling up, but inconsistent operation, missing features, finicky controls, and an overall feeling of, "Do I really need this?" left me wondering if half-way smart glasses are worth making the trip at all.
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: Price and availability
Even Realities G2 smart glasses were unveiled earlier this year and are now shipping for $599 / £599 / AU$649. If you need prescription lenses, which they do support, be sure to factor that into the price (expect at least another $150). My review unit arrived with my prescription in place, and I often forgot I was wearing them.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Even in monochrome, in-lens displays are a premium feature, which accounts for a price tag that’s considerably more than, say, Meta’s recently launched $299 EssilorLuxottica smart glasses, which do feature a camera and speakers.
- Value: 3.5/5
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: Design
- Thin, light, and durable
- Premium materials
- Mostly look like regular glasses
- Comfortable
- Stem bulbs look a little odd but are mostly hidden
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Even Realities G2 display smart glasses are easily the most normal-looking smart glasses I've ever seen or worn. The gray titanium-and-magnesium frames are thin, light, and quite stylish. Where many smart glasses are bulky, heavy, or uncomfortable (or look ridiculous), Even Realities G2 frames are as comfortable as my regular prescription glasses. Yes, the stems end in pill-shaped nodules that house sensors and the batteries, but those elements are mostly hidden behind the ears.
The glasses ship with extra stem covers for comfort and a larger set of nose pads, though I was fine with the default set. There’s also an included charging case.
I didn’t think they looked bad, though my wife, who noticed that, unlike standard glasses, the fronts of the G2 lenses are flat and reflective, called them weird. “They don’t have cameras," I added hopefully.
I asked her if she could see anything on the lens, meaning the display I was viewing. She said no, but still remained unmoved. Some people are never gonna love smart glasses of any stripe, even ones I think look almost like regular glasses.
- Design score: 4/5
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: Display
- Solid waveguide technology
- Low resolution but mostly fit for purpose
- Virtually large enough to be useful
- Plenty bright
Even Realities G2 glasses use micro-LEDs embedded in the frames and waveguide technology, which basically guides the 640 x 350 monochrome (day-glo green) imagery in front of both eyes. Remarkably, the embedded displays are almost imperceptible to the naked eye (even with content running on them).
With my prescription lenses, the single-floating-image effect is perfect. The bright green imagery looks like a monochrome, 15-inch display floating in front of my face. It sits slightly above my eyeline, meaning I could easily look below the display to see what’s in front of me or just slightly up to see the display. It’s not so high on the frame that if you’re looking at the display, someone will think you’re not looking at them.
Even in daylight, the 1,200 nit display is clear, sharp, and very viewable. There are settings to adjust the display brightness, and while the resolution sounds low, you don’t need much for what is essentially CRT-grade imagery.
- Display score: 4/5
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: Software and Performance
- There aren't a lot of features
- Main menu access takes practice
- Teleprompt is a highlight
- News feed is nice to have
- Translate could be useful if you remember to pre-set your language choices for the location
- Navigation purposely is missing a key feature
- No real access to smartphone features
- AI shows promise but has noted limited access
While you might imagine a certain level of complexity with smart glasses, Even Realities keeps it pretty simple. The Dashboard, which you raise with a double tap on one of the stem sensors (or on the optional ring), reminds me of one of those old 1990s personal assistant devices or even a slightly more informative digital clock. There’s a large time readout on the left, with smaller, dare I call them digital watch-like complication elements arrayed around it. At the top is the day and date. To the right is the battery life of the glasses and, if you have it, the R1 smart ring. On the bottom left is the local temperature, and to the right of that is the number of notifications. To the right is a large square news feed.
With another sensor tap, I can open the feed and swipe backwards on the sensor to scroll through it. One more tap opens a news item, which, yes, I can scroll through by swiping on the stem sensor. You can see why someone might want to opt for the R1 ring. Who wants to be touching and swiping near their ear all the time?
Double taps pull you back out of the news feed, all the way to the Dashboard.
One of the less obvious interactions is how you bring up the main menu. I must admit, it took me a while to get the hang of the tap-and-hold gesture to open it. Once you master that — assuming you do — you get just seven options:
- Notifications
- Conversate
- Teleprompt
- Translate
- Navigate
- Dashboard
- Silent Mode
You can swipe up or down to go through them and tap to open one. The gesture-based control system is so finicky that I often ended up in the wrong place, and there’s no confirmation; the system simply starts, for instance, “Coversate,” which is basically a speech-to-text note-taking app.
More interesting is Teleprompt, the one feature that could potentially be the reason someone invests in these glasses. As the name suggests, it puts a teleprompter that no one else can see in front of your face.
To test it, I imported some text into the app (it supports txt, Docx, and PDFs). The app lets you expand or contract the margins, which controls the length of each line you read, but it lacks a way to control the line spacing — a key teleprompter feature. On the glasses, the text appears in front of you, and voice recognition detects you saying each word. As a result, there’s no need to mess with speed or stop and start the text scroll. It’s all controlled by your voice. That’s pretty cool.
Unfortunately, you might look a little odd while using it. I took a picture of myself while reading a script and noticed that I was looking up instead of at the audience in front of me. The key to teleprompters is that they're usually projected over, say, a camera lens, so you are reading while looking directly into the camera. To use Even Realities G2 for this task, you have to look up just a little bit.
Navigate launches turn-by-turn directions, but you can’t do much until you put locations in the iPhone app’s navigation section. I added my home and office addresses and then used them to start navigating from my current location. The only two navigation options are walking or cycling. That's because Even Realities intentionally excluded driving directions, as they might be too distracting in a heads-up display. I disagree with their exclusion.
Glancing at monochrome, see-through, heads-up directions while driving should not be distracting, but I'm not going to argue with the safety concern. Still, I suggested to them that they think about enabling driving directions that can be reviewed before starting the trip and then use detection of the iPhone's Driving Mode to disable that feature as soon as you start driving.
As for what navigation looks like, there’s a small turn-by-turn map on the lower left, distance and time to destination on the upper right, time and a walking icon on the upper left, and next turn on the lower left. Another tap on the sensor shows the full map route, which is a bright green line on a dimmer green map with no labels. I'm not sure how useful that is.
The Translate feature works pretty well, although despite the onboard mics, it does not auto-detect languages. Instead, I had to choose the to-and-from-translation languages in the app. Then, when I played a Spanish-language video, I watched the live translation on screen. Basically, before you go to a different country, you’d want to pre-load the appropriate language settings.
Silent mode instantly turns the G2 frames into dumb glasses, silencing all notifications and ensuring the screen doesn’t turn on, which it can even when you tip your head up. To un-silence it, you put one finger on each sensor.
Of course, there is AI, in the form of Even AI, which I summoned by saying, “Hey Even”. It wasn't the best at listening and getting my requests right, and there are many, many things it cannot do. Even AI has no access to your phone at large, just the app and its relatively limited features.
I did have some success. For instance, when I asked about the latest news on tech companies, I got a nice summary that I could read on the display.
I struggled to get notifications working, though. I was unaware of texts, Slacks, and incoming emails – basically anything I really needed.
Things did not improve when I tried to get clever. I had this idea that I could have the shopping list in my iPhone Notes app float in front of me while I walked around the grocery store. Yet, when I asked Even AI to read my files from the Notes app, it told me it couldn’t access them, but I could access the App’s Quick List. So I tried to build a Quick List, but every time I tried, the glasses would state “Quick List saved” before I even gave it a list. Then it had a bug where it told me the “Command execution” failed. Not useful.
- Performance score: 3.5/5
Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses: Battery
- Small-ish battery on the glasses (to save the design)
- Sizable battery is included in charging case
Even Realities G2 smart glasses are equipped with a 192mAh battery rated to last two days. My first charge ran out after three days of intermittent use. The included charging case has a 2,000mAh battery for up to seven recharges.
Considering there’s no camera, I would expect a longer battery life, but I think Even Realities purposely sacrificed some battery capacity for its exceptionally svelte style.
- Battery score: 3.5/5
Should you buy the Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses?
| Even Realities Even G2 Smart Glasses Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Comment | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | A bit pricey for what they do. You end up paying a premium for the impressive waveguide technology and their normal-glasses style. | 3.5/5 | 
| Design | The rare smart glasses that's thin, light, and kind of attractive, if you ignore the oddness of the flat lenses (only on the front). | 4/5 | 
| Display | The low resolution waveguide displays are used to mostly good effect here. Everything is bright, sharp, and readable. | 4.5/5 | 
| Software and Performance | Even Realities software and operation on the G2 smart glasses is a true mixed bag, with inconsistent performance and only occasional delight. The relatively spare features do not really sell it as a must-have wearable. | 3.5/5 | 
| Battery | Tiny batteries on the glasses can stretch to a few days use, but it's the charging case that saves the day. | 3.5/5 | 
Buy it if…
You want camera-free smart glasses
The Even Realities G2 does away with the one thing that's freaking people out — at least when it comes to smart glasses
You want on your face teleprompter
The voice-activated teleprompter feature is cool
Don’t buy it if…
You wanted full-featured smart glasses 
Even Realities G2 offers baseline features and decent AI, but it's not enough to make this a truly compelling wearable
You don’t want to spend almost twice as much as the nearest smart glasses
Even Realities G2 offers less for more, reminding you how expensive it is to build in-lens display wear.
You want cameras and audio
These glasses are not the smart glasses for you
Also consider
Weighing just 76g, the X3 Pro proves that cutting-edge AR hardware no longer has to crush your nose. The display is a genuine glimpse of the future. But the future has a small battery, and the X3 Pro's 245mAh cell is, alongside the price, the device's biggest obstacle.
Read our RayNeo X3 Pro review
Xreal Air 2
If you want to stick with Xreal, the Xreal Air 2 or its electrochromic dimming-enhanced Xreal Air 2 Pro are both solid options that cost a little less – though expect a slightly lower-quality image and noticeably inferior audio.
Read our Xreal Air 2 review
Meta Quest 3
While not a direct competitor to Xreal’s glasses, the Quest 3 is an XR product that you should consider if you want to experience what VR and MR have to offer – it’s simply superb.
Read our Meta Quest 3 review
How I tested the Even Realities G2 display smart glasses
I spent the last week or so wearing these glasses instead of my normal prescription eyewear. I tried all the features and sometimes used the smart ring to control them.
- First reviewed September 2026

articles.title: La élite de las matemáticas teme que se queden vacías de sentido ante los avances de la IA
articles.text: El matemático Terence Tao es uno de los 25 destacados matemáticos que han firmado la carta sobre IA La tecnología tiene un efecto paradójico: ofrece resultados que satisfacen nuestros deseos mermando nuestras habilidades. La agricultura proporcionó cantidades ingentes de alimentos, haciendo que los humanos dejaran de reconocer infinidad de vegetales comestibles, el GPS hace que todo el mundo llegue a tiempo hasta a los lugares más difíciles, pese a ser la generación menos orientada de la historia, y la escritura mermó la capacidad de memorizar. Ahora, un grupo de 25 ganadores de la medalla Fields (el Nobel de las matemáticas) advierte en una carta de que la inteligencia artificial puede ampliar el impacto de corrosión de las capacidades humanas a través de resultados irrefutables en las matemáticas, una de las más excelsas actividades humanas, vaciándolas de sentido. articles.title: Cloudflare Tests Cache Transcoding to Reduce Storage Requirements
articles.text:
Cloudflare recently described a prototype called Cache Transcoding that compresses eligible cache content, mainly uncompressed text such as HTML, JSON, CSS, and JavaScript, using Zstandard before storing it on disk. The hyperscaler estimates that the approach could provide petabytes of additional effective cache capacity, although broader testing is still needed.
According to the article, the additional processing required is relatively small, as the content is compressed once when it enters the cache and decompressed when served. Compression reduced the size of eligible content by about 2.8 times, allowing existing servers to store more data and reducing the amount of data transferred between data centers.
To achieve this, Cloudflare relies on Zstandard, the lossless compression algorithm developed by Facebook for real-time use, together with Pingora, its Rust-based proxy framework. Aashi Patel writes:
A small increase in CPU gives Cloudflare petabytes of effective cache capacity and reduces the data transferred between our data centers. The encoding cost is paid once when an asset enters the cache. The storage and bandwidth savings continue every single time that asset is reused.
Cloudflare's Cache Transcoding only compresses uncompressed responses that contain compressible text, return successfully, and are at least 4 KiB. It excludes range requests, precompressed or binary content, and responses with an unknown size. The threshold avoids processing many small objects while sacrificing only about 1% of eligible data, and both this threshold and the Zstandard compression level can be adjusted based on CPU and storage trade-offs. Patel adds:
Transcoding does not mean compressing everything. Images, video, and fonts are usually compressed already. In our traffic sample, this media slice represented 21.4% of requests but 63.3% of bytes. Compressing it again would burn CPU for nothing.
According to Cloudflare, compressible text such as HTML, JSON, CSS, and JavaScript accounted for 67.3% of requests and 22.3% of bytes. Of this content, about 71% arrived uncompressed and could be effectively compressed.
Source: Cloudflare blog
While some practitioners question the use of the word "transcoding" for an encode/decode approach, others on Hacker News discuss the compression options. As Cloudflare initially considered limiting transcoding to popular content, user MayeulC writes:
Weird, I would have compressed cold content instead, if the goal was to save on CPU time during decode.
User CodesInChaos asks instead:
I'm confused by how this affects range requests. Without compression, those can be easily satisfied by reading the relevant part of the cached complete file. But how are they handled now?
Tests were performed with and without Tiered Cache to measure the impact of compression on local caching and transfers between cache tiers. The prototype remains under development, with further testing planned across different compression levels, content types, object sizes, and cache scenarios.

articles.title: Opinion: To build Canada’s innovation economy, we need to deploy the wealth we already have| BetaKit
articles.text:
Liam Gill is the lead of the Capital Program at MaRS Discovery District, where he helps Canada’s most promising early-stage companies connect with the capital they need to scale.
This week, Prime Minister Mark Carney will gather global financiers in Toronto for the country’s first-ever Canada Investment Summit. The message will be clear: Canada needs foreign capital to drive economic growth. While more foreign direct investment helps, it also distracts from a bigger problem: Canada isn’t deploying the wealth it already has. In a world where economic sovereignty is increasingly important, building a resilient, innovation-driven economy starts with unlocking domestic capital.
Consider the Dominion List, which tracks Canadian founders building companies in the United States; there are currently 517 US technology companies with a Canadian founder, worth a combined $574 billion CAD, with 56 valued at over $1 billion US ($1.4 billion CAD). For context, all of Canada’s startups combined raised just $9.13 billion CAD last year, and this country is home to only 33 startups valued at over $1 billion USD. This isn’t a comparison between US entrepreneurs and Canadian entrepreneurs; it’s a reminder that Canadian founders are currently contributing more to the US economy than Canada’s.
Canada doesn’t have a capital shortage. It has an incentive problem.
That’s not their fault. Canada has the talent, but what it doesn’t have, for founders who want to scale, is accessible capital. So they go where they can get it.
This does not need to be the case.
We have capital. Canada is home to nearly 177,000 families worth more than $7.5 million. These are exactly the households that fuel angel investing everywhere else in the world. In the US, more than 300,000 active angel investors made over 70,000 deals last year, worth more than $25 billion USD ($34 billion CAD) combined. In Canada, angel investors made just 490 deals worth $114 million CAD, about 0.33% of what their US counterparts invested.
Canada doesn’t have a capital shortage. It has an incentive problem. We’ve built an economic system that incentivizes this money to sit in non-productive assets like GICs and real estate instead of productive assets like technology startups that create jobs, tax revenues and economic growth.
The exodus of founders to the US should worry Canadians even more, given that 88 percent of Dominion List founders were educated at Canadian, publicly funded universities, meaning our taxpayer dollars are subsidizing US growth. The trend is accelerating; more than half of the companies on the list were founded in 2023 or later.
Some of the biggest names on the list, OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI, were founded or built in part by people educated in Toronto. Modern AI itself was invented at the University of Toronto. Given that, it is not surprising Torontonians are behind so much of the field’s progress. What is surprising, unfortunately, is that we still haven’t found a way to get our own high-net-worth individuals to back these talented researchers so they can build world-class companies at home instead of somewhere else.
RELATED: Tracking the Canadian capital commitments surrounding Carney’s investment summit
The National Angel Capital Association quantified just how large this gap is, finding that Canada faces an annual pre-seed and seed-stage funding shortfall of roughly $195 million and a Series A funding deficit of $250 million. Together, those gaps have cost Canada’s three largest technology hubs (Toronto-Waterloo, Vancouver and Montreal) an estimated $92 billion in lost ecosystem value over the past six to eight years.
If Prime Minister Mark Carney wants to build Canada’s economy on the foundation of its own talent and entrepreneurs, he needs to unlock the domestic capital to fund it. That means tax incentives for investors backing innovative startups—the kind the US and UK already offer. It also means educating Canadians who built wealth in manufacturing or real estate on the returns technology investments have historically delivered. US technology angel investors averaged a 27 percent internal rate of return, significantly outpacing public markets or real estate.
As we invite the world to invest in Canada, the clearest signal we can send is that we believe in our own potential enough to invest in ourselves. Foreign capital should complement and amplify domestic capital, not replace it. We have a real chance to combine both to build world-class companies here at home. But if Canadians won’t invest in Canada, why would anyone else?
The opinions and analysis expressed in the above article are those of its author, and do not necessarily reflect the position of BetaKit or its editorial staff. It has been edited for clarity, length, and style.
Image courtesy Julian Gentile via Unsplash.

articles.title: Waymo pulls over, calls cops on riders with a ghost gun
articles.text:
Two people were arrested in San Fransico while riding around in a Waymo robotaxi after the cab pulled over and called the cops on them. The riders were juveniles in possession of a loaded AR-style ghost gun and were taken to a juvenile hall. While the police report did not specify who was operating the autonomous car, Waymo later confirmed it was one of its vehicles to the Los Angeles Times.
Waymo pulls over, calls cops on riders with a ghost gun
Your robotaxi can and will snitch on you.
Your robotaxi can and will snitch on you.
A spokesperson told the LA Times that a “violation of our terms of service involving a firearm” was detected. At which point the car pulled over and alerted the authorities.
Earlier this year, a Waymo faked having mechanical problems to pull over when two passengers were drinking alcohol and firing a toy gun out of the back of the car. In that instance, the riders Waymo snitched on were also juveniles. So let this be a lesson to teens: if you’re gonna do dumb stuff, don’t do it in the back of a robotaxi.
