articles.title: HP OmniBook Ultra 14 review - the allrounder laptop for work, play and entertainment - Tech Guide
articles.text:
- RATING
HP OmniBook Ultra is superb all-rounder laptop for that customer who wants to work hard and play hard and be entertained. It can certainly deliver in all those areas with ease with performance to satisfy even the most demanding users.
HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 is a lot of laptop. It’s capable and powerful and can meet all your PC needs while being an excellent tool for AI to improve your efficiency and creativity.
This is the latest consumer PC laptop offering from HP and they’ve taken all their learnings over the years of releasing compelling products and shaped it beautifully into the OmniBook Ultra.
Design-wise the OmniBook Ultra is slick. It is thin (10.7mm) and light (1.28kg) and made of forge-stamped aluminium, which helps keep down the weight and increase the strength so it can easily handle day-to-day usage on the move.
HP has put the laptop through 20 military standard tests so don’t think that its light and thin chassis isn’t up to the task.
It has a matte finish with glossy edges.
For the period we were using it as our daily driver it did feel thinner and lighter than our go to 14-inch MacBook Pro.
And it was so light we’d forget we had it in our backpack – in fact I had to check several times that I’d remembered to pack it.
The first thing that catches your eye is the stunning 3K OLED touchscreen which has remarkable brightness and accurate colour thanks to a colour gamut that covers 100 per cent of DCI-P3.
It’s a brilliant workspace that you won’t tire of looking at.
It has up to 1,100 nits peak brightness and a 120 Hz refresh rate.
The full-sized keyboard has nice-sized keys with decent travel to make typing easy and quiet.
But what you also get is a massive trackpad offers an easy way to navigate interact with the system.
Also onboard is a 5MP webcam, which can be used to unlock your computer with Windows Hello facial recognition.
Naturally it’s an ideal tool for any video conferencing.
Video quality through this camera is good, not great and It could use some finessing in terms of looking your best for presentations and video calls.
And for added peace of mind there is a shutter so you can physically cover the camera when not in use.
The device is powered by the Intel Core Ultra X9 Series 3 processor which means it not only provides solid performance but it can also easily handle demanding AI workloads on device.
On the performance side the HP OmniBook Ultra certainly delivered but we appreciate the fact that the laptop can do a lot more for power users because our workflow didn’t really challenge it too much.
The unit we received for review had a 1TB solid-state drive with 32GB of LPDDR5x SDRAM and was running Windows 11.
But let’s just say if you are running high-end applications and even the latest games, it is more than up to the task.
It also has a vapour chamber on board to keep things cool if you are pushing the unit to its limit.
The chip comes with Intel’s ARC B390 GPU which will delight gamers demanding better graphics performance that they would receive on a generic Intel CPU.
The 70Wh battery was also one of its best features, running for up to 20 hours before we needed to reach for the charger.
For us that was nearly two full workdays.
In terms of connectivity there is a USB-C port and a headphone jack on the left edge. And two other USB-C ports on the right.
It would have been nice to see an HDMI port or perhaps even a memory card slot but the design couldn’t accommodate it.
The HP OmniBook Ultra that we reviewed is available now and is priced at $3,499.
VERDICT
HP OmniBook Ultra is superb all-rounder laptop for that customer who wants to work hard and play hard and be entertained. It can certainly deliver in all those areas with ease with performance to satisfy even the most demanding users.

articles.title: Personne ne comprend ce nouveau panneau de signalisation : voici ce qu'il signifie précisément
articles.text:
Deux nouveaux panneaux de signalisation ont été placés en Catalogne, près de la frontière franco-espagnole. Si le panneau P-33 est facile à comprendre, le panneau P-35 est un peu plus technique. C’est ce qui ressort des commentaires sur les réseaux sociaux, mais aussi d’une partie de ceux qui réagissaient à notre article. Nous revenons aujourd’hui avec plus de précision sur sa signification et les mesures à prendre lorsqu’on le croise sur une route.
La signification du panneau P-35
Ce panneau de signalisation, représentant deux véhicules ainsi que des flèches noires qui se croisent, annonce une section de voies à entrecroisement. En d’autres termes, les trajectoires de plusieurs véhicules peuvent se croiser lors de changements de voie. Par exemple, un véhicule peut entreprendre une manœuvre pour quitter la voie sur laquelle il se trouve, tandis qu’un autre, arrivant d’une voie parallèle, tentera de s’y insérer.
Le problème est le suivant : les véhicules qui quittent la voie peuvent avoir tendance à ralentir, tandis que ceux qui tentent de s’y insérer vont plutôt accélérer. Cette différence de vitesse entre les véhicules peut alors augmenter le risque de collisions latérales. À noter que ce type de configuration routière est assez fréquent sur les autoroutes et les voies rapides : un même tronçon de voie peut notamment être utilisé par les véhicules qui s’insèrent sur l’autoroute et ceux qui cherchent à la quitter. En général, ce panneau est positionné entre 150 et 500 mètres avant le début d’une voie de croisement.
Pour éviter tout accident, il est conseillé d’adapter sa vitesse aux autres véhicules et de vérifier ses angles morts et ses rétroviseurs afin de repérer les véhicules qui accélèrent pour tenter de s’insérer sur la voie. La Direction générale de la circulation espagnole (DGT) rappelle que les automobilistes doivent respecter les règles de priorité : le véhicule qui s’insère doit céder le passage aux véhicules déjà présents sur la voie. Elle souligne également que les changements de voie doivent s’effectuer progressivement, tout en conservant une distance de sécurité suffisante à tout moment.
La signification du panneau P-33
Rappelons au passage la signification du panneau P-33. Celui-ci indique tout simplement une entrée dans une zone où la visibilité peut être réduite à cause du brouillard, de la neige, de la pluie ou de fumées. Pour être plus précis, ce panneau de signalisation existait déjà, mais son cryptogramme a été modifié. L’ancien pouvait laisser croire qu’il alertait sur des risques de chutes d’objets ou de pierres. Afin d’éviter toute confusion, le cryptogramme a donc été modifié, les lignes horizontales indiquant plus clairement un problème visible depuis l’habitacle de la voiture, et non une chute de pierres venant du ciel.
Si vous rencontrez ce panneau, il faut donc adapter sa conduite à la visibilité et aux conditions de route.

articles.title: Voilà à quoi ressemble la nouvelle carte du remake de Zelda Ocarina of Time
articles.text:
Avec son remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Nintendo entend bien conserver l’esprit de l’original. Les images montrées lors du Nintendo Direct consacré aux 40 ans de Zelda prouvent que l’épisode culte de la Nintendo 64 n’a rien perdu de son charme et que cette nouvelle version semble particulièrement fidèle à l’aventure originale.
Après une longue vidéo de gameplay, c’est au tour de la carte du jeu d’être dévoilée par Nintendo. L’éditeur a partagé de nouvelles images ce 13 septembre 2026 sur le site officiel japonais du jeu, dont cette nouvelle carte d’Hyrule. Ce premier aperçu de la réinterprétation de l’Hyrule classique semble très proche de l’original, avec toutefois quelques menues différences qui font déjà bouillir les fans les plus impatients.
Stylisée à la manière d’un vieux parchemin, la nouvelle carte présente les lieux les plus emblématiques de la région, tels que la Cité d’Hyrule, la Forêt Kokiri ou encore la Vallée Gerudo. Au premier coup d’œil, elle ressemble fortement à celle de l’original, avec une disposition générale des lieux quasiment identique, même si beaucoup plus de détails sont présents. En y regardant de plus près, au-delà d’une représentation plus précise du monde qui aidera à repérer certains lieux, quelques éléments montrent de vrais changements.
La carte du remake de Zelda Ocarina of Time ajoute de nouveaux éléments
En dehors de sa forme, beaucoup plus carrée, à la manière de l’Hyrule de Breath of the Wild, cette nouvelle carte présente déjà plusieurs différences avec celle du jeu original. La plus évidente se trouve aux alentours du château d’Hyrule, dont les environs semblent avoir été considérablement agrandis. On distingue désormais plusieurs maisons et bâtiments autour de l’édifice, là où le château apparaissait beaucoup plus isolé dans l’Ocarina of Time de 1998.
Le village Cocorico semble lui aussi avoir été légèrement modifié. Sa disposition paraît différente de celle que l’on connaissait sur Nintendo 64, avec notamment de nouveaux éléments visibles autour des habitations. La zone située entre le village et le cimetière semble également plus développée, même s’il faudra attendre de voir le jeu pour déterminer précisément ce qui a changé.
Certaines zones semblent aussi avoir été redessinées ou légèrement déplacées. Les chemins qui relient les différentes régions d’Hyrule ne correspondent pas toujours exactement à ceux de l’original, tandis que certains reliefs et éléments du décor ont été repositionnés. La carte donne ainsi l’impression d’un monde que Nintendo a réorganisé par endroits, sans pour autant bouleverser sa structure générale.
Différents points d’intérêt apparaissent également sur la carte, là où l’original était parfois beaucoup plus dépouillé. On ignore encore si Link pourra réellement explorer ces nouveaux lieux, mais cela donne dans tous les cas à Hyrule une dimension bien plus vaste que dans le jeu original et devrait favoriser l’exploration.

articles.title: Infineon RISC-V for Automotive at Hot Chips 2026
articles.text:
Since we covered many of the other talks, we also had a draft of the Infineon RISC-V for Automotive talk for Hot Chips 2026 ready. We figured, why not give this talk some exposure too? Let us get to it.
Infineon RISC-V for Automotive at Hot Chips 2026
Infineon opened with the compute demands facing automotive microcontrollers. Chassis, powertrain, and ADAS applications together want real-time low latency, power efficiency, and security on top of the highest integrity levels and functional safety, all on a single part.
Architecture work starts with the move from domain architecture toward zone control units and eventually full car computers. Former domain controllers evolve into central car computers handling ADAS, infotainment, and vehicle motion, while body and comfort functions consolidate into zones that share wiring and cut harness weight and cost. In automotive, the wiring harness is a huge deal.
Infineon lays out the real-time areas that every automotive part must handle. Fast control loops such as E-motor control need deadlines under 10 ms and interrupt latencies in the tens of nanoseconds, while strategic functions like vehicle management tolerate multiple seconds and 10 ms interrupt latency. We heard some of this in the Waymo Sensor Fusion Processor at Hot Chips 2026 talk.
With zone architecture in place, the open question is how much intelligence each zone controller should carry. Path A uses optimized multi-domain zone controllers that partially consolidate endpoint ECUs and support local power distribution, while Path B keeps zone controllers as low-complexity I/O aggregators with no intelligence of their own.
Infineon says that Option A is the more advantageous path. Keeping local tactics and latency-sensitive control loops in the zone while global strategies and OEM value sit in the central compute shrinks the vehicle attack surface, eases maintenance, and cuts system cost by consolidating endpoint ECUs and decentralizing power distribution.
Real zone controllers integrate workloads with very different compute demands. Real-time control, DSP and AI inference, low-power service layers, and audio processing all land on one part, so the compute architecture must scale across high-end multi-domain zones and low-end body zones while still delivering good power, performance, and area.
A super-integrated zone controller pushes heterogeneity further by adding an MPU island alongside the MCU. Offloading non-real-time critical workloads to a POSIX adaptive software stack frees the real-time core, enables faster boot and wake than a full SoC, and helps a zone scale from L2 toward L2+ and L3.
Against that backdrop, Infineon makes the case for RISC-V, which feels a bit like RISC-V over Arm given many of the other solutions out there. A single open and scalable ISA avoids IP-level lock-in, eases knowledge sharing, and brings ecosystem synergies across automotive, IoT, and industrial use.
Standardization depends on the right profiles. Within the RVI AUTO-SIG discussion, Infineon argues the distinction is less about auto versus non-auto and more about defining industry-grade safety- and security-related products, starting from a base such as RV32E and I plus M and U and adding optionalities for supervisor mode, floating point, vectors, and hypervisor support. If you want to learn more about profiles there was an Update on RISC-V Standards and Adoption at Hot Chips 2026.
Scalability depends as much on the software stack as on the ISA. Infineon points to virtualization as a key requirement so an RVM-based system can host multiple workloads and software domains cleanly.
RISC-V specifies the ISA rather than implementation details. Instruction latency, memory hierarchy, cache coherency, and functional safety features such as lock-step and error tracking stay in the hands of the silicon designer, which is where automotive differentiation happens.
Infineon says that in practice, detailed ISA aspects matter less than microarchitectural optimization, and for MCUs the winning attributes are memory, connectivity, specific hardware, sourcing, and final BOM cost, with the availability of automotive-qualified toolchains deciding who succeeds.
Infineon closes by tying RISC-V to concrete zone controller roles. RISC-V can accelerate zone control units, but application and cost fit are driven by factors beyond the ISA, such as SoC architecture, ecosystem enablement, and ease of deployment, and long-term adoption depends on standardized hardware-software interfaces and toolchain support.
That mix of open ISA freedom and the need for dependable, toolchain-backed automotive silicon frames where RISC-V fits as zone architectures mature.
Final Words
Infineon frames RISC-V as an ISA that removes the lock-in, but the market will be won on auto-qualified toolchains, SoC architecture, and ecosystem enablement rather than the instruction set alone. Hopefully, the automotive folks are able to support multiple ISAs unless one clearly pulls ahead. This was another neat talk, but probably one that was a bit less traditional STH coverage area focused.

articles.title: Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
articles.text:
Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half
A breakthrough nanolaser could let future computer chips communicate with light, potentially doubling down on speed while cutting energy use in half.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Technical University of Denmark
- Summary:
- Scientists have created an ultra-small nanolaser that could eventually allow microchips to transmit information with light instead of electricity, potentially making computers faster while cutting energy use roughly in half. Thousands of the lasers could fit on a single chip, opening possibilities for more efficient data centers, smartphones, and advanced medical sensors.
- Share:
The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.
In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.
"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.
Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.
Using Light Inside Computer Chips
Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.
Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.
Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.
The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.
Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers
The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.
At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.
When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.
The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.
Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use
The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.
Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.
In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.
Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Technical University of Denmark. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Meng Xiong, Yi Yu, Yury Berdnikov, Simon Klinck Borregaard, Adrian Holm Dubré, Elizaveta Semenova, Kresten Yvind, Jesper Mørk. A nanolaser with extreme dielectric confinement. Science Advances, 2025; 11 (51) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adx3865

articles.title: ConnectWise Patches ScreenConnect Vulnerability Exploited in Worm-Like Attacks
articles.text:
ConnectWise has released urgent patches for a critical-severity vulnerability in the ScreenConnect remote access and support software that has been exploited in worm-like attacks.
Tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score of 9.9/10), the security defect is described as a missing authorization and improper privilege management issue.
The bug creates “a condition in the ScreenConnect client that may allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances,” ConnectWise explains in its advisory.
In early September, cybersecurity firm Huntress warned that the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild since August 20.
As part of the observed incidents, a modified ScreenConnect instance was used to deploy four VBScript files designed to establish persistence and propagate to other ScreenConnect clients.
The hackers used social engineering to trick victims into executing rogue ScreenConnect clients, which then checked for active sessions to push the VBScript payload to connected targets.
ConnectWise resolved the flaw in ScreenConnect version 26.6.5 and urged users to apply the fixes as soon as possible. As a temporary mitigation, it recommends disabling the TransferFiles permission in ScreenConnect.
“The ScreenConnect 26.6.5 patch includes updates to strengthen client and session handling for file-transfer and file-execution actions,” ConnectWise notes.
On Friday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days, as mandated by BOD 26-04.

articles.title: New Bernie Sanders bill would ban superintelligent AI and threaten developers with 20 years in prison
articles.text:
What just happened? Bernie Sanders, one of the most vocal opponents of unregulated AI and the race toward superintelligence, has announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act alongside Rep. Greg Casar. One of the more worrying sections for anyone who refuses to adhere to these restrictions is the penalties: ignore them, and the punishment is up to 20 years in prison. That's similar to the penalty for unlawfully developing nuclear weapons.
The first paragraph of the announcement states that the Act would stop AI oligarchs from building machines humans cannot control.
The Act would permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules.
Beyond the United States' borders, it also directs the US to pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world.
 – Sen. Bernie Sanders (@SenSanders) September 12, 2026
"The leaders of the major AI companies publicly acknowledge that they do not fully understand the technology and that it is escaping their control," Sanders said. "The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs."
"Despite its potential deadly consequences, cutting-edge AI technology is less regulated than the average food truck. That must change," Casar said.
The Act would ban the development or deployment of superintelligence, pause advanced AI development, and work to ban superintelligence around the world.
The Act would also establish a new cabinet-level federal agency to "safeguard the public from the dangers of AI." The agency will monitor frontier AI systems at all stages of the lifecycle for dangerous capabilities, supervise the removal of dangerous capabilities, and supervise the destruction of artificial superintelligence.
The penalties section makes it clear that violators face more than a slap on the wrist. "Entities shall be subject to the corporate death penalty, and persons shall be subject to not more than 20 years in prison," it warns.
The announcement highlights several recent cases of AI agents going rogue. There was the incident in which roughly 1,200 agents escaped to the open internet and exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files through an unauthorized message board. Around 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack. The agents also experimented with altering their records to conceal how they had completed tasks. OpenAI is now facing a Sentate probe over what happened.
Reuters reported that investigators also found unauthorized OpenAI agent communications on more than 10 previously undisclosed websites, including wikis and university link shorteners.
There were also incidents involving Anthropic agents, and fears were exacerbated last week when one of the company's former researchers warned the AI race could end in human extinction.
Sanders previusly warned OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta to pause AI development or face Senate action.
Many Americans are moving to an anti-AI stance, whether because of fears of extinction, the building of more data centers, the automation-driven layoffs, or simply the amount of slop proliferating across the internet.
But pro-AI politicians, including President Trump, say slowing AI development is a national security risk and leaves the US in a weakened position against rivals such as China. Trump recently said data center protesters are "making a mistake." It'll certainly be interesting to see how much support Sander's legislation gains.

articles.title: Canada, Ukraine tap Canadian drone companies in binational deal |
articles.text:
More than $50 million in contracts will be doled out to a group of Canadian companies involved in drone manufacturing and engineering, after the Canadian and Ukrainian governments signed deals to advance access to drones for both countries last week.
The news: On Sept. 10, the Government of Canada announced it had signed four deals with Ukraine to increase access to drones and drone manufacturing for both countries. Among the deals signed is the Defence Drone Initiative Marketplace (DDIM) Supply Arrangement, a national digital procurement platform to acquire drones and counter-drone systems for the Canadian military and coast guard.
From the source: “Canada and Ukraine forged a new partnership which will equip the Canadian Armed Forces with world-leading drone capabilities, create jobs across Canada, and support Ukraine as they fight to achieve a just and lasting peace,” Carney said in a press release last week.
The context: Among the initial contracts awarded to support the development of the DDIM framework are six Canadian companies who collectively are receiving contracts worth up to $50 million. Those companies include Beonyx out of Quebec, which develops and manufactures uncrewed ground vehicles; AVSS out of New Brunswick and Ontario, which manufactures and assembles drone parachute recovery systems; Volatus Aerospace, a Montréal-based company providing integrated uncrewed aerial systems and drone technologies; Ontario’s Twenty20 Insight, which provides counter-drone systems; Objexis AI, an AI-imbued platform for avionics and mission systems; and Saskatchewan’s Draganfly, which builds and engineers drone hardware and software.
RELATED: Sentinel R&D at centre of Russian accusations that Canada is a “warmonger”
Final thought: The deal builds upon previous collaborative drone investments between the two nations. In May, Ukraine’s Airlogix announced a partnership with Canada’s Sentinel R&D to expand collaboration on drone production. It also comes at a moment of heightened economic and geopolitical uncertainty for Canada as it faces an increasingly hostile neighbour to the south. Unlike Ukraine, Canada does not have a large drone arsenal. The deal with Ukraine, alongside broader, accelerating defence spending, positions Canada for both expanded economic opportunity and establishing a drone fleet of its own.

articles.title: He dejado de usar Google Maps en Android Auto por esta función tan buena de Waze
articles.text:
Hacía años que estaba utilizando Google Maps en el móvil y también en el coche. Me gustaba la interfaz y, aunque la opción de alertas en carretera era mejorable, a mí me servía. Hace unas semanas cambié de opinión y en mi coche ahora siempre utilizo Waze. ¿Lo mejor? Por algo que ni siquiera sabía que existía y que encontré de casualidad. Y, si tú sigues utilizando Google Maps en Android Auto, es probable que este detalle también te haga cambiar de opinión.
Que Google Maps no tiene el mejor sistema de alertas y avisos es una realidad. De la mayoría de cosas no te alerta, los radares se muestran en pantalla, pero no hay aviso sonoro y las circunstancias climatológicas no las tiene demasiado en cuenta. Es justo el segmento donde Waze saca pecho, y por este motivo lo instalé en un viaje durante este verano.
La sensación fue buena, la interfaz me gustó y el sistema de alertas en carretera es perfecto, pero no fue por esto por lo que dejé de utilizar Google Maps. A la siguiente semana, ya de vuelta a la rutina, estaba conduciendo por mi ciudad y de repente me saltó un aviso en la pantalla del coche: "Alerta: Semáforo con cámara".
Iba conduciendo por un lugar que conocía perfectamente, por lo que no había fijado ninguna ruta: Waze simplemente estaba corriendo en segundo plano porque días antes lo utilicé para viajar. ¿Cuál fue mi sorpresa? Que el sistema de alertas de este GPS es capaz de avisarte siempre, incluso cuando conoces la ruta y no has fijado ir de punto A a punto B.
La joya oculta de Waze: los avisos de radares y cámaras llegan incluso cuando no estás en ruta
No sé cuánto tiempo lleva esta función activa, pero me pareció bastante buena. Es similar a la app de Radarbot, la cual detecta si tienes algún radar cerca en tu ubicación y te va avisando sobre la marcha. La buena noticia es que Waze lo hace con todo: coches parados en la carretera, radares, cámaras en semáforos, cámaras de cinturón y un largo etcétera.
No es necesario decirle: "Voy de Toledo a Madrid" para que te avise de los radares de esa carretera. Tú simplemente puedes iniciar la conducción, ejecutar Android Auto y, de forma automática, Waze conocerá tu posición para indicarte si cerca de donde pasas hay algo que debas tener en cuenta. Es perfecto para recibir estos avisos en esos trayectos que conoces a la perfección y que no pones en el GPS todos los días.
Conectar el móvil a Android Auto y tener el servicio de alertas funcionando sin tener que hacer nada es lo que me ha convencido, de una vez por todas, para pasarme a Waze y dejar Google Maps como una app para buscar restaurantes y lugares, pero no como mi GPS.

articles.title: Your car is selling your data
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on cars, data privacy, and autonomous vehicles, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Your car is selling your data
The amount of data about you that many cars collect — and sell to third parties — is staggering.
How it started
Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission issued an unprecedented penalty against General Motors: a five-year ban on selling customer data to consumer reporting agencies and third-party data brokers.
For years, GM had been collecting all sorts of data on its customers — such as how often they sped or whether they drove at night — and selling it to brokers to generate risk profiles for insurance companies. More often than not, drivers were unaware of the degree to which their data was being collected. Many had unknowingly consented to it by signing up for an OnStar connected services plan, which activated a feature called Smart Driver that collected their driving data.
GM was then turning around and sharing that data with two data brokers, LexisNexis and Verisk, both of which work with the insurance industry. In a 2024 blockbuster investigative report by The New York Times, some drivers said their insurance rates went up as a result of the data collection. The enrollment process was so confusing that many vehicle owners had no idea their data was being shared. Under the settlement with the FTC, GM has to make it easier for drivers to turn off location tracking, as well as enable them to access and delete their data collected by the automaker.
But GM isn’t the only automaker vacuuming up data on its customers. A team of researchers from the Mozilla Foundation spent months examining the privacy policies of all the major car companies for a report they were working on in 2023. Their conclusion: Every single one had “horrible privacy and security,” said Jen Caltrider, who helped author the study. Not only that, but customers were forced to accept overlapping policies for the car, the connected services, the smartphone app, and the financial services through which they received their loan — all of which included data collection provisions.
“And so it was really overwhelming trying to understand what was going on,” Caltrider said.
There has been plenty of corroborating evidence for this. Consumer Reports published its own investigation last year that concluded “nearly every automaker that sells cars in the U.S. is similarly collecting and sharing so-called ‘driver behavior data’ with other companies and continues to do so.”
Cars are particularly problematic compared to phones because the privacy controls are less intuitive. A smartphone owner can generally find and tweak their privacy settings. With a vehicle, the data collection is spread across multiple systems and policies, making it much harder for consumers to understand what is happening. It feels like a free-for-all because automakers are collecting enormous amounts of information without much public scrutiny.
How it’s going
After GM was penalized as a result of the Times investigation, the issue of data privacy and cars appears to finally be getting some scrutiny. But as is often the case, policymakers may be missing the mark on how to address it.
Last December, a trio of House Republicans introduced the Data Rights for Information and Vehicle Electronics in Real-time, or DRIVER, Act. According to these lawmakers, the bill “reaffirms a basic principle: if you own the vehicle, you should own the data it generates.”
But while the bill would give vehicle owners a bit more control over their data, it would also allow automakers to continue gathering and selling it to third-party data brokers, which makes it a nonstarter for privacy advocates. As Caltrider notes, access and deletion rights are not the same thing as preventing excess collection in the first place. If an automaker can collect enormous amounts of information and the consumer must then go through an arduous process to discover what was collected and request that it be deleted, the burden remains on the individual. Most privacy advocates would rather see a system in which automakers simply do not collect so much information to begin with.
The issue has even risen to the level of MAGA World. Last July, Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, sent a letter to Congress outlining the administration’s policy priorities for the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization bill. Tucked in the letter was a new concept called “the Freedom Car,” which Duffy described as Americans’ right to “drive disconnected and non-automated” vehicles. The proposal would ban the government from requiring that vehicles be equipped with automated driving systems or have the capability to transmit data wirelessly — which, to my knowledge, no one is trying to do.
What happens next
It’s unclear whether the DRIVER Act or the Freedom Car will ever clear the hurdles in Washington to become real policies. What is clear is that there is significant demand for simpler vehicles. People are asking why they can’t just buy a car without all the sensors and data collection. They look at new concepts like the Slate Truck and wonder whether they could also use something more bare-bones.
Sure, consumers may accept useful safety equipment such as backup cameras, but many don’t want their vehicle tracking everything they do — and they definitely don’t want to see ads on their vehicle screens. (BMW, I’m looking at you.) Nor do they want Flock cameras tracking their every movement while they drive down the street.
But automakers have every incentive to keep collecting data because there is money to be made from it. As long as the broader data economy rewards companies for gathering and monetizing information, there’s little reason for automakers to voluntarily abandon the practice.
By the way
- Every automaker has its own privacy page where vehicle owners can submit requests, including opting out of data collection. Of course, they’re all buried under mountains of legalese, so good luck finding it.
- Same goes for all the smartphone apps for connected car services. Changing your privacy settings in those apps is generally a little easier.
Read this
- The New York Times’ investigation into GM’s data collection program is worth a read, if just for the flabbergasted reactions from drivers who couldn’t understand why their insurance rates were going up.
- Edmunds and Consumer Reports both did the work to ask every automaker for their data collection policies. There’s a lot of variety across the industry.
- These Redditors are crowdsourcing a list of new cars (from 2019 onward) that aren’t digitally connected and/or transmitting data to the car company’s servers. Spoiler alert: It’s a pretty short list!

articles.title: Canada needs growth-stage capital, too
articles.text:
When should one look a gift billion in the mouth?
Prime Minister Mark Carney has once again cajoled the international spotlight onto Canada, and the nation’s financial sector responded in kind, committing some $100 billion CAD in new capital before the Canada Investment Summit has even begun. The commitments are extensive enough that BetaKit has compiled a running tracker to keep tabs on them all.
Despite the nation’s capital allocators finally getting the hint that building Canada might require significant homegrown investment, a number of Statler and Waldorfs in Canadian tech have emerged to heckle from the balcony box. I won’t name names, but their main complaint seems to be that little, if any, of these investment commitments will find purchase amongst our early-stage innovators.
Sitting in the cheap seats, I find this assessment both true and mildly infuriating.
Here’s why: venture capital is one of the few sectors where trickle-down economics actually works. The US absolutely dwarfs Canada when it comes to venture investment (some $320 billion USD to $8 billion CAD in 2025), and part of the reason why Valley VCs cut large cheques so quickly is that they know, whatever their stage of investment, a ready amount of follow-on capital from the next stage is available. A few billion in growth-stage capital from Canada’s financial sector won’t eliminate the disparity, but it should make it easier for Canadian early-stage VCs to sling cheques with more confidence.
This won’t fully solve Canada’s early-stage capital gap, nor will it address the fundraising struggles of emerging VCs, or our generational entrepreneur diaspora. But solutions are judged by the problems they try to solve, not those they don’t. Progress is progress!
It’s fun to heckle performers on stage, but also futile. For those interested in solutions, might I suggest putting your money where your mouth is? We’ll add it to our tracker.

Join the Canada Fintech Forum in Montréal on September 14-15, 2026, and connect with the institutions, startups, investors, policymakers, and technology leaders shaping the evolution of financial services. Two days of high-value content, strategic networking, and opportunities.

Inside Carney’s pitchbook

The summit will bring 100 global investors to Toronto to try to attract more than $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years; BetaKit is already tracking the biggest cash commitments.

Making Canada AI literate
AI Minister Evan Solomon was in Edmonton this week to unveil the National AI Literacy Initiative, a cornerstone deliverable of Canada’s broader national AI strategy. BetaKitsat down with Amii CEO Cam Linke to learn more about the $13-million program’s curriculum, which launches on Sept. 21.
From Vancouver with love
Zach Oldham, the 23-year-old co-founder of AI adtech startup Gravity, moved from Vancouver to San Francisco to build his startup. He hopes his business grows big enough to one day return and stimulate the Canadian tech ecosystem.
Waterloo Tech Week returns
The second annual Waterloo Tech Week runs until Sept. 17, with nearly 60 events organized by students, venture capital companies, and local tech organizations across the region. Event co-director Maggie Lu said the event is “putting companies in direct contact with high-signal builders.”

To prepare for an increase to 65 million annual passengers, Toronto Pearson is testing an opt-in facial-verification e-gate program to speed up boarding times and reduce friction for travellers.

The Smart Cities AI Challenge at the ALL IN 2026 conference is bridging the gap between Canadian AI startups and the public sector by having selected innovators pitch their solutions for real-world urban challenges.
What’s next for trust, innovation, and co-creation in the Canadian FinTech ecosystem?
Ahead of the 2026 Canada FinTech Forum, Mastercard is supporting local fintech startups through co-creation by helping them build customer trust, bring their products to market, and scale globally.
Deals and dollars
Who cashed in, or out, this week:
- Ultimarii raised a $13-million Series A round to expand its regulatory intelligence platform across Canada and the United States (Calgary)
- Weston family-backed Wittington Ventures closed $180 million for its third VC fund for climate, commerce, and consumer-focused tech startups (Toronto)

Data point

The share of domestic growth rounds led by Canadian investors in the last decade—and one of the reasons RBC is launching a billion-dollar growth fund.
The refresh
Reject subscriptions, embrace self-hosting
Subscription services have swallowed up much of our digital lives and have been met with a reactionary swell of desire for personal ownership of physical media. As YouTuber Matteo puts it, “I want to own everything I use.” If that resonates with you, this guide walks you through how to set up your own self-hosting system (using Canadian open-source software Tailscale, to boot).
Sold Out. That’s what happened with the Accelerator Centre’s Scale Canadian Tech Connect Mixer, co-presented by Graphite Ventures.
The question is why? We believe much has to do with what’s happening right now with the economy. Canada’s next generation of global companies needs conviction, capital, and community behind them more than ever. Just ask Carol Leaman, co-founder of Axonify. Carol is featured in Graphite’s latest Scale Canadian Founder Series episode, discussing the riskiest bet of her career and the discipline behind one of Canada’s biggest enterprise software exits.

articles.title: 3 nouveaux modèles par jour : la cadence folle de la Chine menace la qualité des batteries
articles.text:
Eldorado de la voiture électrique, la Chine sort en moyenne trois nouveaux modèles chaque jour. Ce rythme ultra soutenu permet de dynamiter le marché intérieur en proposant des produits toujours plus compétitifs pour le plus grand bonheur des consommateurs. Le problème, c’est que certains fournisseurs n’arrivent plus à suivre la cadence. C’est le cas des fabricants de batterie, qui sont au bord de la rupture.
Robin Zeng, président de CATL, explique que la tension n’a jamais été aussi grande sur les accumulateurs. Plus de 600 nouveaux modèles électriques ont été lancés en Chine depuis le début de l’année. Cela représente en moyenne trois lancements par jour, ce qui n’est clairement pas sans conséquences en amont. Avec une demande augmentant de manière exponentielle, les contrôles qualité s’accélèrent tout autant.
Des contrôles qualité bâclés au détriment de la sécurité
Selon le dirigeant, puisque les cycles de validation sont désormais expédiés à toute allure pour satisfaire les commandes, plusieurs lots de batteries ne seraient plus conformes au cahier des charges. Zeng n’a cependant pas précisé quels fournisseurs et marques étaient concernés par la chose. Quoi qu’il en soit, ces annonces tombent dans un contexte ultra concurrentiel où les prix des voitures électriques ont atteint un niveau inédit.
Inédit vers le bas, bien entendu, et cela est tiré par le montant des cellules lithium fer phosphate inférieur à 0,045 € le wattheure. Pour que les fournisseurs de batteries s’assurent une rentabilité minimale, l’accélération de la production est inévitable, au détriment de la qualité, comme souvent. Aujourd’hui, avec un taux de défaut d’une partie par million, un milliard de cellules produites pourrait contenir jusqu’à 1 000 cellules défectueuses.
Déjà des millions d’euros de plaintes et des rappels massifs
Les conséquences pour l’automobiliste sont évidentes : une autonomie plus faible, une recharge plus lente et un comportement thermique plus instable impactant la consommation. Ces problèmes sont déjà devenus réalité en Chine, avec des multiples affaires impliquant des centaines de milliers de véhicules. En décembre 2025, une filiale de Geely a par exemple porté plainte contre le fournisseur chinois Sunwoda.
Suite à des cellules défaillantes fournies entre juin 2021 et décembre 2023, la compagnie a réclamé près de 300 millions d’euros de dommages et intérêts. Plus récemment, ce n’étaient pas moins de 213 000 GAC Aion qui ont été sujettes à d’importantes pertes de puissance de leurs batteries fournies par CALB. Inquiétant, d’autant plus que la Chine produit près de 70 % du volume mondial de batteries.
Un risque direct pour les voitures électriques importées en Europe
Il n’est donc pas impossible que des packs défectueux soient déjà en circulation dans certains véhicules en Europe. Bref, il n’y a qu’une seule solution au problème : prêter une plus grande attention aux batteries produites en affinant les contrôles. Cela signifie donc réduire la cadence de production, chose que beaucoup de fabricants ne seraient certainement pas prêts à faire…

articles.title: iOS 27 im Überblick: Diese Funktionen könnt ihr auch in Deutschland nutzen
articles.text:
Stellt euch vor, ein neues Betriebssystem erscheint, aber die beste Funktion könnt ihr nicht benutzen. So dürfte es Nutzer:innen gehen, die das neue iOS 27 installieren. Herzstück des Updates ist die neue KI-Version von Siri, genannt Siri AI. In Europa wird sie vorerst nicht zum Funktionsumfang auf dem iPhone gehören. Lediglich auf dem Mac lässt sich die Assistenz ausprobieren, wenn die Sprache auf Englisch gestellt ist.
Abseits davon hat Apple nur einige wenige Funktionen und Neuheiten auf der WWDC 2026 vorgestellt. Einige bleiben euren Augen sogar verborgen, ihr sollt aber trotzdem davon profitieren. Denn das Unternehmen verspricht mehr Geschwindigkeit beim Öffnen von Apps und bei der Dateiübertragung, ein höheres Arbeitstempo auf alten iPhones und praktische Kleinigkeiten, die etwa dafür sorgen, dass nicht zugestellte Nachrichten automatisch erneut verschickt werden.
Kosmetische Neuheiten
Mini-Uhr im Sperrbildschirm
Euch stört die große Zeitanzeige im Sperrbildschirm? Dann gibt euch Apple jetzt die Möglichkeit, die Uhr winzig klein anzuzeigen. Dazu haltet ihr im Sperrbildschirm das Wallpaper gedrückt, tippt auf Anpassen und dann auf die Uhr. Rechts neben Schrift & Farbe gibt es ein neues Symbol, das die Uhrzeit und das Datum verkleinert und in einer Zeile zusammenfasst.
Finetuning für Liquid Glass
2025 hatte Apple mit iOS 26 die Designsprache Liquid Glass eingeführt. Der neue Look mit transparenten Schaltflächen kam nicht bei jedem gut an. Mit einem Update hat Apple deswegen schnell nachgeholfen. In den Display-Einstellungen können Nutzer:innen seitdem auswählen, ob die Elemente des Systems transparent erscheinen oder eine gewisse Deckkraft bieten sollen, damit dahinterliegender Text nicht durchschimmert. Mit iOS 27 führt Apple nun einen Schieberegler ein, mit dessen Hilfe ihr stufenlos zwischen den beiden Optionen wechseln und den Grad der Deckkraft nach Belieben anpassen könnt. Ihr findet die Einstellung, wenn ihr unter Bildschirm und Helligkeit den Punkt Liquid Glass auswählt.
Neue Funktionen für Apple Intelligence
Deutlich mehr Vergnügen mit iOS 27 werdet ihr hierzulande haben, wenn ihr ein iPhone 15 Pro (Max) oder ein neueres Modell besitzt. Dann profitiert ihr zumindest ein wenig von einigen neuen Apple-Intelligence-Funktionen.
Fotos neu ausrichten
Ihr habt ein schickes Foto von euch, aber der Winkel passt nicht ganz? Eine neue Funktion in der Fotos-App kann euch helfen, die Person vor der Kamera besser auszurichten. Spatial Reframing nennt sich das Feature. Dazu öffnet ihr ein Foto in der Fotos-App, danach die Bearbeitungsansicht, und tippt dann unten rechts auf Werkzeuge. Hier wählt ihr Neu ausrichten aus und könnt den Winkel bis zu einem gewissen Grad anpassen. Danach geht das Bild in die Cloud und wird neu berechnet.
Fotos erweitern
Ähnlich funktioniert das Feature Foto erweitern. Der Weg ist derselbe wie bei der Neuausrichtung. Klickt auf das Bearbeitungssymbol in der Fotos-App, dann auf Werkzeug, dann auf Erweitern. Nun zoomt ihr einfach so weit aus dem Bild heraus, wie ihr es erweitern wollt. Den Rest übernimmt Apple Intelligence.
Mitteilungen von Safari erhalten
Mit iOS 27 könnt ihr euch von Safari erinnern lassen, wenn etwas auf einer Webseite passiert. Das ist etwa dann praktisch, wenn ihr darauf wartet, dass Tickets endlich in den Verkauf gehen, oder ihr keine Nachricht von eurer Lieblingsseite verpassen wollt. Um eine Benachrichtigung einzurichten, surft ihr zunächst auf die richtige Seite, tippt dann auf die drei Striche neben der Adresszeile und wählt Mitteilung an mich aus. Jetzt beschreibt ihr in natürlicher Sprache, woran Safari euch erinnern soll. Ihr könnt zusätzlich eine Zeit und eine Frequenz auswählen, in der euch der Browser Mitteilungen schicken soll. Abschließend tippt ihr oben rechts auf den Haken. Im Anschluss wird auf der entsprechenden Seite oben ein Banner angezeigt. Hier könnt ihr auf Bearbeiten tippen und dann unten auf Löschen, um die Notification wieder zu entfernen.
Eigene Browser-Erweiterung vibecoden
Nach ähnlichem Muster könnt ihr Safari auch um eigene Addons erweitern. Tippt erneut auf die drei Striche und wählt dann Erweiterung beschreiben aus. Hier könnt ihr aus vorgefertigten Aktionen wählen oder unten bei Etwas anderes beschreiben … in natürlicher Sprache eure Wunscherweiterung eintippen. In unserem Fall soll Safari auf Rezeptseiten den üblichen SEO-Text außen vor lassen und direkt das Rezept in die Zwischenablage kopieren. So können wir es einfach in einer Notiz speichern. Klickt im Anschluss auf Erstellen. Um die Erweiterung zu nutzen, tippt erneut auf die drei Striche und wählt sie dann auf entsprechenden Webseiten aus. Tippt ihr stattdessen auf Erweiterungen verwalten, könnt ihr dem Ganzen auch einen passenden Namen und ein Symbol geben.
Tabs automatisch ordnen
Wer im Web surft und Links Tab für Tab öffnet, kann irgendwann den Überblick im Chaos verlieren. Auch hier soll Safari unterstützen, indem der Browser Tabs automatisch sortiert. Dazu öffnet ihr die Tab-Übersicht, tippt auf die drei Punkte und klickt unter Tabs ordnen nach auf Themen automatisch erstellen.
Kurzbefehle vibecoden
Die Kurzbefehle-App kann sehr praktisch für Shortcuts und Automationen sein – wenn man damit umzugehen weiß. Mit iOS 27 vereinfacht Apple den Umgang damit. Genau wie bei den Safari-Erweiterungen könnt ihr Kurzbefehle jetzt vibecoden. Dazu tippt ihr in der App einfach auf das Plus, um einen neuen Kurzbefehl zu erstellen, und beschreibt dann, was er tun soll. Tippt zum Beispiel “Aktiviere um 22 Uhr den Energiesparmodus” ein, um eben jene Automation zu erstellen.
Eigene KI-Bilder erstellen
Mit Apple Intelligence hat das Unternehmen den sogenannten Image Playground eingeführt. Mit der App lassen sich eigene KI-Bilder erstellen. Seit Bestehen waren die Möglichkeiten aber stark begrenzt. Das ändert sich mit iOS 27. Erstmals gibt Apple euch die Möglichkeit, eigene, realistische Bilder zu erstellen. Dazu tippt ihr in der App auf das Plus und wählt Beliebiger Stil aus. Zusätzlich könnt ihr festlegen, ob ihr ein quadratisches Bild erstellen lassen wollt, ein Hintergrundbild oder ein Bild im Hoch- oder Querformat. Tippt dann euren Prompt ein und anschließend auf den Pfeil. Auf die selbe Art lassen sich auch Fotos aus der Mediathek modifizieren.
Funktionen speziell für Eltern
Mit Apple Intelligence liefert Apple zudem neue Funktionen für Eltern aus. Sie können festlegen, welche Apps für den Nachwuchs zum Start erlaubt sein werden, welche Websites die Kids ansurfen dürfen und wie lange sie Apps und Spiele nutzen dürfen. Neue Filter warnen außerdem in Facetime-Anrufen und Nachrichten, wenn sensible Inhalte gezeigt werden. Die Steuerung der Features soll über ein neu gestaltetes Dashboard einfach gelingen.
Diese Features kommen später
Wie in den vergangenen Jahren werden nicht alle Features sofort zur Verfügung stehen. iOS 27 soll zum Beispiel die Möglichkeit bieten, Passwörter in der gleichnamigen App automatisch zu wechseln, wenn diese zu schwach sind oder kompromittiert wurden. Die Funktion ist allerdings mit einem Sternchen gekennzeichnet. „Kommt mit einem zukünftigen Softwareupdate“, steht darunter.
Mit Verspätung dürfte dann auch Siri AI in der EU eintreffen. Die ursprüngliche Version von Apple Intelligence hatte es schließlich zunächst ebenfalls nicht auf die hiesigen iPhones geschafft. Monate später hatte Apple die KI-Funktionen dann doch nachgeliefert.

articles.title: Pourquoi une invocation de Final Fantasy VII Revelation a nécessité une réunion de crise
articles.text:
Si vous avez joué au Final Fantasy VII original, alors vous savez que l’une des materia les plus prisées et puissantes n’est autre que l’invocation des Chevaliers de la Table Ronde. Pour l’obtenir, il fallait toutefois se mouiller la nuque, et pas qu’un peu. Il fallait se rendre dans une grotte située sur une île accessible uniquement à dos du Chocobo d’Or (capable de traverser les océans profonds).
Pour débloquer un Chocobo d’Or, il fallait soit se lancer dans la capture et l’élevage de Chocobos pour faire des croisements, soit affronter l’Arme Rubis, située dans le désert du Gold Saucer. En bref, soit un processus long et fastidieux, soit un combat difficile.
Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde feront leur retour dans Final Fantasy VII Revelation. Il ne sera a priori pas nécessaire de devenir éleveur de Chocobos. En revanche, il faudra les combattre.
L’invocation iconique de Final Fantasy VII sera difficile à avoir dans Revelation
Sortie
Final Fantasy VII Revelation est attendu pour le 8 avril 2027 sur PS5, Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch 2 et PC.
Réalisateur de Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Naoki Hamaguchi a confirmé que les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde seront bien de la partie. Les développeurs n’auraient pas pu faire autrement au regard du statut culte de cette invocation. Dans une interview accordée à MinnMax et publiée le 10 septembre, il prévient toutefois : « En raison de la puissance de la materia du jeu original, nous en avons fait un ennemi très formidable. » Dans le sens puissant du terme.
Preuve que Square Enix a pris le sujet très au sérieux ? Il y a eu une réunion de crise pour refaire ce boss, jugé décevant dans la première proposition. C’est Teruki Endo, directeur des combats, qui a suggéré l’idée de rendre les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde plus forts. Avec le sourire, Naoki Hamaguchi confie : « On a donc organisé une réunion d’urgence avec l’ensemble des directeurs, comme le directeur artistique et le directeur d’animation. J’ai dû expliquer à tout le monde qu’Endo voulait rendre ce boss plus puissant, et qu’il fallait qu’on reparte à zéro. »
En résumé, nul besoin d’accoupler des Chocobos pendant des heures et des heures pour récupérer l’invocation. Il sera toutefois nécessaire de la terrasser, et ce ne sera pas une sinécure à en juger par les propos de Naoki Hamaguchi. Elle aura en prime droit à son propre scénario. Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde se mériteront aussi dans Final Fantasy VII Revelation. Comme dans le RPG original.

articles.title: Hackers exploit Tencent app flaw to deploy GrayRabbit malware
articles.text:
Threat actors linked to a China-aligned espionage group are exploiting a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-51990) in Tencent’s Sogou Input Method for Windows to deploy the GrayRabbit backdoor.
Researchers at cybersecurity company Gen Digital warn that the security issue is a one-click remote code execution (RCE) flaw.
"We observed this vulnerability actively exploited in the wild by the UNC3569 threat group to deploy the GRAYRABBIT backdoor through a crafted link," Gen Threat Labs says.
Sogou Input Method is a popular Windows application that lets users type Chinese characters using a standard keyboard and also offers a custom link handler and a built-in web browser using an outdated Chromium engine.
Developed by Chinese tech giant Tencent, Sogou Input Method reportedly has hundreds of millions of installations in China.
Gen Threat Labs reports that UNC3569 chains three weaknesses in the product:
- an unvalidated command-line argument injection in the sgbiz: URI
- an unrestricted URL navigation in a CEF-based webview
- an outdated, unsandboxed Chromium browser engine
The attack chain starts with the victim clicking a crafted sgbiz: custom URI, causing Windows to invoke Sogou’s biz_helper.exe protocol handler, which passes attacker-controlled command-line arguments to the legitimate SGMyInput.exe executable without validating them.
The attacker-injected arguments open Sogou’s skincenter component and instruct its embedded Chromium webview to load an attacker-controlled URL. Sogou does not restrict the URL’s scheme or destination.
In the third stage, a malicious page exploits a known vulnerability in Sogou’s outdated Chromium 80 engine. Because the browser runs without a sandbox and with important web-security protections disabled, the exploit achieves code execution and installs the GrayRabbit backdoor.
In 2024, Google researchers described GrayRabbit as a modular malware family and linked it to UNC3569, a China-based threat actor operating across both the cybercrime and cyber contractor-for-hire ecosystems.
The malware sample that Gen Threat Labs analyzed is a more mature 64-bit variant with an expanded command set and RC4-encoded command-and-control (C2) configuration.
Its capabilities include process execution, opening interactive reverse shells, uploading and downloading files, collecting system and user information, and reflectively loading plugins in the host’s memory.
Gen Threat Labs reported their findings to Tencent on April 9, and the software vendor deployed a fix in Sogou Input Method version 16.3.0.3498, released on April 21.
The patch validates the URL arguments accepted through the protocol handler, permits only HTTPS, and restricts navigation to approved domains related to Sogou and Tencent.
However, the researchers warned that the underlying browser remains outdated and still runs without a sandbox, with many web security protections disabled.

articles.title: Ce ventilateur Shark rafraîchit l'air jusqu'à 6 °C et coûte 110 € de moins grâce à cette offre — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pour bien anticiper les prochaines vagues de chaleur et aborder les pics de température en toute sérénité l’été prochain, s’équiper au bon moment est essentiel. C’est là que le Shark FlexBreeze ProMist tire son épingle du jeu. À la fois ventilateur sans fil et brumisateur, il s’utilise aussi bien dans votre salon que sur une terrasse ou dans le jardin. Sa conception nomade vous permet de rafraîchir efficacement n’importe quelle zone, alors qu’il perd 110 euros de son prix.
Le Shark FlexBreeze ProMist, c’est quoi ?
- Sa brumisation qui abaisse la température ressentie jusqu’à 6 °C
- Son autonomie sans fil allant jusqu’à 24 heures à vitesse 1
- Son usage 4-en-1 : intérieur ou extérieur, sur pied ou sur table
Habituellement affiché à 279 euros, le Shark FlexBreeze ProMist tombe à 169 euros sur le site de SharkNinja.
Un ventilateur pensé pour vous suivre partout
La grande force du Shark FlexBreeze ProMist, c’est sa mobilité. Pensé pour s’adapter à votre quotidien, il passe en un clin d’œil du mode sur pied au mode sur table : un simple bouton suffit pour modifier sa configuration. Et grâce à sa batterie sans fil offrant jusqu’à 24 heures d’autonomie (à la vitesse la plus faible et sans brumisation), vous pouvez l’emporter partout avec vous, du salon à la terrasse et même en pique-nique dans un parc.
Côté performances, sa brise peut porter jusqu’à 20 mètres, avec une large oscillation à 180° et 5 vitesses pour s’ajuster précisément à vos envies. En intérieur, son fonctionnement reste très silencieux, ce qui permet de le laisser tourner la nuit sans troubler votre sommeil ou de travailler à côté en toute tranquillité.
En revanche, avec ses 7 kg sur la balance, on le déplace facilement d’une pièce à l’autre, un peu moins à bout de bras sur une longue distance.
La brumisation qui fait la différence
Le vrai argument du ProMist, c’est son réservoir intégré et amovible, qui diffuse une fine brume sans raccordement à un tuyau. D’après la marque, l’effet est immédiat avec une baisse de température ressentie pouvant aller jusqu’à 6 °C, à condition, bien sûr, d’y verser une eau bien fraîche.
Le réservoir offre jusqu’à 60 minutes de brumisation par recharge, avec trois modes au choix, et sa conception résistante à l’eau et aux UV lui permet de rester dehors sous le soleil comme sous une averse. Il faudra simplement penser à remplir le réservoir régulièrement pour profiter de l’effet rafraîchissant.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro et iPhone Duo : après l'officialisation, quelles rumeurs étaient vraies et lesquelles se sont trompées ?
articles.text:
iPhone 18 Pro et iPhone Duo : après l'officialisation, quelles rumeurs étaient vraies et lesquelles se sont trompées ?
Avant chaque présentation d’un nouveau smartphone d’Apple, c’est la foire aux rumeurs pendant des mois. Mais maintenant que les iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max et iPhone Duo sont officiels, est-ce que les informations partagées ici et là avant la keynote de la firme de Cupertino étaient vraies ? On fait le point sur tout ce qui avait été prédit, ce qui s’est avéré vrai, mais aussi les loupés des divulgateurs et autres insiders.
Ah, les rumeurs, un grand classique avant la sortie d'un nouvel iPhone. Et nous ne blâmons pas les autres : on pratique nous-même l'exercice en suivant les divulgâcheurs réputés pour leurs indiscrétions puis les partageons. Mais maintenant que cette nouvelle génération est officielle avec les iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max et iPhone Duo, c'est l'heure du bilan en vérifiant quelles rumeurs avaient tapé juste et celles qui se sont trompées.
Après l'officialisation, l'heure du bilan des rumeurs
Parlons déjà de la première grosse rumeur, celle de l’existence d’un smartphone pliable chez Apple. Il faut dire que la concurrence comme Samsung, Xiaomi ou Huawei propose déjà pareil modèle et Apple faisait figure de retardataire. Finalement, cette rumeur était vraie et l’iPhone Duo fut présenté en grande pompe par la firme de Cupertino.
Par contre, loupé pour le nom chez les insiders qui parlaient d'iPhone Fold ou iPhone Ultra. Nous n'avons en tout cas pas vu le suffixe "Duo"” passer avant qu'il soit dévoilé par Apple.
Les rumeurs disaient que l’iPhone Duo ne serait pas compatible avec l’Apple Pencil et pourtant, c’est bel et bien le cas. Quant à iOS 27, les rumeurs parlaient d’un affichage Parallel View qui s’adapte au format de l’iPhone Duo. Apple l’a finalement officialisé sous le nom de Split View.
L’autre rumeur qui a circulé et s’est avérée exacte, c’est l’absence d’iPhone 18 d’entrée de gamme lors de cette keynote. Selon les rumeurs que l’on vérifiera à nouveau au moment de l’officialisation, c’est au printemps 2027 que débarquera cette version. On parle aussi de l’iPhone 18e et de l’iPhone Air 2 à cette date.
Apple aurait apparemment fait le choix de séparer cette génération. La stratégie serait de d’abord proposer l’iPhone 18 Pro à la rentrée et ensuite la version moins coûteuse pour relancer les ventes quelques mois plus tard. Au niveau des rumeurs sur le design, c’était très proche de la réalité. Les divulgateurs et autres insiders parlaient d’un écran de 6,3 et 6,9 pouces pour les iPhone 18 Pro et iPhone 18 Pro Max, c’était exact.
Pareil pour le châssis en aluminium et une esthétique très proche des iPhone 17 Pro. Les rumeurs évoquaient aussi une Dynamic Island plus petite et c’est le cas. Les informations parlaient bien les coloris bordeaux, glacier, argent et noir qui se sont vérifiées à la présentation.
Des rumeurs fausses, d'autres vraies
Pour la photographie, le bilan est beaucoup plus mitigé. Le capteur principal de 48 mégapixels a bien une ouverture variable avec quatre valeurs entre f/1,48 et f/4. Mais pour le capteur frontal de 24 mégapixels évoqué par les rumeurs, c’est loupé. Apple propose une caméra Center Stage de 18 mégapixels. Loupé aussi pour Camera Control puisque des informations parlaient d’une disparition de certaines fonctionnalités tactiles. Finalement, Apple a tout conservé.
La puce A20 Pro faisait partie des prédictions les plus solides. On parlait déjà d’une gravure en 2 nm par TSMC avant même l’officialisation. Toutefois, les rumeurs évoquaient d’un gain proche de 18 % pour les cœurs CPU en termes de rapidité. Apple annonce plutôt 20 % mais là, peut-être que le chiffre a été un chouïa gonflé pour faire bien plus beau et rond que 18 %.
Et surprise, il y a des nouveautés de cette nouvelle génération que les rumeurs n’ont pas évoquées et qu’Apple a réussi à garder secrètes jusqu'au bout. L’iPhone 18 Pro introduit Apple Reference Image pour créer la référence signée d’une photographie et donc vérifier si elle a été modifiée, notamment par l’IA.
Alors quel bilan après des mois de fuites lorsque l’on compare aux informations officielles autour de l’iPhone 18 Pro et de l’iPhone Duo ? Les rumeurs ont tapé juste la plupart du temps, notamment au niveau du matériel. Mais c’est pour les détails que le bilan est plus mitigé avec des noms faux pour l’iPhone Duo ou encore une surestimation de la capacité du capteur frontal de l’iPhone 18 Pro.

articles.title: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
articles.text:
Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
A new quantum computing method can make advanced operations more than 1,000 times faster, potentially removing a major barrier to reliable quantum machines.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Chalmers University of Technology
- Summary:
- Researchers have found a way to perform certain quantum operations more than 1,000 times faster, cutting thousands of repeated control cycles down to just one. The advance could reduce errors and bring reliable, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality.
- Share:
Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.
Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.
Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone
A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.
Traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.
"The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information
To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.
Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.
"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.
Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster
Working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.
That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.
Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.
"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," says Lei Du.
Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut
The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.
These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.
"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.
Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers
The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.
Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.
"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.
The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.
"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.
More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control
*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.
Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.
One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.
More About the Research
The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.
The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, Lingzhen Guo. Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (6) DOI: 10.1103/tnb8-3m8m

articles.title: Waving the AI bubble red flags | BetaKit
articles.text:
We’ve had a lot of leaders on The BetaKit Podcast talking about AI recently: as a powerful new tool (like Cohere’s Nick Frosst), or a component of Canada’s sovereignty and prosperity (like AI Minister Evan Solomon). We’ve even had author Cory Doctorow on to discuss what happens after the AI bubble bursts.
“They’re building AI that they’re selling as so powerful that it is exceeding its limitations.”
But we’ve never really discussed the bubble itself.
There are good reasons for this. We’re not economists, and the bubble is so big, growing so fast, and so weirdly shaped that it seems hard to grasp onto and contextualize for healthy debate and discussion. But it can no longer be ignored.
So we’re going to dig in. Helping me to identify and wave a curated selection of red flags in the air is BetaKit managing editor Sarah Rieger.
Keeping a conversation about AI topical and timely is tough sledding. This episode was recorded before Nvidia’s Hugging Face acquisition was confirmed, a whole bunch of (additional) OpenAI executives had departed the company, and a whole bunch of (additional) agentic AI cyberattacks were revealed. It was most certainly recorded before Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk released statements calling for a slower pace to AI development (although perhaps we have that covered while discussing the merits and likelihood of a managed deflation of the AI bubble).
Subscribe: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, Overcast, Pocket Casts, RSS
That said, the core questions at the heart of our conversation remain remarkably pertinent. What is the current state of the AI bubble? How is it impacting the public markets? And how are the public markets impacting the AI bubble?
Let’s dig in.
PRESENTED BY
The BetaKit Podcast is presented by CPPO.
How is prepaid being used as a vital system for moving money across the country?
During this year’s CPPO Symposium, co-founder and Executive Director, Jennifer Tramontana, explained how prepaid powers Canadians to move money across the nation every day digitally. From neo-banks and gig worker wage access to youth money management tools, nearly 50 percent of Canadians now utilize digital-first offerings.
To discover how prepaid innovation is fueling Canada’s digital ecosystem, visit CPPO.ca.
